a round never leaves an interval containing all current values

nodes.statement: $\sum_v\deg(v)\,x_{t}(v)$ does not depend on $t$; without isolated nodes, a round never leaves an interval containing all current values.
nodes.label: lem:basic

nodes.name: Proof of Conservation and range
nodes.statement_short: Double counting over ordered adjacent pairs for conservation; averages stay in an interval.
nodes.statement: Double counting over ordered adjacent pairs; an average of values in an interval stays in it.

nodes.name: Walk weights
nodes.statement_short: Values are stochastic walk-weighted averages of the initial values; with an odd closed walk some length joins every pair.
assumptions: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk
conclusions: $x_t(v)=\sum_u W_t(v,u)\,x_0(u)$ with $W_t$ stochastic and $W_t(v,u)>0$ when a walk of length $t$ joins $v$ and $u$
some length $L$ joins every pair
$x_t(v)=\sum_u W_t(v,u)\,x_0(u)$ with $W_t$ stochastic and $W_t(v,u)>0$ when a walk of length $t$ joins $v$ and $u$

assumptions: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk
conclusions: some length $L$ joins every pair

nodes.statement: $x_t(v)=\sum_u W_t(v,u)\,x_0(u)$ with $W_t$ stochastic and $W_t(v,u)>0$ when a walk of length $t$ joins $v$ and $u$. On a connected graph with an odd closed walk, some length $L$ joins every pair.
nodes.label: lem:walks

nodes.name: Proof of Walk weights
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $t$; parity fixed by the odd closed walk, padded with back-and-forth steps.
nodes.statement: Induction on $t$; for $L$, fix the parity with the odd closed walk and pad with back-and-forth steps.

nodes.name: Convergence to the degree-weighted average
assumptions: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk
conclusions: $x_t(v)\to\bar x$ for every $v$
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk, $x_t(v)\to\bar x$ for every $v$.
nodes.label: thm:conv

nodes.name: Proof of Convergence to the degree-weighted average
nodes.statement_short: Doeblin contraction: all entries of $W_L$ are bounded below, so max-min contracts; the limit is $\bar x$ by conservation.
nodes.statement: All entries of $W_L$ are at least some $\delta>0$, so $\max-\min$ contracts by $1-|V|\delta$ every $L$ rounds (Doeblin); the common limit is $\bar x$ by conservation.

nodes.name: Bipartite graphs
nodes.statement_short: On a connected bipartite graph the $\pm1$ proper 2-colouring flips sign each round, so averaging need not converge.
assumptions: On a connected bipartite graph with at least two nodes
conclusions: the values $\pm1$ of a proper 2-colouring change sign at every round, so they converge nowhere
nodes.statement: On a connected bipartite graph with at least two nodes, the values $\pm1$ of a proper 2-colouring change sign at every round, so they converge nowhere.
nodes.label: thm:bip

nodes.name: Proof of Bipartite graphs
nodes.statement_short: Direct: every neighbour has the opposite colour, so averages flip sign.
nodes.statement: All neighbours of a node have the other colour.

nodes.name: Correction to Lovász's definition of $\lambda$
nodes.statement_short: Lovász's $\lambda$ should be the max, not min, of $|\lambda_2|,|\lambda_n|$, and the survey's $\sqrt{d(v)/d(v)}$ should be $\sqrt{d(v)/d(u)}$.
nodes.statement: Two printed details need a minor correction: Lovász's text defines $\lambda$ as $\min\{|\lambda_2|,|\lambda_n|\}$, a slip for $\max$ (with $\min$ the bound would fail, e.g.\ on a connected bipartite graph), and Theorem~33 of the survey prints $\sqrt{d(v)/d(v)}$ for $\sqrt{d(v)/d(u)}$; the corrected form is formalized (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/averaging/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#rate-bound-and-sequential-averaging-rate-sequential-avg-1}{details}).

nodes.name: Random walk and its spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Transition matrix $P=D^{-1}A$, its symmetrization $N$, the spectral gap parameter $\lambda$ and stationary distribution $\pi$.
nodes.statement: $P=D^{-1}A$ is the transition matrix of the random walk, $N=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$ its symmetric version with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$, $\lambda=\max\{|\lambda_2|,|\lambda_n|\}$ ($0$ if $n<2$), and $\pi(v)=\deg(v)/2m$ with $m$ the number of edges.
nodes.label: def:walk

nodes.name: Matrix form of the dynamics
nodes.statement_short: The averaging dynamics is $x_t=P^tx_0$, and with positive degrees $P$ and $N$ are similar, so $\lambda$ comes from the spectrum of $P$.
conclusions: $P^t(u,v)=W_t(u,v)$ is the probability that the walk from $u$ is at $v$ after $t$ steps, and $x_t=P^tx_0$
$P$ and $N$ have the same characteristic polynomial, so $\lambda$ is computed from the spectrum of $P$
$P^t(u,v)=W_t(u,v)$ is the probability that the walk from $u$ is at $v$ after $t$ steps, and $x_t=P^tx_0$
$P$ and $N$ have the same characteristic polynomial, so $\lambda$ is computed from the spectrum of $P$

nodes.statement: $P^t(u,v)=W_t(u,v)$ is the probability that the walk from $u$ is at $v$ after $t$ steps, and $x_t=P^tx_0$. If every degree is positive, $P$ and $N$ have the same characteristic polynomial, so $\lambda$ is computed from the spectrum of $P$.
nodes.label: lem:walk-bridges

nodes.name: Proof of Matrix form of the dynamics
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $t$, and similarity $P=SNS^{-1}$ with $S=D^{-1/2}$.
nodes.statement: Induction on $t$; $P=SNS^{-1}$ with $S=D^{-1/2}$.

nodes.name: Lovász's bound (Survey Theorem 33)
nodes.statement_short: Walk probabilities converge to stationarity at rate $\lambda^t$, with a $\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}$ factor.
conclusions: $|P^t(u,v)-\pi(v)|\le\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,\lambda^t$ for all nodes $u,v$ and all $t$
nodes.statement: If every degree is positive, $|P^t(u,v)-\pi(v)|\le\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,\lambda^t$ for all nodes $u,v$ and all $t$.
nodes.label: thm:lovasz

nodes.name: Proof of Lovász's bound (Survey Theorem 33)
nodes.statement_short: Spectral: rewrite $P^t$ via the symmetric $N$, project off the top eigenvector $\sqrt\pi$, and bound by Cauchy-Schwarz using contraction by $\lambda$.
nodes.statement: $P^t(u,v)=\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,N^t(u,v)$ and $\pi(v)=\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,s(u)s(v)$ with $s=\sqrt\pi$ a unit eigenvector of $N$ for the eigenvalue $1$. At most one eigenvalue of $N$ exceeds $\lambda$ in absolute value, and then it is $1$ with eigenvector $s$; so $N$ contracts $s^\perp$ by $\lambda$, and $N^t(u,v)-s(u)s(v)=\langle Qe_u,N^tQe_v\rangle$ with $Q=I-ss^\top$ is at most $\lambda^t$ by Cauchy--Schwarz.

nodes.name: Non-bipartite graphs
assumptions: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk
conclusions: $\lambda<1$
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk, $\lambda<1$.
nodes.label: lem:lambda-lt-one

nodes.name: Proof of Non-bipartite graphs
nodes.statement_short: An eigenvalue of modulus 1 gives a non-converging or non-constant solution of the dynamics, contradicting convergence.
nodes.statement: An eigenvalue $\mu$ of $N$ with $|\mu|=1$ gives a vector $y$ with $x_t=\mu^ty$ for the dynamics started at $y$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:conv} $\mu=-1$ is impossible and $\mu=1$ forces $y$ constant, so $1$ is a simple eigenvalue and all others have absolute value below $1$.

nodes.name: Rate of the averaging dynamics
nodes.statement_short: Averaging values approach the $\pi$-weighted average at rate $\lambda^t$.
conclusions: $|x_t(u)-\sum_v\pi(v)x_0(v)|\le\lambda^t\sum_v\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,|x_0(v)|$
nodes.statement: If every degree is positive, $|x_t(u)-\sum_v\pi(v)x_0(v)|\le\lambda^t\sum_v\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,|x_0(v)|$.
nodes.label: cor:avg-rate

nodes.name: Proof of Rate of the averaging dynamics
nodes.statement_short: Write the error as $\sum_v(P^t(u,v)-\pi(v))x_0(v)$ and apply Lovász's bound.
nodes.statement: $x_t(u)-\sum_v\pi(v)x_0(v)=\sum_v(P^t(u,v)-\pi(v))x_0(v)$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:lovasz}.

nodes.name: Edge step
nodes.statement_short: The gossip step on edge $(i,j)$ is the matrix $W_{ij}$ averaging $x_i,x_j$; $\bar W_P$ and $\bar W=I-L/2m$ are the expected steps.
nodes.statement: A step on the edge $(i,j)$ multiplies the state by $W_{ij}=I-\frac12(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^\top$; a run applies the steps of a list of oriented edges in order. For a stochastic matrix $P$ (given as a kernel), $\bar W_P=I-\bar D/2n+(P+P^\top)/2n$ with $\bar D_{ii}=\sum_j(P_{ij}+P_{ji})$, and $\bar W=I-L/2m$ with $L$ the Laplacian.
nodes.label: def:edge-matrix

nodes.name: Properties of an edge step
nodes.statement_short: $W_{ij}$ averages two coordinates, is doubly stochastic and a symmetric projection.
conclusions: $W_{ij}x$ replaces $x_i$ and $x_j$ by their average and keeps the other values
$W_{ij}$ is doubly stochastic and a symmetric projection, $W_{ij}^\top W_{ij}=W_{ij}$
nodes.statement: $W_{ij}x$ replaces $x_i$ and $x_j$ by their average and keeps the other values; $W_{ij}$ is doubly stochastic and a symmetric projection, $W_{ij}^\top W_{ij}=W_{ij}$.
nodes.label: lem:edge-matrix

nodes.name: Proof of Properties of an edge step
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation using $(e_i-e_j)^\top(e_i-e_j)=2$.
nodes.statement: Direct computation; $(e_i-e_j)^\top(e_i-e_j)=2$ for $i\ne j$.

nodes.name: Expected step (Survey equations (4) and (5))
nodes.origin_citation: Boyd, Ghosh, Prabhakar, Shah 2006; Becchetti, Clementi, Natale 2020
nodes.statement_short: The expected gossip matrix is $\bar W_P$ for node-driven contacts and $\bar W$ for uniform edges; on regular graphs both equal $(1-1/n)I+P/n$.
assumptions: If a uniformly random node $i$ contacts $j$ with probability $P_{ij}$
if a uniformly random oriented edge is selected
conclusions: $\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W_P$
$\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W$
both equal $(1-1/n)I+P/n$

assumptions: If a uniformly random node $i$ contacts $j$ with probability $P_{ij}$
conclusions: $\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W_P$

assumptions: if a uniformly random oriented edge is selected
conclusions: $\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W$
both equal $(1-1/n)I+P/n$

nodes.statement: If a uniformly random node $i$ contacts $j$ with probability $P_{ij}$, then $\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W_P$; if a uniformly random oriented edge is selected, then $\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W$. On a $d$-regular graph with $d>0$ and $P=D^{-1}A$ both equal $(1-1/n)I+P/n$.
nodes.label: thm:mean-step

nodes.name: Proof of Expected step (Survey equations (4) and (5))
nodes.statement_short: Entrywise expansion of $W_{ij}$ and counting darts out of each node.
nodes.statement: Entrywise expansion of $W_{ij}(a,b)=\delta_{ab}-\frac12(\delta_{ia}-\delta_{ja})(\delta_{ib}-\delta_{jb})$; there are $\deg(a)$ darts out of $a$ and $2m=nd$ darts in all.

nodes.name: First and second moments
nodes.statement_short: For uniform random edges, $\mathbb E[W^\top W]=\bar W$, and the expected state after $t$ steps is $\bar W^tx_0$.
assumptions: For a uniformly random oriented edge
after $t$ independent uniformly random oriented edges
conclusions: $\mathbb E[W^\top W]=\bar W$ and $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$
$\mathbb E[x_t]=\bar W^tx_0$

assumptions: For a uniformly random oriented edge
conclusions: $\mathbb E[W^\top W]=\bar W$ and $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$

assumptions: after $t$ independent uniformly random oriented edges
conclusions: $\mathbb E[x_t]=\bar W^tx_0$

nodes.statement: For a uniformly random oriented edge, $\mathbb E[W^\top W]=\bar W$ and $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$; after $t$ independent uniformly random oriented edges, $\mathbb E[x_t]=\bar W^tx_0$.
nodes.label: thm:moments

nodes.name: Proof of First and second moments
nodes.statement_short: Projection identity $W^\top W=W$; first moment by induction on $t$ and linearity of expectation.
nodes.statement: $W^\top W=W$; for the first moment, induction on $t$ and linearity of expectation.

nodes.name: Clustered regular graph
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Trevisan, SODA 2017
nodes.statement_short: Two-cluster $d$-regular graph with $b$ cross neighbours, cluster indicator $\chi$, third eigenvalue bound $\lambda$, blue/strong-reconstruction colouring and time $T(n,\delta)$.
nodes.statement: $G$ is $d$-regular on two clusters $V_1,V_2$ of $n$ nodes, each node having $b$ neighbours in the other cluster; $\chi=\mathbb 1_{V_1}-\mathbb 1_{V_2}$, $P=A/d$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots$, $\lambda=\max_{i\ge3}|\lambda_i|$. Node $v$ is blue at round $t$ if $x_t(v)\ge x_{t-1}(v)$; a coloring is a strong reconstruction if no color appears in both clusters. $T(n,\delta)=\lceil\log(4n^3)/\log(1+\delta)\rceil+1$.
nodes.label: def:clustered

nodes.name: Lemma C.1
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Trevisan, SODA 2017
nodes.statement_short: Averaging from signs stays within $\lambda^t\sqrt{2n}$ of its projection onto $\mathbb 1$ and $\chi$.
conclusions: $|x_t(v)-\alpha_1-\alpha_2(1-2b/d)^t\chi(v)|\le\lambda^t\sqrt{2n}$ with $\alpha_1=\langle x,\mathbb 1\rangle/2n$, $\alpha_2=\langle x,\chi\rangle/2n$
nodes.statement: If $\lambda<1-2b/d$ and $x\in\{\pm1\}^{2n}$, then $|x_t(v)-\alpha_1-\alpha_2(1-2b/d)^t\chi(v)|\le\lambda^t\sqrt{2n}$ with $\alpha_1=\langle x,\mathbb 1\rangle/2n$, $\alpha_2=\langle x,\chi\rangle/2n$.
nodes.label: lem:c1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma C.1
nodes.statement_short: Spectral decomposition: $\mathbb 1$ and $\chi$ span the top eigenspace (Bessel equality), and $P$ contracts the complement by $\lambda$.
nodes.statement: $\mathbb 1$ and $\chi$ are eigenvectors with eigenvalues $1$ and $1-2b/d$, both above $\lambda$; at most two eigenvalues exceed $\lambda$ in absolute value, so by equality in Bessel's inequality their eigenvectors lie in $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbb 1,\chi\}$, and $P$ contracts the orthogonal complement of this plane by $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Deterministic core
nodes.statement_short: After $T(n,\delta)$ rounds, the sign of each node's last change reveals its cluster, given a nonzero initial correlation with $\chi$.
assumptions: On a connected clustered graph with $1-2b/d>(1+\delta)\lambda$
conclusions: $\operatorname{sgn}(x_{t-1}(u)-x_t(u))=\operatorname{sgn}(\langle x,\chi\rangle\chi(u))$
nodes.statement: On a connected clustered graph with $1-2b/d>(1+\delta)\lambda$, if $x\in\{\pm1\}^{2n}$ and $\langle x,\chi\rangle\ne0$, then for $t\ge T(n,\delta)=O(\log n/\delta)$, $\operatorname{sgn}(x_{t-1}(u)-x_t(u))=\operatorname{sgn}(\langle x,\chi\rangle\chi(u))$.
nodes.label: thm:core

nodes.name: Proof of Deterministic core
nodes.statement_short: Parity, connectivity and the choice of $t$ make the main term of Lemma C.1 dominate the error.
nodes.statement: $|\langle x,\chi\rangle|\ge2$ by parity, $b\ge1$ by connectivity, $d<2n$, and $(1+\delta)^{t-1}\ge4n^3$, so the main term of Lemma~\ref{lem:c1} dominates the errors.

nodes.name: Lemma B.1, exact form
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Trevisan, SODA 2017
conclusions: $P(\langle x,\chi\rangle=0)=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n\le1/\sqrt{\pi n}$
nodes.statement: For uniform $x\in\{\pm1\}^{2n}$, $P(\langle x,\chi\rangle=0)=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n\le1/\sqrt{\pi n}$.
nodes.label: lem:b1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.1, exact form
nodes.statement_short: Bijection between zeros and $n$-subsets, then Wallis' product bound on the central binomial.
nodes.statement: $x\mapsto\{v: x(v)=\chi(v)\}$ maps the zeros bijectively to the $n$-subsets; Wallis' product.

nodes.name: Strong reconstruction (Theorem 3.2)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Trevisan, SODA 2017
conclusions: With probability at least $1-1/\sqrt{\pi n}$, the coloring is a strong reconstruction at every round $t\ge T(n,\delta)$
nodes.statement: With probability at least $1-1/\sqrt{\pi n}$, the coloring is a strong reconstruction at every round $t\ge T(n,\delta)$.
nodes.label: thm:strong

nodes.name: Proof of Strong reconstruction (Theorem 3.2)
nodes.statement_short: Combine the deterministic core with Lemma B.1.
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:core} and Lemma~\ref{lem:b1}.

nodes.name: Correction to the proof of Theorem 4.1 (opportunistic averaging)
nodes.statement_short: The original proof of Theorem 4.1 wrongly bounds $\mathbb E\|z^{(0)}\|^2$ by $1/n$ (it is $n-2$); the conclusion holds with separate bookkeeping.
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem~4.1 needs a minor correction: its last step uses $\mathbb E\|z^{(0)}\|^2\le 1/n$, while for uniform signs $\mathbb E\|z^{(0)}\|^2=n-2$. The conclusion still holds, and the formal proof uses its own bookkeeping (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/averaging/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#averaging-whenever-you-meet-opportunistic-avg-3}{details}).

nodes.name: Opportunistic averaging (Algorithm 1)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Manurangsi, Natale, Pasquale, Raghavendra, Trevisan, ESA 2018
nodes.statement_short: Each round a random edge is activated; first-time nodes draw a random sign; endpoints average their values.
nodes.statement: One uniformly random edge is activated per round; a node activated for the first time draws a uniform sign, and both endpoints take the average of their two values. The rounds are i.i.d. uniform darts of $G$.
nodes.label: def:opp

nodes.name: Deferred decisions
nodes.statement_short: The opportunistic protocol equals the averaging process started from the coin values, with conserved sum.
conclusions: A uniform dart is a uniform edge
a node holds a value exactly when it has been activated, and the protocol's values are those of the averaging process started from the coins $\sigma$
the sum of the values is conserved
nodes.statement: A uniform dart is a uniform edge; a node holds a value exactly when it has been activated, and the protocol's values are those of the averaging process started from the coins $\sigma$; the sum of the values is conserved.
nodes.label: lem:opp-model

nodes.name: Proof of Deferred decisions
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the list of rounds; each edge carries two darts.
nodes.statement: Induction on the list of rounds; every edge carries two darts.

nodes.name: Expected step (equations (1), (2), (15))
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Manurangsi, Natale, Pasquale, Raghavendra, Trevisan, ESA 2018
nodes.statement_short: The step matrix is a symmetric projection with mean $\bar W=I-L/2m$, giving the expected state and the second moment.
conclusions: $W_t$ is a symmetric projection
$\mathbb E[W]=\bar W=I-L/2m$ is symmetric and doubly stochastic
$\mathbb E[x^{(t)}]=\bar W^tx^{(0)}$ and $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$
nodes.statement: $W_t$ is a symmetric projection, $\mathbb E[W]=\bar W=I-L/2m$ is symmetric and doubly stochastic, $\mathbb E[x^{(t)}]=\bar W^tx^{(0)}$ and $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$.
nodes.label: thm:opp-first

nodes.name: Proof of Expected step (equations (1), (2), (15))
nodes.statement_short: Entrywise computation over darts, then induction on $t$.
nodes.statement: Entrywise computation over the darts; induction on $t$.

nodes.name: Clustered regular graphs (Definition 2.2)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Manurangsi, Natale, Pasquale, Raghavendra, Trevisan, ESA 2018
nodes.statement_short: $d$-regular graph with two equal communities and $b$ cross neighbours; state split along $\mathbb 1$, $\chi$ and the complement; $\lambda_2=2b/d$, $\lambda_3$ a Rayleigh bound.
nodes.statement: $G$ is $d$-regular with communities $V_1$ and $V_2=V_1^c$ of size $n/2$, each node having $b$ neighbours in the other community, $0<b$, $2b<d<n$. The state splits as $x=x_\parallel+y+z$ along $\mathbb 1$, $\chi=\mathbb 1_{V_1}-\mathbb 1_{V_2}$ and their orthogonal complement; $\lambda_2=2b/d$, and $\lambda_3$ enters as a lower bound on the Rayleigh quotient of $L/d$ on the complement.
nodes.label: def:opp-clustered

nodes.name: Theorem 3.1 on clustered regular graphs
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Manurangsi, Natale, Pasquale, Raghavendra, Trevisan, ESA 2018
nodes.statement_short: $\chi$ is an eigenvector of $\bar W$, so the expected state decomposes and the monotonicity/sign criteria hold.
conclusions: $\bar W\chi=(1-\lambda_2/n)\chi$
the expected state decomposes exactly as in Lemma B.1
the monotonicity and sign criteria of Lemmas B.3 and B.4 hold at every node
nodes.statement: $\bar W\chi=(1-\lambda_2/n)\chi$, the expected state decomposes exactly as in Lemma B.1, and the monotonicity and sign criteria of Lemmas B.3 and B.4 hold at every node.
nodes.label: thm:opp-31

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1 on clustered regular graphs
nodes.statement_short: $\bar W$ contracts the complement of $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbb 1,\chi\}$ by $1-\lambda_3/n$.
nodes.statement: $\bar W$ contracts the complement of $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbb 1,\chi\}$ by $1-\lambda_3/n$.

nodes.name: One round (Lemmas C.2 and C.3)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Manurangsi, Natale, Pasquale, Raghavendra, Trevisan, ESA 2018
nodes.statement_short: One-round recursions for the expected squared norm of $z$ and the expected deviation of $\beta$.
conclusions: $\mathbb E\|z'\|^2\le(1-\lambda_3/n)\|z\|^2+\lambda_2\beta^2$
$\mathbb E\,n(\beta'-\gamma)^2\le(1-\lambda_2/n)\,n(\beta-\gamma)^2+\lambda_2\gamma^2 +(4\lambda_2/n^2)(n\beta^2+\|z\|^2)$
nodes.statement: With $\beta=\langle x,\chi\rangle/n$: $\mathbb E\|z'\|^2\le(1-\lambda_3/n)\|z\|^2+\lambda_2\beta^2$ and, for every $\gamma$, $\mathbb E\,n(\beta'-\gamma)^2\le(1-\lambda_2/n)\,n(\beta-\gamma)^2+\lambda_2\gamma^2 +(4\lambda_2/n^2)(n\beta^2+\|z\|^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:opp-onestep

nodes.name: Proof of One round (Lemmas C.2 and C.3)
nodes.statement_short: Use $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$ and Jensen; the variance of $\beta'$ comes from cut darts.
nodes.statement: $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$ and Jensen for $\beta'$; the variance of $\beta'$ comes from the $nb$ darts across the cut.

nodes.name: Second moment analysis (Lemma C.4 and Theorem 4.1)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Manurangsi, Natale, Pasquale, Raghavendra, Trevisan, ESA 2018
nodes.statement_short: In the right time window the state stays close in mean square to its initial $\chi$-component.
conclusions: $\mathbb E\|y^{(t)}+z^{(t)}-y^{(0)}\|^2\le3\lambda_2t/n$
nodes.statement: If $100\lambda_2\log n\le\lambda_3$ and $3(n/\lambda_3)\log n\le t\le n/(4\lambda_2)$, then $\mathbb E\|y^{(t)}+z^{(t)}-y^{(0)}\|^2\le3\lambda_2t/n$.
nodes.label: thm:opp-41

nodes.name: Proof of Second moment analysis (Lemma C.4 and Theorem 4.1)
nodes.statement_short: Unroll the two one-round recursions and average over the initial signs.
nodes.statement: Unroll the two recursions from any state; average over the signs ($\mathbb E\|y^{(0)}\|^2=1$, $\|z^{(0)}\|^2\le n$).

nodes.name: Non-ephemeral good nodes (Lemma 4.2)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Manurangsi, Natale, Pasquale, Raghavendra, Trevisan, ESA 2018
nodes.statement_short: Under a spectral gap condition, w.p. $1-\varepsilon$ most nodes stay $\varepsilon$-good throughout the phase.
conclusions: with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ at least $(1-3\varepsilon)n$ nodes are $\varepsilon$-good at every round of the phase $6(n/\lambda_3)\log n\le t\le12(n/\lambda_3)\log n$
nodes.statement: If $\lambda_2/\lambda_3\le\lambda_3\varepsilon^4/(c\log^2n)$, then with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ at least $(1-3\varepsilon)n$ nodes are $\varepsilon$-good at every round of the phase $6(n/\lambda_3)\log n\le t\le12(n/\lambda_3)\log n$.
nodes.label: thm:opp-42

nodes.name: Proof of Non-ephemeral good nodes (Lemma 4.2)
nodes.statement_short: Good nodes stay good; bad rounds counted in expectation via restarted second-moment bounds; anti-concentration handles small components.
nodes.statement: Good nodes averaged only with good nodes of their community stay good; the bad rounds of the phase are counted in expectation from the second-moment bounds restarted at the start of the phase, and small initial cut components are handled by anti-concentration of $\langle\sigma,\chi\rangle$.

nodes.name: Sign recovery and weak reconstruction
nodes.statement_short: Most nodes keep their community's sign during the phase, giving a $6\varepsilon$-weak reconstruction with probability about $1/2$.
conclusions: with probability at least $1-4\varepsilon$ at least $(1-4\varepsilon)n$ nodes have the sign of their community's initial average throughout the phase
with probability at least $1/2-6\varepsilon$ the signs of the values are a $6\varepsilon$-weak reconstruction at every round of the phase
nodes.statement: Under the hypothesis of Lemma 4.2, with probability at least $1-4\varepsilon$ at least $(1-4\varepsilon)n$ nodes have the sign of their community's initial average throughout the phase, and with probability at least $1/2-6\varepsilon$ the signs of the values are a $6\varepsilon$-weak reconstruction at every round of the phase.
nodes.label: thm:opp-main

nodes.name: Proof of Sign recovery and weak reconstruction
nodes.statement_short: Good nodes have the right sign unless one community sum is tiny relative to the other; bound those and the sign-disagreement probability.
nodes.statement: A good node has the sign of $2S_h/n$ unless $|S_1|\le\varepsilon|S_2|$ or $|S_2|\le\varepsilon|S_1|$ (each of probability at most $\varepsilon+1/\sqrt{n/2+1}$); $S_1S_2<0$ with probability at least $1/2-1/\sqrt{n/2+1}$.

nodes.name: Reactions, networks, counts
nodes.statement_short: Bimolecular reactions $A+B\to C+D$, networks of them, count vectors of $n$ molecules, and firing a reaction.
nodes.statement:
A reaction $A + B 	o C + D$ consumes the unordered pair $\{A, B\}$ of species and produces the unordered pair $\{C, D\}$; a network is a nonempty finite set of reactions whose products differ from their reactants. A count vector of $n$ molecules gives the number $x_a$ of molecules of each species $a$, with $\sum_a x_a = n$; firing an applicable reaction $r$ replaces $x_a$ by $x_a - 
u_a + 
u'_a$, with $
u$, $
u'$ the reactant and product multiplicities.
nodes.label: def:crn

nodes.name: Mass-action propensity
nodes.statement: With rate constant $k$, the propensity of $r$ at $x$ is $a_r(x) = k \prod_a \binom{x_a}{\nu_a}$ (Gillespie's combinatorial form), and $a_0(x) = \sum_r a_r(x)$.
nodes.label: def:propensity

nodes.name: Propensities
conclusions: the propensity is $k\, x_A x_B$
it is $k \binom{x_A}{2}$
the propensity is $k\, x_A x_B$
it is $k \binom{x_A}{2}$

nodes.statement: For $A + B \to \cdots$ with $A \ne B$ the propensity is $k\, x_A x_B$; for $A + A \to \cdots$ it is $k \binom{x_A}{2}$.
nodes.label: lem:propensity

nodes.name: Proof of Propensities
nodes.statement_short: Only reactant species have nonzero multiplicity in the product formula.
nodes.statement: Only the reactant species have nonzero multiplicity in the product.

nodes.name: Jump chain
nodes.statement: From $x$ with $a_0(x) > 0$ the jump chain fires $r$ with probability $a_r(x)/a_0(x)$; from a terminal state ($a_0(x) = 0$) it stays put.
nodes.label: def:jump

nodes.name: The jump chain jumps
conclusions: the jump chain from $x$ gives weight $0$ to $x$
nodes.statement: If $a_0(x) \ne 0$, the jump chain from $x$ gives weight $0$ to $x$.
nodes.label: lem:jump-self

nodes.name: Proof of The jump chain jumps
nodes.statement_short: A reaction with nonzero propensity is applicable and changes the counts.
nodes.statement: A reaction with nonzero propensity is applicable, and firing an applicable reaction whose products differ from its reactants changes the counts.

nodes.name: The population protocol of a network
nodes.statement_short: Agents hold species; an interaction draws a random ordered pair and a random reaction, firing it if the pair matches its reactants.
nodes.statement: Each of $n \ge 2$ agents holds a species. One interaction draws a uniformly random ordered pair $(u, v)$ of distinct agents and, independently, a uniformly random reaction $r$ of the network; if the species of $u$ and $v$ are the reactants of $r$ the pair reacts and $r$ fires, otherwise nothing changes. The protocol is observed on count vectors; conditioning on the pair reacting gives a kernel on count vectors.
nodes.label: def:pp

nodes.name: Key identity
nodes.statement_short: The probability the random pair has given species, equivalently the reactants of $r$, is proportional to the propensity.
conclusions: The drawn pair has species $\{A, B\}$ with probability $x_A x_B / \binom{n}{2}$ if $A \ne B$, and $\binom{x_A}{2} / \binom{n}{2}$ if $A = B$
it has the reactants of $r$ with probability $a_r(x) / (k \binom{n}{2})$
nodes.statement: The drawn pair has species $\{A, B\}$ with probability $x_A x_B / \binom{n}{2}$ if $A \ne B$, and $\binom{x_A}{2} / \binom{n}{2}$ if $A = B$. Equivalently, it has the reactants of $r$ with probability $a_r(x) / (k \binom{n}{2})$.
nodes.label: lem:pair

nodes.name: Proof of Key identity
nodes.statement_short: Count ordered pairs of distinct agents with the given species.
nodes.statement: There are $n(n-1)$ ordered pairs of distinct agents, $2 x_A x_B$ of them with species $\{A, B\}$ for $A \ne B$, and $x_A(x_A - 1)$ with species $\{A, A\}$.

nodes.name: One interaction
nodes.statement_short: One interaction reacts with probability proportional to $a_0(x)$ and then acts as a mass-action jump.
conclusions: The drawn pair reacts with probability $p = a_0(x) / (k\, |N| \binom{n}{2})$
one interaction is a jump of the mass-action chain with probability $p$ and a no-op otherwise
nodes.statement: The drawn pair reacts with probability $p = a_0(x) / (k\, |N| \binom{n}{2})$, and one interaction is a jump of the mass-action chain with probability $p$ and a no-op otherwise.
nodes.label: thm:step

nodes.name: Proof of One interaction
nodes.statement_short: Average over the uniform reaction and apply the key identity to each reaction.
nodes.statement: Average over the uniform reaction and apply the key identity to each reaction.

nodes.name: CRNs are population protocols
nodes.statement_short: Conditioned on reacting, the population protocol equals the mass-action jump chain as kernels on count vectors.
conclusions: the population protocol conditioned on the drawn pair reacting is the jump chain of mass-action kinetics, from every configuration and hence as kernels on count vectors
nodes.statement: For every rate constant $k > 0$ and $n \ge 2$, the population protocol conditioned on the drawn pair reacting is the jump chain of mass-action kinetics, from every configuration and hence as kernels on count vectors.
nodes.label: thm:crn1

nodes.name: Proof of CRNs are population protocols
nodes.statement_short: By the key identity a reacting interaction fires $r$ with probability proportional to $a_r(x)$; terminal configurations stay put on both sides.
nodes.statement: Conditioned on reacting, the interaction fires $r$ with probability proportional to $a_r(x)$ by the key identity, which is the jump chain; from a configuration where no pair can react both sides stay put.

nodes.name: The approximate-majority network
nodes.statement: Species $X$, $Y$ (the two opinions) and $B$ (blank), and the reactions $X + Y \to X + B$, $X + Y \to Y + B$, $B + X \to X + X$, $B + Y \to Y + Y$ (Angluin, Aspnes and Eisenstat).
nodes.label: def:am

nodes.name: Approximate majority as a population protocol
nodes.statement_short: Explicit jump-chain probabilities for the approximate-majority network and its identification with the conditioned population protocol.
conclusions: the jump chain fires each $X + Y$ reaction with probability $x_X x_Y / D$, $B + X \to X + X$ with probability $x_B x_X / D$ and $B + Y \to Y + Y$ with probability $x_B x_Y / D$
a drawn pair reacts with probability $D / (4 \binom{n}{2})$
the jump chain is the population protocol conditioned on reacting
nodes.statement: With $D = 2 x_X x_Y + x_B (x_X + x_Y) > 0$, the jump chain fires each $X + Y$ reaction with probability $x_X x_Y / D$, $B + X \to X + X$ with probability $x_B x_X / D$ and $B + Y \to Y + Y$ with probability $x_B x_Y / D$; a drawn pair reacts with probability $D / (4 \binom{n}{2})$; and the jump chain is the population protocol conditioned on reacting.
nodes.label: thm:am

nodes.name: Proof of Approximate majority as a population protocol
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate the general results with $a_0(x)=kD$.
nodes.statement: Instances of the general results, with $a_0(x) = k D$.

nodes.name: Correction to Lemma 5 of Angluin et al. for a single agent
nodes.statement_short: With one agent no encounter happens, so the original protocols fail; here agents start with their single-agent output, correct for all $n\ge1$.
nodes.statement: Their Lemma~5 needs a minor correction for a population of a single agent: no encounter happens, and if a lone agent keeps its state, its output stays $0$ even when the predicate holds. The protocols formalized here start each agent with its single-agent output and are correct for every $n\ge1$ (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/crn/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#semilinear-predicates-are-stably-computable-stable-crn-3-easy-direction}{details}).

nodes.name: Population protocols with input and output
nodes.statement_short: Input, output and transition functions; encounters, reachability and output-stable configurations.
nodes.statement: A population protocol has an input function $I : X \to Q$, an output function $O : Q \to \{0, 1\}$ and a transition function $\delta : Q \times Q \to Q \times Q$. An encounter of an ordered pair $(u, v)$ of distinct agents replaces their states $p, q$ by $\delta(p, q)$; reachability is the reflexive-transitive closure of encounters. A configuration is output-stable with output $b$ if in every configuration reachable from it every agent outputs $b$.
nodes.label: def:protocol

nodes.name: Stable computation
nodes.statement_short: A protocol stably computes $\varphi$ if every reachable configuration can reach an output-stable one with output $\varphi$.
nodes.statement: A protocol stably computes a predicate $\varphi$ on input count vectors if, for every nonempty population and every input assignment $\iota$, every configuration reachable from $I \circ \iota$ can reach an output-stable configuration with output $\varphi$ of the input counts. A predicate is stably computable if a protocol with finitely many states stably computes it.
nodes.label: def:stable

nodes.name: Uniqueness
conclusions: A protocol stably computes at most one predicate on nonzero count vectors
nodes.statement: A protocol stably computes at most one predicate on nonzero count vectors.
nodes.label: lem:stable-unique

nodes.name: Proof of Uniqueness
nodes.statement_short: Reach an output-stable configuration for one predicate, then for the other; the outputs agree.
nodes.statement: From the initial configuration of a population with the given counts, reach an output-stable configuration for the first predicate and then one for the second: they agree.

nodes.name: Boolean closure
assumptions: For every Boolean function $\xi$ of two arguments
conclusions: so is $\xi(\varphi, \psi)$
the class is closed under negation, conjunction and disjunction
nodes.statement: For every Boolean function $\xi$ of two arguments, if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are stably computable then so is $\xi(\varphi, \psi)$; in particular the class is closed under negation, conjunction and disjunction.
nodes.label: thm:boolean

nodes.name: Proof of Boolean closure
nodes.statement_short: Parallel composition of the two protocols on pairs of states.
nodes.statement: Parallel composition: states are pairs, both components make their own transition in every encounter, and the output of $(p_1, p_2)$ is $\xi(O_1 p_1, O_2 p_2)$.

nodes.name: Threshold predicates
conclusions: the predicates $\sum_i a_i x_i < c$ and $\sum_i a_i x_i \ge c$ are stably computable
nodes.statement: For integers $a_i$ and $c$, the predicates $\sum_i a_i x_i < c$ and $\sum_i a_i x_i \ge c$ are stably computable.
nodes.label: thm:threshold

nodes.name: Proof of Threshold predicates
nodes.statement_short: Leader-election protocol accumulating the weighted count, with outputs initialised for single agents; the second form by negation.
nodes.statement: Each agent holds a leader bit, an output bit and a count in $[-s, s]$, starting from $a_i$; an encounter involving a leader merges the leaders into the initiator, which takes as much of the sum of the two counts as fits in $[-s, s]$, and both agents set their output to whether the initiator's count is below $c$. Unlike the original protocol, an input starts with output bit $[a_i < c]$, which is needed for a population of one agent. The second form is the negation.

Each agent holds a leader bit, an output bit and a count in $[-s, s]$, starting from $a_i$; an encounter involving a leader merges the leaders into the initiator, which takes as much of the sum of the two counts as fits in $[-s, s]$, and both agents set their output to whether the initiator's count is below $c$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the leader protocol accumulating counts in $[-s,s]$.
nodes.name: Leader protocol

nodes.statement: Unlike the original protocol, an input starts with output bit $[a_i < c]$, which is needed for a population of one agent.
nodes.statement_short: Initial output bits fix the single-agent case.
nodes.name: Single-agent fix

nodes.statement: The second form is the negation.
nodes.statement_short: The $\ge c$ form follows by negation.

Remainder predicates
conclusions: the predicate $\sum_i a_i x_i \equiv c \pmod m$ is stably computable
nodes.statement: For integers $a_i$, $c$ and $m > 0$, the predicate $\sum_i a_i x_i \equiv c \pmod m$ is stably computable.
nodes.label: thm:remainder

nodes.name: Proof of Remainder predicates
nodes.statement_short: The same leader protocol with counts in $\mathbb{Z}/m$.
nodes.statement: The same leader protocol with counts in $\mathbb{Z}/m$: the initiator takes the sum of the two counts and the responder gets $0$.

nodes.name: Semilinear predicates
nodes.statement: The Boolean combinations of threshold and remainder predicates.
nodes.label: def:semilinear

nodes.name: Semilinear predicates are stably computable
conclusions: The truth set of every such predicate is a semilinear set of count vectors
every such predicate is stably computable
nodes.statement: The truth set of every such predicate is a semilinear set of count vectors, and every such predicate is stably computable.
nodes.label: thm:semilinear

nodes.name: Proof of Semilinear predicates are stably computable
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the Boolean combination using threshold, remainder and Boolean closure.
nodes.statement: Induction on the Boolean combination, with the two preceding theorems and Boolean closure; for the first part, semilinear sets are closed under complement, intersection and union.

nodes.name: Stable decision by a network
nodes.statement_short: A network stably decides $\varphi$ if every reachable count vector can reach one where all present species vote $\varphi(x)$ forever.
nodes.statement: A network with an injective input map $I : X \to S$ and an output map $O : S \to \{0, 1\}$ stably decides $\varphi$ if, from the initial count vector with $x_i$ molecules of $I(i)$ and nothing else, every reachable count vector can reach one in which, now and in every count vector reachable from it, every present species votes $\varphi(x)$.
nodes.label: def:crn-stable

nodes.name: Protocols are networks
nodes.statement_short: Protocol transitions form a bimolecular network with the same reachable counts, so every stably computable (semilinear) predicate is stably decided by a CRN.
conclusions: The transitions $p + q \to \delta_1(p, q) + \delta_2(p, q)$ that change $\{p, q\}$ form a count-conserving bimolecular network whose reachable count vectors are the counts of the configurations reachable in the protocol
every stably computable predicate, and in particular every Boolean combination of threshold and remainder predicates, is stably decided by such a network
nodes.statement: The transitions $p + q \to \delta_1(p, q) + \delta_2(p, q)$ that change $\{p, q\}$ form a count-conserving bimolecular network whose reachable count vectors are the counts of the configurations reachable in the protocol. Hence every stably computable predicate, and in particular every Boolean combination of threshold and remainder predicates, is stably decided by such a network.
nodes.label: thm:transfer

nodes.name: Proof of Protocols are networks
nodes.statement_short: Encounters change counts as the corresponding reaction; tagging input states keeps the input map injective.
nodes.statement: Encounters change counts exactly by the corresponding reaction. Tagging the input states keeps the input map injective and provides a transition that changes the multiset of states.

nodes.name: Corrections to Theorems 1, 2 and 4 of Mertzios et al.
nodes.statement_short: Minor fixes: types and an index in Theorem 1, closest opposite ambassadors in Theorem 2, and a monotone coupling plus absorption in Theorem 4.
nodes.statement: The proofs of Theorems~1, 2 and~4 need minor corrections: in Theorem~1 the type of two agents and one set index are corrected; in Theorem~2 ambassadors of the same color can block each other, which a closest pair of opposite ambassadors avoids; in Theorem~4 the monotonicity step is stated without proof (it follows from a monotone coupling), and the bound $1/2$ also needs absorption with probability $1$ (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/crn/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#majority-on-graphs-with-very-small-local-memory-graphmajority-crn-4}{details}).

nodes.name: Protocols on an interaction graph
nodes.statement_short: Encounters along oriented edges of $G$; stable computation on $G$ for inputs in a domain, and on all connected graphs.
nodes.statement: On a graph $G$ on the agents, an encounter is an oriented edge $(u, v)$ of $G$ (initiator $u$, responder $v$). Reachability and output stability on $G$ are defined as before with encounters along edges of $G$. A protocol stably computes $\varphi$ on $G$ for inputs in a domain $D$ if, for every input whose count vector lies in $D$, every configuration reachable on $G$ can reach an output-stable configuration with output $\varphi$; it stably computes $\varphi$ on graphs if it does so on every connected graph.

nodes.name: The complete graph
conclusions: these notions are those of Definition~\ref{def:stable}: stable computation on the complete graphs of all nonempty populations, with the trivial domain, is stable computation

nodes.name: The ambassador protocol
nodes.statement_short: 4-state protocol: colour plus ambassador bit; opposite ambassadors annihilate, ambassadors move to empty vertices and paint them.
nodes.statement: A state is a color and a bit saying whether the vertex holds an ambassador; every agent starts with an ambassador of its input color, and the output is the color. Two ambassadors of different colors annihilate; an ambassador meeting a vertex without ambassador moves there and paints it; nothing else changes. This is the table of Figure~1, with $4$ states, and the protocol is symmetric.
nodes.section: 25 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:ambassador

nodes.name: Invariants
conclusions: The number of ambassadors of each color starts at the input count and never increases
the difference between red and green ambassadors never changes

nodes.name: Proof of Invariants

nodes.name: Annihilation and spreading
nodes.statement_short: On connected graphs, opposite ambassadors can be annihilated pairwise, and a single remaining colour can be spread to an output-stable colouring.
assumptions: If all ambassadors have color $b$ and there is one
conclusions: a configuration with one ambassador of each color fewer is reachable
the all-$b$ coloring is reachable, and it is output-stable
a configuration with one ambassador of each color fewer is reachable

assumptions: If all ambassadors have color $b$ and there is one
conclusions: the all-$b$ coloring is reachable, and it is output-stable

nodes.statement: On a connected graph, while both colors have ambassadors, a configuration with one ambassador of each color fewer is reachable. If all ambassadors have color $b$ and there is one, the all-$b$ coloring is reachable, and it is output-stable.

nodes.name: Proof of Annihilation and spreading
nodes.statement_short: Strong induction on the distance between a red and a closest green ambassador; spreading by induction on distance then on the number of other-colour vertices.
nodes.statement: Take a red ambassador and a closest green one. The red ambassador walks along a shortest path, moving onto vertices without ambassador and handing over to red ambassadors it meets, until it meets the green one (strong induction on the distance). Spreading is similar, by induction on the distance to a vertex of the other color and then on the number of such vertices.

nodes.statement: Take a red ambassador and a closest green one. The red ambassador walks along a shortest path, moving onto vertices without ambassador and handing over to red ambassadors it meets, until it meets the green one (strong induction on the distance).

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: The 4-state ambassador protocol stably computes majority on every connected graph; ties must be excluded.
assumptions: for every input with a majority
conclusions: The ambassador protocol stably computes majority on every connected graph
With one red and one green agent, a configuration is reachable from which no output-stable configuration is reachable, so ties must be excluded
nodes.statement: The ambassador protocol stably computes majority on every connected graph, for every input with a majority. With one red and one green agent, a configuration is reachable from which no output-stable configuration is reachable, so ties must be excluded.

nodes.name: Proof of MNRS14, Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Annihilate pairs until only majority ambassadors remain (invariant), then spread their colour.
nodes.statement: From every reachable configuration, annihilate pairs until only ambassadors of the majority color remain (there is one by the invariant), then spread that color. Configurations without ambassadors are frozen.

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: No protocol with at most 3 states stably computes majority even on complete graphs, so 4 states are minimal.
conclusions: No protocol with at most $3$ states stably computes majority, ties excluded, on the complete graphs of all nonempty populations, hence on all connected graphs
$4$ is the minimal number of states
nodes.statement: No protocol with at most $3$ states stably computes majority, ties excluded, on the complete graphs of all nonempty populations, hence on all connected graphs. With Theorem~\ref{thm:ambassador}, $4$ is the minimal number of states.

nodes.name: Proof of MNRS14, Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: a single-state output forces two inputs with different majorities to reach a common configuration after adding two agents.
nodes.statement: A single agent never interacts, so both outputs occur, and one output $b$ has a single state $q_1$. On $3$ agents, the inputs $(b, b, \lnot b)$ and $(b, b, b)$ both reach the configuration in which every agent is in $q_1$. Adding two agents of input $\lnot b$ and running the same encounters on the first three agents, inputs with majority $\lnot b$ and $b$ reach a common configuration, a contradiction.

nodes.statement: A single agent never interacts, so both outputs occur, and one output $b$ has a single state $q_1$.

nodes.name: Approximate majority on a graph
nodes.origin_citation: Angluin, Aspnes, Eisenstat 2008; Mertzios, Nikoletseas, Raptopoulos, Spirakis 2014
nodes.statement_short: One-way 3-state rule realising the approximate-majority reactions along uniformly random oriented edges of $G$.
nodes.statement: The one-way rule: the initiator never changes; an initiator $X$ or $Y$ turns an opposite responder blank and recruits a blank responder. Its effective transitions are exactly the reactions of the approximate-majority network. Each step activates a uniformly random oriented edge of $G$.
nodes.section: 25 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:am-graph

nodes.name: Winning probabilities
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{win}_t(s)$: probability of unanimity in $s$ at time $t$ from a random placement; nondecreasing, with limit the convergence probability.
nodes.statement: With $m$ agents of type $Y$ placed on a uniformly random $m$-set and $X$ elsewhere, $\mathrm{win}_t(s)$ is the probability that every agent is $s$ at time $t$. Unanimity is absorbing, so $\mathrm{win}_t(s)$ is nondecreasing in $t$, and its supremum, the convergence probability, is its limit.
nodes.section: 25 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:winprob

nodes.name: Coupling and symmetry
nodes.statement_short: The rule is monotone for $Y<B<X$, so the all-$X$ probability is monotone in the start; swapping $X,Y$ commutes with the dynamics.
conclusions: the rule is monotone in both states, so the probability that every agent is $X$ at time $t$ is monotone in the initial configuration
Exchanging $X$ and $Y$ commutes with the dynamics
nodes.statement: For the order $Y < B < X$ the rule is monotone in both states, so the probability that every agent is $X$ at time $t$ is monotone in the initial configuration. Exchanging $X$ and $Y$ commutes with the dynamics.

nodes.name: MNRS14, Corollary 1
nodes.statement_short: A regular family of subsets has a system of distinct representatives; hence an injective choice of $(n-m)$-subsets $A_S\subseteq S$.
assumptions: A family of $r$-element subsets of a finite universe, with at most as many sets as elements, in which every element lies in the same number $d \ge 1$ of sets
conclusions: has a system of distinct representatives
every $m$-set $S$ of agents contains an $(n - m)$-subset $A_S$, with $S \mapsto A_S$ injective on the $m$-sets
nodes.statement: A family of $r$-element subsets of a finite universe, with at most as many sets as elements, in which every element lies in the same number $d \ge 1$ of sets, has a system of distinct representatives. In particular, if $n \le 2m$, every $m$-set $S$ of agents contains an $(n - m)$-subset $A_S$, with $S \mapsto A_S$ injective on the $m$-sets.

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 4, at every finite time
nodes.statement_short: At every time the minority's winning probability is at most the majority's.
assumptions: On every graph with an edge
conclusions: at every time $t$ the probability that the minority $X$ has won is at most the probability that the majority $Y$ has won
the same holds for the convergence probabilities
nodes.statement: On every graph with an edge, if $n \le 2m$, at every time $t$ the probability that the minority $X$ has won is at most the probability that the majority $Y$ has won; hence the same holds for the convergence probabilities.

nodes.name: Proof of MNRS14, Theorem 4, at every finite time
nodes.statement_short: Compare placements via the injection $S\mapsto A_S$ using monotone coupling and symmetry, then average over $m$-sets.
nodes.statement: For each $m$-set $S$, the configuration with $X$ exactly on $A_S$ lies below the one with $X$ exactly on $S$, which is the swap of the placement with $Y$ on $S$. By monotonicity and symmetry, the minority wins from the first with probability at most the probability that the majority wins from the placement on $S$. The first configuration is the placement on the $m$-set $A_S^c$, and $S \mapsto A_S^c$ is a bijection of the $m$-sets, so averaging over $S$ gives the inequality (eqs.~(18) to~(23)).
nodes.section: 25 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.statement: For each $m$-set $S$, the configuration with $X$ exactly on $A_S$ lies below the one with $X$ exactly on $S$, which is the swap of the placement with $Y$ on $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the configuration on $A_S$ with the swapped placement on $S$.
nodes.name: Comparison configurations

nodes.statement: By monotonicity and symmetry, the minority wins from the first with probability at most the probability that the majority wins from the placement on $S$.

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 4
nodes.statement_short: On connected graphs the protocol is absorbed in a consensus a.s., and converges to the majority with probability at least $1/2$.
assumptions: from every configuration with a non-blank agent
conclusions: the protocol is absorbed in all-$X$ or all-$Y$ with probability tending to $1$
it converges to the majority with probability at least $1/2$

assumptions: from every configuration with a non-blank agent
conclusions: the protocol is absorbed in all-$X$ or all-$Y$ with probability tending to $1$
it converges to the majority with probability at least $1/2$

nodes.statement: On a connected graph, from every configuration with a non-blank agent, the protocol is absorbed in all-$X$ or all-$Y$ with probability tending to $1$. Hence, if $n \le 2m$ and $m \le n$, it converges to the majority with probability at least $1/2$.

nodes.name: Proof of MNRS14, Theorem 4
nodes.statement_short: Opinions spread along edges and all-blank is unreachable, so the finite chain is absorbed; convergence probabilities sum to 1.
nodes.statement: An initiator $s \ne B$ activated twice on the same responder makes it $s$, so an opinion present spreads to all agents along the edges of a connected graph, and all-blank is never reached. Absorption in a finite chain follows, and the two convergence probabilities sum to $1$.

nodes.name: Scope of the formalized Theorem 7
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 7 is formalized as Section 5.1 computes it: agents learn whether their own colour is the plurality colour.
nodes.statement: Theorem~7 is formalized as the protocol of Section~5.1 computes it: every agent learns whether its own colour is the plurality colour, not the winner's label (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/crn/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#deterministic-exact-majority-and-plurality-exactmajority-crn-5}{details}).

nodes.name: Stable computation with general outputs
nodes.statement_short: A protocol stably marks agents with $g(x,i)$ if every reachable configuration can reach one where each agent forever outputs $g$ of its input.
nodes.statement: For an output map $O : Q \to Y$ into any type and a target $g(x, i) \in Y$ depending on the input counts $x$ and on an agent's input $i$, a protocol stably marks the agents with $g$ if, for every nonempty population, every configuration reachable from the initial one can reach a configuration from which every agent $v$ forever outputs $g(x, \iota(v))$. Stable computation of $f$ is the case $g(x, i) = f(x)$; with the protocol's Boolean output it is Definition~\ref{def:stable}.
nodes.label: def:em-marks

nodes.name: The static protocol
nodes.statement_short: Six-state exact-majority protocol with strong and weak states; opposite strong states annihilate and strong states recruit.
nodes.statement: Colours are in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. The six states are the strong states $[x]$ and the weak states $\langle x \rangle$, $x \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$, of weight $x$ and $0$. The states $[1]$ and $[-1]$ annihilate into $[0], [0]$; a strong $[x]$ turns a weak state into $\langle x \rangle$, and, for $x \ne 0$, turns $[0]$ into $\langle x \rangle$. The output of $[x]$ and $\langle x \rangle$ is $x$.
nodes.label: def:em-static

nodes.name: Lemmas 1 and 2
conclusions: the weight sum equals the colour sum $S$
the sum $R$ of the absolute weights does not increase
a configuration with $R = |S|$ is reachable
nodes.statement: Along every execution the weight sum equals the colour sum $S$, the sum $R$ of the absolute weights does not increase, and a configuration with $R = |S|$ is reachable.
nodes.label: lem:em-static

nodes.name: Proof of Lemmas 1 and 2
nodes.statement_short: Exhaustive check over the 36 encounter pairs; bringing opposite weights together decreases $R$.
nodes.statement: Check the encounters (by computation over the $36$ pairs); while weights of both signs are present, bring two of them together, which decreases $R$.

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Theorem 3
conclusions: The static protocol stably computes $\operatorname{sign}(\#1 - \#(-1))$: all agents eventually and forever output $1$, $-1$, or $0$ for a tie
nodes.statement: The static protocol stably computes $\operatorname{sign}(\#1 - \#(-1))$: all agents eventually and forever output $1$, $-1$, or $0$ for a tie.
nodes.label: thm:em-static

nodes.name: Proof of GHMSS16, Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Once $R=|S|$ a strong agent of the majority sign exists and recruits all agents into a closed set of states with that output.
nodes.statement: Once $R = |S|$, every weight is $0$ or $s = \operatorname{sign} S$ and a strong agent $[s]$ exists (for $s = 0$, a strong state is never lost). It recruits every agent into the states of output $s$, a set closed under the transitions.

nodes.name: The dynamic protocol
nodes.statement_short: Eight-state colour-blind variant: strong states cancel and recruit; an external colour change shifts the weight; runs in groups.
nodes.statement: The eight states are the strong states $[-2], \dots, [2]$ and the weak states $\langle -1 \rangle, \langle 0 \rangle, \langle 1 \rangle$. Opposite strong states cancel as far as possible, and strong states recruit weak ones and $[0]$ as in the static protocol; the transitions do not read the colours. When an external force changes a colour $c$ to $c'$, the state becomes $[w + c' - c]$, $w$ its weight. For Section~5 the protocol runs separately in groups of agents, with encounters inside a group.
nodes.label: def:em-dynamic

nodes.name: Invariants of Section 3
nodes.statement: In every group the colour sum equals the weight sum, every agent's weight is within $1$ of its colour, and every group contains a strong state. The initial configuration $[c_a]$ satisfies them.
nodes.label: def:em-dyninv

nodes.name: Lemmas 4 and 5
nodes.statement_short: The invariants are preserved by encounters and colour changes, absolute weights do not increase, and a configuration without opposite weights is reachable.
conclusions: The invariants are preserved by encounters inside groups and by colour changes
The sum of the absolute weights does not increase, and a configuration without opposite weights in a group is reachable
nodes.statement: The invariants are preserved by encounters inside groups and by colour changes. The sum of the absolute weights does not increase, and a configuration without opposite weights in a group is reachable.
nodes.label: lem:em-dynamic

nodes.name: Proof of Lemmas 4 and 5
nodes.statement_short: Encounter-by-encounter finite check; a colour change shifts the weight and makes the state strong.
nodes.statement: Encounter by encounter (by computation over the finite state space); a colour change moves the weight by the change of colour and makes the state strong.

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Section 3
nodes.statement_short: From invariant-satisfying configurations, each group stabilizes on the sign of its colour sum, even after finite interleavings of colour changes.
assumptions: From every configuration satisfying the invariants
conclusions: a configuration is reachable from which every agent forever outputs the sign of the colour sum of its group

after any finite interleaving of encounters and colour changes the dynamic protocol stabilizes on the sign of the final colour sum, and without the force it stably computes $\operatorname{sign}(\#1 - \#(-1))$
nodes.statement: From every configuration satisfying the invariants, a configuration is reachable from which every agent forever outputs the sign of the colour sum of its group. Hence after any finite interleaving of encounters and colour changes the dynamic protocol stabilizes on the sign of the final colour sum, and without the force it stably computes $\operatorname{sign}(\#1 - \#(-1))$.
nodes.label: thm:em-dynamic

nodes.name: Proof of GHMSS16, Section 3
nodes.statement_short: After Lemma 5 nonzero weights share the group's sign and a strong agent exists (third invariant); it recruits the group.
nodes.statement: After Lemma~5, every nonzero weight in a group has the sign $s$ of the group's colour sum, and a strong agent of weight sign $s$ exists in the group (the third invariant gives it in the tie case). It recruits the group into the states of output $s$.

nodes.name: Driving the dynamic protocol
nodes.statement_short: The driven protocol runs $D$ alongside a dynamic protocol, applying the force whenever an agent's derived colour changes.
nodes.statement: Given a protocol $D$, a colour map from its states to $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ and a group map that $D$ never changes, the driven protocol runs $D$ and a copy of the dynamic protocol: in an encounter $D$ makes its transition, the dynamic protocol makes its transition if the two agents are in the same group, and each agent whose colour changed applies the state change of the force.
nodes.label: def:em-drive

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.statement_short: The driven protocol keeps the invariants, and if $D$ stably marks eventual colours it stably marks each agent with its group's colour-sum sign.
assumptions: If $D$ stably marks the agents with their eventual colours
conclusions: Along every execution of the driven protocol the invariants of Section~3 hold for the derived colours
the driven protocol stably marks every agent with the sign of the eventual colour sum of its group
Along every execution of the driven protocol the invariants of Section~3 hold for the derived colours

assumptions: If $D$ stably marks the agents with their eventual colours
conclusions: the driven protocol stably marks every agent with the sign of the eventual colour sum of its group

nodes.name: Proof of Composition
nodes.statement_short: Each encounter is a dynamic-protocol encounter plus two colour changes; after $D$ stabilizes, apply the Section 3 theorem per group.
nodes.statement: An encounter is an encounter of the dynamic protocol inside a group followed by two colour changes. Once $D$ has stabilized, the colours are fixed and Theorem~\ref{thm:em-dynamic} applies in every group.

nodes.name: Absolute-Majority
nodes.statement_short: $k$ static protocols on label bits drive a dynamic protocol that checks whether an agent's label is the majority label.
nodes.statement: Every agent keeps its label $l$ and runs $k$ copies of the static protocol on the bits $l[i]$, read as $\pm 1$. They drive a copy of the dynamic protocol, with colour $1$ if every copy currently reports the agent's own bit and $-1$ otherwise. An agent outputs the reported majority bits if its dynamic protocol outputs $1$, and none otherwise. The specification is the colour held by more than half of the agents, if any.
nodes.label: def:em-absolute

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Theorem 6
conclusions: Absolute-Majority stably computes the absolute majority colour, or reports that there is none, with $2^k \cdot 6^k \cdot 8 \le 2^{4k+3}$ states
nodes.statement: Absolute-Majority stably computes the absolute majority colour, or reports that there is none, with $2^k \cdot 6^k \cdot 8 \le 2^{4k+3}$ states.
nodes.label: thm:em-absolute

nodes.name: Proof of GHMSS16, Theorem 6
nodes.statement_short: The bit copies stabilize; then colour 1 marks the majority label, and the composition theorem applies with one group.
nodes.statement: The $k$ copies stabilize on the majority bits one at a time. Then the colour of an agent is $1$ exactly when its label consists of the majority bits, so the eventual colour sum is positive if and only if that label is held by more than half of the agents, and the composition theorem applies with a single group.

nodes.name: Relative-Majority
nodes.statement_short: Stage-wise tournament over label prefixes, each stage a dynamic protocol in prefix groups; plurality colour with lexicographic tie-break.
nodes.statement: Stages $i = k - 1, \dots, 0$: the agents whose labels share the prefix $l[0..i-1]$ form a group, and a copy of the dynamic protocol runs in each group, with colour $l[i]$ (as $\pm 1$) for the agents that won all the stages above $i$ and $0$ for the others. An agent wins stage $i$ if its colour is $-1$ and the stage outputs $-1$, or its colour is $1$ and the stage outputs $0$ or $1$. The protocol is the $k$-fold iteration of the driven protocol, the colours being derived from the states. The plurality colour is the most frequent one, ties broken in favour of the lexicographically largest label.
nodes.label: def:em-relative

nodes.name: The duel
assumptions: Once the stages above $i$ have stabilized
conclusions: the duel of stage $i$ between the winners of the two groups extending a prefix $p$ selects the winner of the group of $p$
The winner of the whole population is the plurality colour
nodes.statement: Once the stages above $i$ have stabilized, the duel of stage $i$ between the winners of the two groups extending a prefix $p$ selects the winner of the group of $p$. The winner of the whole population is the plurality colour.
nodes.label: lem:em-duel

nodes.name: Proof of The duel
nodes.statement_short: The group's colour sum is the count difference of the two sub-winners; ties go to the larger label.
nodes.statement: The colour sum of the group of $p$ is the difference of the counts of the two group winners, and ties go to the larger label.

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Theorem 7
nodes.statement_short: Relative-Majority stably marks the agents of the plurality colour using $2^{4k}$ states.
conclusions: Relative-Majority stably marks the agents of the plurality colour: eventually and forever, every agent outputs whether its own colour is the plurality colour
It has $2^k \cdot 8^k = 2^{4k}$ states
nodes.statement: Relative-Majority stably marks the agents of the plurality colour: eventually and forever, every agent outputs whether its own colour is the plurality colour. It has $2^k \cdot 8^k = 2^{4k}$ states.
nodes.label: thm:em-relative

nodes.name: Proof of GHMSS16, Theorem 7
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the levels using the composition theorem and the duel lemma.
nodes.statement: Induction on the levels: level $m$ stably marks every agent with whether its label wins its group of prefix length $k - m$, by the composition theorem and the duel lemma.

nodes.statement: Let $\varphi$ equal $\varphi_A$ on an event $A$ and $\varphi_B$ on an event $B$, and let $S$ be the event of lying in neither. If $\E_{x_0}\varphi(X_T)=\varphi(x_0)$ and $m\le\varphi-\varphi_B\le M$ on $S$, then $\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_B-(\varphi_A-\varphi_B)\Pr_{x_0}(X_T\in A)$ lies between $m\Pr_{x_0}(X_T\in S)$ and $M\Pr_{x_0}(X_T\in S)$. Hence, if $\varphi_A\ne\varphi_B$, the conservation law holds for every $T$ and $\Pr_{x_0}(X_T\in S)\to0$, then $\Pr_{x_0}(X_T\in A)\to(\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_B)/(\varphi_A-\varphi_B)$; if moreover $A$ is absorbing, this is the supremum of the finite-time probabilities.

nodes.name: Proof of Finite-horizon optional stopping
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise decomposition of $\varphi-\varphi_B$, take expectations, bound the residual, squeeze for the limit.
nodes.statement: Pointwise, $\varphi-\varphi_B=(\varphi_A-\varphi_B)1_A+(\varphi-\varphi_B)1_S$ (on $A\cap B$ both sides vanish). Take expectations at time $T$ and bound the last term by monotonicity. For the limit, take $M=-m=\sum_a|\varphi(a)-\varphi_B|$ and squeeze. If $A$ is absorbing, the finite-time probabilities increase, so their limit is their supremum.

conclusions: $\Pr(X\ge\E X+\lambda)\le e^{-2\lambda^2/n}$

nodes.statement: Let $X=\sum_{i<n}Y_i(\omega_i)$ with independent uniform coordinates. If each $Y_i$ is $\{0,1\}$-valued, $\Pr(X\ge\E X+\lambda)\le e^{-2\lambda^2/n}$. nodes.name: Proof of Hoeffding and Bernstein inequalities
nodes.statement_short: Exponential moment method: Markov on $e^{tX}$, bound each factor (Hoeffding's lemma, or a Bernstein-type exponential bound), optimize $t$.
nodes.statement: Markov's inequality applied to $e^{tX}$, which factors over the coordinates. Hoeffding's lemma bounds each Bernoulli factor; for Bernstein, $e^y\le1+y+y^2/(2(1-u/3))$ for $y\le u<3$ bounds each factor, and $t$ is chosen as $\lambda/(\sigma^2+b\lambda/3)$.

nodes.name: Chernoff bounds for independent Bernoulli trials
nodes.origin_citation: Mitzenmacher & Upfal, Probability and Computing, Theorems 4.4, 4.5, Exercise 4.7
assumptions: Let $X=\sum_iX_i$ be a sum of independent $\{0,1\}$-valued trials with $\Pr(X_i=1)=p_i$, and let $\mu_L\le\mu=\sum_ip_i\le\mu_H$.
conclusions: \Pr(X\ge(1+\delta)\mu_H)\le\Bigl(\frac{e^{\delta}}{(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}}\Bigr)^{\mu_H} \le e^{-\delta^2\mu_H/(2+\delta)},
\Pr(X\le(1-\delta)\mu_L)\le\Bigl(\frac{e^{-\delta}}{(1-\delta)^{1-\delta}}\Bigr)^{\mu_L} \le e^{-\delta^2\mu_L/2}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicative Chernoff upper and lower tail bounds for sums of independent 0/1 trials, with mean bounds $\mu_L\le\mu\le\mu_H$.
nodes.statement: Let $X=\sum_iX_i$ be a sum of independent $\{0,1\}$-valued trials with $\Pr(X_i=1)=p_i$, and let $\mu_L\le\mu=\sum_ip_i\le\mu_H$. For $\delta>0$, \[\Pr(X\ge(1+\delta)\mu_H)\le\Bigl(\frac{e^{\delta}}{(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}}\Bigr)^{\mu_H} \le e^{-\delta^2\mu_H/(2+\delta)},\] and for $0<\delta<1$, \[\Pr(X\le(1-\delta)\mu_L)\le\Bigl(\frac{e^{-\delta}}{(1-\delta)^{1-\delta}}\Bigr)^{\mu_L} \le e^{-\delta^2\mu_L/2}.\] The trials are $\{0,1\}$-valued observables of the coordinates of an independent product of distributions, independent biased coins (counting the heads in any subset), or the coordinates of one uniform round (Mitzenmacher--Upfal, \emph{Probability and Computing}, Theorems 4.4 and 4.5 with Exercise 4.7).
nodes.label: thm:chernoff

nodes.name: Proof of Chernoff bounds for independent Bernoulli trials
nodes.statement_short: Exponential moment method with $1+x\le e^x$ per factor, $t=\log(1\pm\delta)$, and elementary logarithm bounds for the closed forms.
nodes.statement: Markov's inequality applied to $e^{tX}$, which factors over the coordinates; each factor is $1+p_i(e^t-1)\le e^{p_i(e^t-1)}$, so $\E e^{tX}\le e^{\mu_H(e^t-1)}$ for $t\ge0$ and $\E e^{tX}\le e^{\mu_L(e^t-1)}$ for $t\le0$. Take $t=\log(1+\delta)$, respectively $t=\log(1-\delta)$. The closed forms follow from $\log(1+\delta)\ge2\delta/(2+\delta)$ (the first term of the series of $\log\frac{1+x}{1-x}$ at $x=\delta/(2+\delta)$) and $(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta)\ge-\delta+\delta^2/2$.

nodes.name: Bound the MGF factor by factor via Markov on $e^{tX}$
nodes.statement: Markov's inequality applied to $e^{tX}$, which factors over the coordinates; each factor is $1+p_i(e^t-1)\le e^{p_i(e^t-1)}$, so $\E e^{tX}\le e^{\mu_H(e^t-1)}$ for $t\ge0$ and $\E e^{tX}\le e^{\mu_L(e^t-1)}$ for $t\le0$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the MGF factor by factor via Markov on $e^{tX}$

nodes.name: Derive the closed forms from elementary log inequalities
nodes.statement: Take $t=\log(1+\delta)$, respectively $t=\log(1-\delta)$. The closed forms follow from $\log(1+\delta)\ge2\delta/(2+\delta)$ (the first term of the series of $\log\frac{1+x}{1-x}$ at $x=\delta/(2+\delta)$) and $(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta)\ge-\delta+\delta^2/2$.

nodes.name: Lower tails, MGF and parametric Chernoff bounds
assumptions: Let $X=\sum_{i<n}Y_i(\omega_i)$ with independent uniform $\{0,1\}$-valued coordinates and $\mu=\E X$.
conclusions: $\Pr(X\le\E X-\lambda)\le e^{-2\lambda^2/n}$
a $\{0,1\}$ coordinate has variance at most its mean
$\E e^{tX}\le\exp(\mu(e^t-1))$
$\Pr(X\le(1-\delta)\E X)\le\exp(-\delta^2\E X/2)$ for $0\le\delta<1$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower Hoeffding tail, MGF bound $\E e^{tX}\le\exp(\mu(e^t-1))$, parametric Chernoff tails and the multiplicative lower tail for 0/1 sums.
nodes.statement: Let $X=\sum_{i<n}Y_i(\omega_i)$ with independent uniform $\{0,1\}$-valued coordinates and $\mu=\E X$. Then $\Pr(X\le\E X-\lambda)\le e^{-2\lambda^2/n}$, and a $\{0,1\}$ coordinate has variance at most its mean. For every real $t$, $\E e^{tX}\le\exp(\mu(e^t-1))$; hence $\Pr(X\ge k)\le\exp(\mu(e^t-1)-tk)$ for $t\ge0$ and $\Pr(X\le k)\le\exp(\mu(e^t-1)-tk)$ for $t\le0$. If $\E X\le\mu\le k$ with $\mu>0$, then $\Pr(X\ge k)\le\exp(k-\mu-k\log(k/\mu))$; if $0<k\le\mu\le\E X$, then $\Pr(X\le k)\le\exp(k-\mu-k\log(k/\mu))$. Finally $\Pr(X\le(1-\delta)\E X)\le\exp(-\delta^2\E X/2)$ for $0\le\delta<1$.
nodes.label: thm:chernoffmgf

nodes.name: Proof of Lower tails, MGF and parametric Chernoff bounds
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the lower Hoeffding tail to the upper one, bound the MGF factorwise, then choose $t=\log(k/\mu)$.
nodes.statement: The lower Hoeffding tail is the upper one for $1-Y_i$. For the MGF bound, $e^{tY}=1+(e^t-1)Y$ on $\{0,1\}$ and $1+y\le e^y$, factor by factor; Markov's inequality applied to $e^{tX}$ gives the tails, and $t=\log(k/\mu)$ the closed forms (the exponent is monotone in $\mu$ in the right direction). The last bound is the lower bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:chernoff} with $\mu_L=\E X$ (trivial for $\delta=0$).

nodes.name: Elementary tail bounds and monotonicity
conclusions: Probability is monotone in the event.
Markov's inequality $\Pr(X\ge c)\le\E X/c$ for $X\ge0$, $c>0$
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of probability, Markov's inequality and union bound, one-round success bound, monotone occupation of absorbing events, and $e^{-2\log n}=1/n^2$.
nodes.statement: Probability is monotone in the event. An observable $f\le1$ with $f(b)<1$ at a point of positive weight has expectation $<1$. Markov's inequality $\Pr(X\ge c)\le\E X/c$ for $X\ge0$, $c>0$; in particular $\Pr(\sum_iY_i(\omega_i)\ge1)\le\sum_i\E Y_i$ for nonnegative coordinates. One round of $\mathrm{step}$ lands in an event with probability at least $1-\E[\mathrm{bad}]$ when $\mathrm{bad}\ge0$ is at least $1$ on every miss. If $f\le Kf$, then $n\mapsto K^nf(a)$ is nondecreasing; in particular the occupation probability of an absorbing event is nondecreasing in time. Finally $e^{-2\log n}=1/n^2$ for $n\ge1$, and $\log n>0$ forces $n\ge1$.
nodes.label: lem:tail

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary tail bounds and monotonicity
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise indicator comparisons integrated by monotonicity; induction on time for kernel statements.
nodes.statement: Pointwise comparisons of indicators, integrated by monotonicity of the expectation; for the kernel statements, induction on time with $K^{n+1}f=K^n(Kf)$.

nodes.name: Nested phases
assumptions: Let $A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_T$ be sets of states such that from $A_i$ the chain stays in $A_i$ with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ and, for $i<T$, enters $A_{i+1}$ with probability at least $1-\nu$.
conclusions: From $A_1$, after $\ell T$ steps the chain is in $A_T$ with probability at least $1-T(\ell\varepsilon+\nu^\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: If each of nested state sets is retained w.p. $\ge1-\varepsilon$ and the next is entered w.p. $\ge1-\nu$, after $\ell T$ steps the last is reached w.p. $\ge1-T(\ell\varepsilon+\nu^\ell)$.
nodes.statement: Let $A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_T$ be sets of states such that from $A_i$ the chain stays in $A_i$ with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ and, for $i<T$, enters $A_{i+1}$ with probability at least $1-\nu$. From $A_1$, after $\ell T$ steps the chain is in $A_T$ with probability at least $1-T(\ell\varepsilon+\nu^\ell)$.
nodes.label: thm:phases

nodes.name: Proof of Nested phases
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over phases: per phase, bound leaving probability by $\ell\varepsilon$ and missing probability by $\nu^\ell$.
nodes.statement: Track the indicator of lying outside a set. In $\ell$ steps the chain leaves $A_i$ with probability at most $\ell\varepsilon$, and misses $A_{i+1}$ in all $\ell$ steps with probability at most $\nu^\ell$. Sum over the $T$ phases.
