k-party 2-Choices
nodes.origin_citation: Elsässer, Friedetzky, Kaaser, Mallmann-Trenn, Trinker, arXiv:1602.04667
nodes.statement_short: Each node samples two nodes and adopts their colour if they agree; defines colour counts $c_i$ and $\mathrm{twice}_i$.
nodes.statement: Colours lie in any type with decidable equality. In a round every node samples two nodes uniformly at random (independently, with replacement) and adopts their colour if the two samples hold the same colour; otherwise it keeps its own. $c_i$ is the number of nodes of colour $i$, and the number of nodes whose two samples both hold $i$ is denoted $\mathrm{twice}_i$.
nodes.label: def:two-choices

nodes.name: Basic facts and two colours
nodes.statement_short: Consensus is fixed, extinct colours stay extinct, two colours give the median rule, and colour $i$ dominates the binary process of its indicator.
conclusions: Consensus configurations are fixed
$c_i'\le c_i+\mathrm{twice}_i$, so an extinct colour stays extinct
On two colours the rule is the median of the own colour and the two samples
every node that holds \texttt{true} in the binary median process started from the indicator of colour $i$ holds colour $i$
nodes.statement: Consensus configurations are fixed; $c_i'\le c_i+\mathrm{twice}_i$, so an extinct colour stays extinct. On two colours the rule is the median of the own colour and the two samples. For the same rounds, every node that holds \texttt{true} in the binary median process started from the indicator of colour $i$ holds colour $i$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-basic

nodes.statement_short: Direct check of the adoption rule; for domination, the new-colour indicator dominates the median of indicators; induct on rounds.
nodes.statement: A node that does not hold $i$ adopts $i$ only if both samples hold $i$. With two colours, the new colour is the majority among the own colour and the two samples, that is, their median. For the domination, the indicator of $\{\text{new colour}=i\}$ is at least the median of the three indicators, and the median is monotone; induct on the rounds.

nodes.name: Extinction
nodes.statement: A node that does not hold $i$ adopts $i$ only if both samples hold $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Adoption needs both samples.

nodes.name: Two colours
nodes.statement: With two colours, the new colour is the majority among the own colour and the two samples, that is, their median.
nodes.statement_short: Majority of three is the median.

nodes.name: Domination
nodes.statement: For the domination, the indicator of $\{\text{new colour}=i\}$ is at least the median of the three indicators, and the median is monotone; induct on the rounds.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone median; induct on rounds.

nodes.name: One-round expectations (including Observation 2.1)
nodes.statement_short: Exact one-round expected colour counts, order preservation in expectation, and a lower bound on the expected growth of the leading gap.
conclusions: $c_r\le c_s$ implies $\E c_r'\le\E c_s'$ (Observation~2.1)
If every colour other than $i$ has at most $b$ nodes, then $S\le c_i^2+(n-c_i)b$
If $a$ and $b$ are the sizes of the largest and the second largest colour, then $\E(a'-b')\ge(a-b)(1+(a/n)(1-a/n))$
nodes.statement: $\E c_i'=c_i(1+c_i/n-S/n^2)$; hence $c_r\le c_s$ implies $\E c_r'\le\E c_s'$ (Observation~2.1), and $\E(c_i'-c_j')=(c_i-c_j)(1+(c_i+c_j)/n-S/n^2)$. If every colour other than $i$ has at most $b$ nodes, then $S\le c_i^2+(n-c_i)b$. If $a$ and $b$ are the sizes of the largest and the second largest colour, then $\E(a'-b')\ge(a-b)(1+(a/n)(1-a/n))$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-expect

nodes.statement_short: Per-node colour probabilities summed; monotonicity of $c\mapsto c(1+c/n-S/n^2)$; aggregation bound on $S$.
nodes.statement: A node ends in colour $i$ with probability $(c_i/n)^2+[x_v=i](1-S/n^2)$; sum over the nodes. The map $c\mapsto c(1+c/n-S/n^2)$ is increasing on $c\ge0$ since $S\le n^2$. The aggregation bound is $\sum_{j\ne i}c_j^2\le b\sum_{j\ne i}c_j=b(n-c_i)$, and with $S\le a^2+nb$ the gap formula gives the last bound.

nodes.name: Expectation
nodes.statement: A node ends in colour $i$ with probability $(c_i/n)^2+[x_v=i](1-S/n^2)$; sum over the nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Per-node probability summed.

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: The map $c\mapsto c(1+c/n-S/n^2)$ is increasing on $c\ge0$ since $S\le n^2$.
nodes.statement_short: The map is increasing.

nodes.name: Aggregation
nodes.statement: The aggregation bound is $\sum_{j\ne i}c_j^2\le b\sum_{j\ne i}c_j=b(n-c_i)$, and with $S\le a^2+nb$ the gap formula gives the last bound.
nodes.statement_short: Aggregation bound and gap formula.

nodes.name: One-round concentration
nodes.statement_short: Bernstein-type lower tails for the leading gap and the leading count after one round.
assumptions: colour $i$ be a largest colour, with $a=c_i>0$ nodes, and $j\ne i$
conclusions: For every $\lambda\ge0$, $\Pr(a'-c_j'\le\E(a'-c_j')-\lambda)\le\exp(-\lambda^2/(20a^2/n+4\lambda/3))$ and $\Pr(a'\le\E a'-\lambda)\le\exp(-\lambda^2/(4a^2/n+2\lambda/3))$
if $128\sqrt{n\log n}\le g\le a$, both probabilities are at most $n^{-12}$ for $\lambda=ga/(8n)$ and $\lambda=ag/(4n)$ respectively
nodes.statement: Let colour $i$ be a largest colour, with $a=c_i>0$ nodes, and $j\ne i$. For every $\lambda\ge0$, $\Pr(a'-c_j'\le\E(a'-c_j')-\lambda)\le\exp(-\lambda^2/(20a^2/n+4\lambda/3))$ and $\Pr(a'\le\E a'-\lambda)\le\exp(-\lambda^2/(4a^2/n+2\lambda/3))$. In particular, if $128\sqrt{n\log n}\le g\le a$, both probabilities are at most $n^{-12}$ for $\lambda=ga/(8n)$ and $\lambda=ag/(4n)$ respectively.
nodes.label: lem:tc-conc

nodes.statement_short: Sums of independent bounded per-node contributions with small variances; apply Bernstein's inequality.
nodes.statement: Both quantities are sums of independent per-node contributions bounded by $1$ in absolute value. A node of colour $i$ or $j$ contributes only when it leaves its colour, which has probability at most $S/n^2\le a/n$, and any other node joins $i$ or $j$ with probability at most $2a^2/n^2$. Bounding each variance by the second moment about the node's current contribution gives $\mathrm{Var}(a'-c_j')\le10a^2/n$ and $\mathrm{Var}(a')\le2a^2/n$; apply Bernstein's inequality. The exponents are then at least $(g^2/(1344n))\ge12\log n$.

nodes.name: Independent sums
nodes.statement: Both quantities are sums of independent per-node contributions bounded by $1$ in absolute value.
nodes.statement_short: Sums of independent bounded contributions.

nodes.name: Contribution probabilities
nodes.statement: A node of colour $i$ or $j$ contributes only when it leaves its colour, which has probability at most $S/n^2\le a/n$, and any other node joins $i$ or $j$ with probability at most $2a^2/n^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound per-node change probabilities.

nodes.name: Bernstein
nodes.statement: Bounding each variance by the second moment about the node's current contribution gives $\mathrm{Var}(a'-c_j')\le10a^2/n$ and $\mathrm{Var}(a')\le2a^2/n$; apply Bernstein's inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Variance bounds and Bernstein's inequality.

nodes.name: Exponents
nodes.statement: The exponents are then at least $(g^2/(1344n))\ge12\log n$.
nodes.statement_short: Exponents at least $12\log n$.

nodes.name: The distance increases (Lemma 2.2)
nodes.origin_citation: Elsässer, Friedetzky, Kaaser, Mallmann-Trenn, Trinker, arXiv:1602.04667 (Lemma 2.2)
nodes.statement_short: The gap between the two largest colours grows by a factor $1+a/(4n)$ in one round w.h.p.
assumptions: colour $i$ is the largest, with $a=c_i\le n/2$ nodes, $j$ is the second largest, with $b=c_j$ nodes, and $a-b\ge z\sqrt{n\log n}$
conclusions: $a'-b'>(a-b)(1+a/(4n))$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$
nodes.statement: There are constants $z,C>0$ such that, whenever $\log n\ge C$: if colour $i$ is the largest, with $a=c_i\le n/2$ nodes, $j$ is the second largest, with $b=c_j$ nodes, and $a-b\ge z\sqrt{n\log n}$, then $a'-b'>(a-b)(1+a/(4n))$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-distance

nodes.statement_short: Expected-gap bound from one-round expectations plus Bernstein concentration.
nodes.statement: Take $z=128$ and $C=2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-expect} and $a\le n/2$, $\E(a'-b')\ge(a-b)(1+a/(2n))$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-conc} with $\lambda=(a-b)a/(8n)$, the gap falls below $\E(a'-b')-\lambda$ with probability at most $n^{-12}$. No bound on the number of colours is needed.

nodes.name: Expectation and concentration
nodes.statement: Take $z=128$ and $C=2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-expect} and $a\le n/2$, $\E(a'-b')\ge(a-b)(1+a/(2n))$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-conc} with $\lambda=(a-b)a/(8n)$, the gap falls below $\E(a'-b')-\lambda$ with probability at most $n^{-12}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expected gap growth and Bernstein tail.

nodes.name: Remark
nodes.statement: No bound on the number of colours is needed.
nodes.statement_short: No bound on the number of colours needed.

nodes.name: The coupling (Lemma 2.3) as stochastic domination
nodes.origin_citation: Elsässer, Friedetzky, Kaaser, Mallmann-Trenn, Trinker, arXiv:1602.04667 (Lemma 2.3)
nodes.statement_short: A smaller colour's next count is stochastically dominated by a larger colour's next count.
conclusions: $\Pr(c_c'\ge t)\le\Pr(c_b'\ge t)$ for every $t$
nodes.statement: If $c_c\le c_b$, then $\Pr(c_c'\ge t)\le\Pr(c_b'\ge t)$ for every $t$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-stochdom

nodes.statement_short: Construct a measure-preserving bijection of rounds from node and sample-pair permutations mapping the event for $c$ into the event for $b$.
nodes.statement: Choose a permutation $\tau$ of the nodes sending every node of colour $c$ to a node of colour $b$. For every node $v$, the sample pairs that make $v$ end in colour $c$ are at most as many as those that make $\tau(v)$ end in colour $b$: a node of another colour adopts a colour of size $m$ on the $m^2$ pairs with both samples on it, a node of that colour keeps it on the $n^2-S+m^2$ pairs that do not agree on another colour, and both counts increase with $m$. Choose a permutation of the sample pairs embedding the first set into the second. The induced bijection of rounds preserves the uniform distribution and maps the rounds with $c_c'\ge t$ into the rounds with $c_b'\ge t$. The paper's coupling, read literally, needs a minor correction (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/median/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#remarks-on-the-sources}{details}).

nodes.name: Node permutation
nodes.statement: Choose a permutation $\tau$ of the nodes sending every node of colour $c$ to a node of colour $b$.
nodes.statement_short: Map colour $c$ nodes to colour $b$ nodes.

nodes.name: Counting pairs
nodes.statement: For every node $v$, the sample pairs that make $v$ end in colour $c$ are at most as many as those that make $\tau(v)$ end in colour $b$: a node of another colour adopts a colour of size $m$ on the $m^2$ pairs with both samples on it, a node of that colour keeps it on the $n^2-S+m^2$ pairs that do not agree on another colour, and both counts increase with $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare favourable sample-pair counts.

nodes.name: Pair embedding
nodes.statement: Choose a permutation of the sample pairs embedding the first set into the second.
nodes.statement_short: Embed favourable pairs.

nodes.name: Bijection
nodes.statement: The induced bijection of rounds preserves the uniform distribution and maps the rounds with $c_c'\ge t$ into the rounds with $c_b'\ge t$.
nodes.statement_short: Measure-preserving map of rounds gives domination.

nodes.name: Correction note
nodes.statement: The paper's coupling, read literally, needs a minor correction (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/median/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#remarks-on-the-sources}{details}).
nodes.statement_short: Paper's coupling needs a minor correction.

nodes.name: One round of the growth phase
nodes.statement_short: In one growth round the leading colour does not shrink and its lead over every colour grows by $1+a/(8n)$ w.h.p.
assumptions: colour $i$ has $a=c_i\le3n/4$ nodes and leads every other colour by at least $g\ge z\sqrt{n\log n}$
conclusions: with probability at least $1-C/n^2$ after one round $a'\ge a$ and colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $g(1+a/(8n))$
nodes.statement: There are constants $z,C>0$ such that, whenever $\log n\ge C$: if colour $i$ has $a=c_i\le3n/4$ nodes and leads every other colour by at least $g\ge z\sqrt{n\log n}$, then with probability at least $1-C/n^2$ after one round $a'\ge a$ and colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $g(1+a/(8n))$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-growth-round

nodes.statement_short: Expected gap growth via Observation 2.1 and one-round expectations; Bernstein concentration per colour; union bound over colours.
nodes.statement: Take $z=128$ and $C=2$, and let $b$ be the second largest colour. For every other colour $j$, Observation~2.1 gives $\E c_j'\le\E b'$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-expect} $\E(a'-c_j')\ge(a-b)(1+(a/n)(1-a/n))\ge g(1+a/(4n))$ since $a\le3n/4$. Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-conc} with $\lambda=ga/(8n)$ bounds the failure for $j$ by $n^{-12}$. The aggregation bound gives $\E a'-a\ge ag/(4n)$, so $a'<a$ has probability at most $n^{-12}$. A union bound over the at most $n$ colours present gives the failure probability $2/n^2$. This replaces the coupling of Lemma~2.3, and the range $a\le3n/4$ (instead of $n/2$) closes the gap before the two-colour phase.

nodes.name: Expected gap
nodes.statement: Take $z=128$ and $C=2$, and let $b$ be the second largest colour. For every other colour $j$, Observation~2.1 gives $\E c_j'\le\E b'$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-expect} $\E(a'-c_j')\ge(a-b)(1+(a/n)(1-a/n))\ge g(1+a/(4n))$ since $a\le3n/4$.
nodes.statement_short: Observation 2.1 and expectations bound the expected gap growth.

nodes.name: Concentration
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-conc} with $\lambda=ga/(8n)$ bounds the failure for $j$ by $n^{-12}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bernstein tail per colour.

nodes.name: Leader does not shrink
nodes.statement: The aggregation bound gives $\E a'-a\ge ag/(4n)$, so $a'<a$ has probability at most $n^{-12}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expected growth of the leader.

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: A union bound over the at most $n$ colours present gives the failure probability $2/n^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over colours.

nodes.name: Remark
nodes.statement: This replaces the coupling of Lemma~2.3, and the range $a\le3n/4$ (instead of $n/2$) closes the gap before the two-colour phase.
nodes.statement_short: Replaces the paper's coupling.

nodes.name: The growth phase
nodes.statement_short: A leading colour reaches $3n/4$ nodes within $O((n/c_i)\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.
assumptions: colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $z\sqrt{n\log n}$
conclusions: after $\lceil C(n/c_i)\log n\rceil$ rounds it holds at least $3n/4$ nodes with probability at least $1-C/n$
nodes.statement: There are constants $z,C>0$ such that, whenever $\log n\ge C$: if colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $z\sqrt{n\log n}$, then after $\lceil C(n/c_i)\log n\rceil$ rounds it holds at least $3n/4$ nodes with probability at least $1-C/n$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-growth-phase

nodes.statement_short: Moving targets with geometrically growing lead, each kept per round w.h.p.; the lead cannot exceed $n$, forcing $3n/4$.
nodes.statement: Take $z=C=128$, $a_0=c_i$, $g_0$ the initial lead and $q=1+a_0/(8n)$. Consider the moving targets ``colour $i$ holds $3n/4$ nodes, or it holds at least $a_0$ nodes and leads every other colour by $g_0q^t$''. Each round leaves them with probability at most $2/n^2$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-round} while $a\le3n/4$, and because a colour holding $3n/4$ nodes keeps them except with probability $n^{-2}$ (Bernstein, drift from the aggregation bound). Since $q^{\lceil128(n/a_0)\log n\rceil}>n$, a lead of $g_0q^t$ is impossible at the end, so the colour holds $3n/4$ nodes.

nodes.name: Moving targets
nodes.statement: Take $z=C=128$, $a_0=c_i$, $g_0$ the initial lead and $q=1+a_0/(8n)$. Consider the moving targets ``colour $i$ holds $3n/4$ nodes, or it holds at least $a_0$ nodes and leads every other colour by $g_0q^t$''.
nodes.statement_short: Fix constants and define moving targets.

nodes.name: Per-round failure
nodes.statement: Each round leaves them with probability at most $2/n^2$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-round} while $a\le3n/4$, and because a colour holding $3n/4$ nodes keeps them except with probability $n^{-2}$ (Bernstein, drift from the aggregation bound).
nodes.statement_short: One-round lemma and Bernstein for staying.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $q^{\lceil128(n/a_0)\log n\rceil}>n$, a lead of $g_0q^t$ is impossible at the end, so the colour holds $3n/4$ nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Lead cannot exceed $n$, so $3n/4$ is reached.

nodes.name: Finishing phase
nodes.statement_short: A colour holding $3n/4$ nodes wins within $\lceil128\log n\rceil$ rounds w.p. $\ge1-128/n$.
conclusions: all nodes hold $i$ after $\lceil128\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-128/n$
nodes.statement: If $\log n\ge128$ and colour $i$ holds at least $3n/4$ nodes, all nodes hold $i$ after $\lceil128\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-128/n$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-finish

nodes.statement_short: Dominate by the binary median process and apply the 2-Choices w.h.p. theorem.
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-basic}, colour $i$ dominates the binary median process started from its indicator, whose gap is at least $n/2\ge128\sqrt{n\log n}$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:whp}.

nodes.name: Plurality consensus (Theorem 1.2 without the adversary)
nodes.origin_citation: Elsässer, Friedetzky, Kaaser, Mallmann-Trenn, Trinker, arXiv:1602.04667 (Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement_short: With $k$ colours, a plurality lead of $z\sqrt{n\log n}$ gives consensus within $O((n/c_i)\log n)\le O(k\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.
assumptions: $\log n\ge C$, for every number $k$ of colours
colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $z\sqrt{n\log n}$
conclusions: all nodes hold $i$ after $\lceil C(n/c_i)\log n\rceil$ rounds, and hence after $\lceil Ck\log n\rceil$ rounds, with probability at least $1-C/n$
nodes.statement: There are constants $z,C>0$ such that, whenever $\log n\ge C$, for every number $k$ of colours: if colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $z\sqrt{n\log n}$, all nodes hold $i$ after $\lceil C(n/c_i)\log n\rceil$ rounds, and hence after $\lceil Ck\log n\rceil$ rounds, with probability at least $1-C/n$.
nodes.label: thm:tc-plurality

nodes.statement_short: Growth phase then finishing phase; consensus is absorbing; $c_i\ge n/k$ for the second form.
nodes.statement: Take $z=128$ and $C=384$: Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-phase}, then Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-finish} from the configuration reached, with failure at most $256/n$; consensus is absorbing, so more rounds do not hurt. For the second form, $c_i\ge n/k$. The paper's proof of Theorem~1.2 needs a minor correction (the range $n/2<a<(1/2+\varepsilon_1)n$ and the time bound), which Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-round} supplies.

nodes.name: Growth then finish
nodes.statement: Take $z=128$ and $C=384$: Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-phase}, then Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-finish} from the configuration reached, with failure at most $256/n$; consensus is absorbing, so more rounds do not hurt.
nodes.statement_short: Apply growth and finishing lemmas.

nodes.name: Second form
nodes.statement: For the second form, $c_i\ge n/k$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $c_i\ge n/k$.

nodes.name: Correction note
nodes.statement: The paper's proof of Theorem~1.2 needs a minor correction (the range $n/2<a<(1/2+\varepsilon_1)n$ and the time bound), which Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-round} supplies.
nodes.statement_short: Paper's proof needs minor correction.

nodes.name: Two colours and almost-sure consensus
nodes.statement_short: Two-colour 2-Choices from a $C\sqrt{n\log n}$ gap wins in $O(\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.; with finitely many colours consensus is a.s.
conclusions: With two colours, a gap of $C\sqrt{n\log n}$ gives consensus on the majority after $\lceil C\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-C/n$, whenever $\log n\ge C$
With finitely many colours, consensus is reached almost surely
nodes.statement: With two colours, a gap of $C\sqrt{n\log n}$ gives consensus on the majority after $\lceil C\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-C/n$, whenever $\log n\ge C$. With finitely many colours, consensus is reached almost surely.
nodes.label: thm:tc-two

nodes.statement_short: Two colours reduce to the binary median process; a positive-probability consensus round plus the absorption theorem.
nodes.statement: On two colours the process is the binary median process (Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-basic}); apply Theorem~\ref{thm:whp}. The round in which every node samples node $0$ twice gives consensus and has positive probability; conclude with the shared absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Few nodes change colour
nodes.statement_short: MGF of $\mathrm{twice}_i$, expected number of disagreeing sample pairs, and at most $\ell$ expected colour changes when colours are small.
conclusions: $\E e^{\theta\,\mathrm{twice}_i}=(1+(c_i/n)^2(e^\theta-1))^n$
The expected number of nodes whose two samples hold different colours is $n-S/n$
if every colour has at most $\ell$ nodes, the expected number of nodes that change colour is at most $\ell$
nodes.statement: The number of nodes that see colour $i$ twice is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli variables of parameter $(c_i/n)^2$, so $\E e^{\theta\,\mathrm{twice}_i}=(1+(c_i/n)^2(e^\theta-1))^n$. The expected number of nodes whose two samples hold different colours is $n-S/n$, and if every colour has at most $\ell$ nodes, the expected number of nodes that change colour is at most $\ell$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-few-changes

nodes.statement_short: Independence of samples; agreement probability $S/n^2$ and $S\le\ell n$.
nodes.statement: The samples of different nodes are independent. Two samples hold the same colour with probability $S/n^2$, and only such nodes can change colour; $S\le\ell n$.

nodes.name: One colour does not grow fast
nodes.statement_short: A colour starting at most $L$ exceeds $L$ within $T$ rounds with probability at most $\exp(-(L-c_i)+(e-1)TL^2/n)$.
conclusions: for every $T$, the probability that $c_i(t)>L$ for some $t\le T$ is at most $\exp(-(L-c_i)+(e-1)TL^2/n)$
nodes.statement: If $c_i\le L$, then for every $T$, the probability that $c_i(t)>L$ for some $t\le T$ is at most $\exp(-(L-c_i)+(e-1)TL^2/n)$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-escape

nodes.statement_short: Induction on the horizon with a stopped exponential supermartingale, then Markov's inequality.
nodes.statement: Induction on the horizon. While $c_i\le L$, $c_i'\le c_i+\mathrm{twice}_i$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-basic}) and, with $\theta=1$, $\E e^{\mathrm{twice}_i}\le\exp((e-1)n(c_i/n)^2)\le\exp((e-1)L^2/n)$, so $e^{c_i(t)-(e-1)tL^2/n}$, stopped when $c_i$ exceeds $L$, is a supermartingale; conclude with Markov's inequality. This replaces the paper's domination by a process with binomial increments.

nodes.name: Induction
nodes.statement: Induction on the horizon.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the horizon.

nodes.name: Supermartingale
nodes.statement: While $c_i\le L$, $c_i'\le c_i+\mathrm{twice}_i$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-basic}) and, with $\theta=1$, $\E e^{\mathrm{twice}_i}\le\exp((e-1)n(c_i/n)^2)\le\exp((e-1)L^2/n)$, so $e^{c_i(t)-(e-1)tL^2/n}$, stopped when $c_i$ exceeds $L$, is a supermartingale; conclude with Markov's inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Stopped exponential supermartingale and Markov.

nodes.name: Remark
nodes.statement: This replaces the paper's domination by a process with binomial increments.
nodes.statement_short: Replaces the paper's binomial domination.

nodes.name: Theorem 5 of Berenbrink et al.
nodes.origin_citation: Berenbrink, Clementi, Elsässer, Kling, Mallmann-Trenn, Natale, PODC 2017 (Theorem 5)
nodes.statement_short: From small colours, no colour exceeds $\max\{2\ell,\gamma\log n\}$ for $n/(\gamma\ell')$ rounds except with probability $1/n$.
assumptions: every colour has at most $\ell$ nodes, $\ell'=\max\{2\ell,\gamma\log n\}$ and $T<n/(\gamma\ell')$
conclusions: the probability that some colour has more than $\ell'$ nodes at some time $t\le T$ is at most $1/n$
nodes.statement: There is a constant $\gamma_0$ such that for every $\gamma\ge\gamma_0$: if every colour has at most $\ell$ nodes, $\ell'=\max\{2\ell,\gamma\log n\}$ and $T<n/(\gamma\ell')$, the probability that some colour has more than $\ell'$ nodes at some time $t\le T$ is at most $1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:tc-lower-strong

nodes.statement_short: Apply the escape lemma with $L=\ell'$ per colour and union bound over colours.
nodes.statement: Take $\gamma_0=8$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-escape} with $L=\ell'$, since $L-c_i\ge\ell'/2$ and $T\ell'^2/n<\ell'/\gamma$, one colour exceeds $\ell'$ with probability at most $\exp(-\ell'(1/2-(e-1)/\gamma))\le n^{-2}$; take a union bound over the at most $n$ colours present. A constant in the paper's proof needs a minor correction ($\gamma\ge36$ instead of $\gamma\ge18$ in its Chernoff step); the theorem is unaffected.

nodes.name: Escape and union bound
nodes.statement: Take $\gamma_0=8$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-escape} with $L=\ell'$, since $L-c_i\ge\ell'/2$ and $T\ell'^2/n<\ell'/\gamma$, one colour exceeds $\ell'$ with probability at most $\exp(-\ell'(1/2-(e-1)/\gamma))\le n^{-2}$; take a union bound over the at most $n$ colours present.
nodes.statement_short: Escape lemma per colour and union bound.

nodes.name: Correction note
nodes.statement: A constant in the paper's proof needs a minor correction ($\gamma\ge36$ instead of $\gamma\ge18$ in its Chernoff step); the theorem is unaffected.
nodes.statement_short: Constant correction in the paper.

nodes.name: 2-Choices needs Omega(n/log n) rounds
nodes.origin_citation: Berenbrink, Clementi, Elsässer, Kling, Mallmann-Trenn, Natale, PODC 2017 (Theorem 1, Simplified)
nodes.statement_short: From colours of size $O(\log n)$, 2-Choices needs $\Omega(n/\log n)$ rounds to reach consensus w.h.p.
assumptions: every configuration in which every colour has at most $\beta\log n$ nodes
conclusions: 2-Choices reaches consensus at some time $t\le T$ with probability at most $1/n$
nodes.statement: For every $\beta>0$ there is $C>0$ such that, from every configuration in which every colour has at most $\beta\log n$ nodes, 2-Choices reaches consensus at some time $t\le T$ with probability at most $1/n$, for every $T$ with $(T+1)C\log n<n$.
nodes.label: thm:tc-lower

nodes.statement_short: Choose $\gamma$ and $C$ so Theorem 5's window contains $T$; consensus would need a colour with $n>\ell'$ nodes.
nodes.statement: Take $\gamma=\max\{8,2\beta\}$ and $C=\gamma^2$. Then $\ell'=\gamma\log n$, the window of Theorem~\ref{thm:tc-lower-strong} contains $T$, and consensus would put $n>\ell'$ nodes on one colour.

nodes.name: Birth-death Moran process
nodes.statement_short: Fitness-proportional parent choice, offspring placed on a uniform neighbour.
nodes.statement: Mutants have fitness $r>0$ and residents fitness $1$. A step chooses a parent $u$ with probability proportional to its fitness and an offspring position $w$ uniformly among the neighbours of $u$ (or $w=u$ if $u$ is isolated); the individual at $w$ is replaced by a copy of the parent.
nodes.label: def:moran

nodes.name: The kernel is well defined
conclusions: The weights of (parent, offspring position) pairs are nonnegative and sum to one
nodes.statement: The weights of (parent, offspring position) pairs are nonnegative and sum to one.
nodes.label: lem:well-defined

nodes.statement_short: Sum over offspring positions first, then fitness over total fitness.
nodes.statement: Sum over the offspring position first: each parent's placement weights sum to one. The remaining sum of fitnesses over the total fitness is one.

nodes.name: Birth mass is $r$ times death mass
nodes.statement_short: On regular graphs the probability of gaining a mutant is $r$ times the probability of losing one.
conclusions: the probability that a step adds a mutant equals $r$ times the probability that it removes one
nodes.statement: On a $d$-regular graph, the probability that a step adds a mutant equals $r$ times the probability that it removes one: both are proportional to the number of edges between the two types, counted from either side.
nodes.label: lem:birth-death

nodes.statement_short: Both masses are the symmetric oriented cut divided by $Fd$; trivial for $d=0$.
nodes.statement: For $d>0$ both masses are the oriented cut divided by $Fd$, weighted by the parent's fitness; the cut is symmetric under swapping endpoints. For $d=0$ both masses vanish.

nodes.name: Invariant potentials
nodes.statement_short: On regular graphs $(1/r)^{\#\text{mutants}}$ (or the mutant count when $r=1$) is a martingale.
conclusions: $(1/r)^{\#\text{mutants}}$ is preserved in expectation by one step
when $r=1$, so is the number of mutants
nodes.statement: On a regular graph, $(1/r)^{\#\text{mutants}}$ is preserved in expectation by one step; when $r=1$, so is the number of mutants.
nodes.label: thm:invariance

nodes.statement_short: The expected change is affine in birth and death masses, which cancel by the birth-death lemma.
nodes.statement: A step changes the number of mutants by $\pm1$ or not at all, so its expectation is affine in the birth and death masses, and these cancel by the previous lemma.

nodes.name: Fixation or extinction
nodes.statement_short: On connected graphs the Moran process is absorbed (fixation or extinction) with probability one.
conclusions: the probability that neither type has taken over tends to zero
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, the probability that neither type has taken over tends to zero.
nodes.label: thm:absorption

nodes.statement_short: Fixation is reachable from every mixed state by induction on residents; apply the finite-chain absorption theorem.
nodes.statement: Constant configurations are absorbing. From a mixed configuration, a mutant adjacent to a resident (which exists by connectivity) reproduces onto it with positive probability; by induction on the number of residents, fixation is reachable. Apply the shared finite-chain absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Absorbing states
nodes.statement: Constant configurations are absorbing.
nodes.statement_short: Constant configurations are absorbing.

nodes.name: Reachability
nodes.statement: From a mixed configuration, a mutant adjacent to a resident (which exists by connectivity) reproduces onto it with positive probability; by induction on the number of residents, fixation is reachable.
nodes.statement_short: Fixation reachable by induction.

nodes.name: Absorption theorem
nodes.statement: Apply the shared finite-chain absorption theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the finite-chain absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Absorption theorem
nodes.statement: Apply the shared finite-chain absorption theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Apply finite-chain absorption.

nodes.name: Fixation from an invariant
nodes.statement_short: An invariant observable equal to 1 at fixation and 0 at extinction equals the fixation probability, given absorption.
assumptions: an observable be invariant in expectation, equal to $1$ on the all-mutant and to $0$ on the all-resident configuration
the all-mutant configuration is absorbing and the probability that neither type has taken over tends to zero
conclusions: the observable is the fixation probability
nodes.statement: Let an observable be invariant in expectation, equal to $1$ on the all-mutant and to $0$ on the all-resident configuration. If the all-mutant configuration is absorbing and the probability that neither type has taken over tends to zero, the observable is the fixation probability.
nodes.label: lem:fixation-limit

nodes.statement_short: Finite-horizon optional stopping from the shared dynamics package with the two constant configurations as targets.
nodes.statement: This is the finite-horizon optional stopping theorem of the shared \texttt{dynamics} package (\texttt{Dynamics.Kernel.iSup\_event\_of\_invariant}, roadmap FND-4) with the two constant configurations as targets: the fixation and unfixed indicators are the corresponding events.

nodes.name: Isothermal theorem
nodes.statement_short: On connected regular graphs the fixation probability of $k$ mutants equals Moran's $(1-r^{-k})/(1-r^{-n})$.
assumptions: On a connected regular graph with $r\neq1$
conclusions: the fixation probability from $k$ mutants is $(1-r^{-k})/(1-r^{-n})$
nodes.statement: On a connected regular graph with $r\neq1$, the fixation probability from $k$ mutants is $(1-r^{-k})/(1-r^{-n})$.
nodes.label: thm:isothermal

nodes.statement_short: Apply the fixation-from-invariant lemma to the normalized potential $(1/r)^{\#\text{mutants}}$, with invariance and absorption theorems.
nodes.statement: Apply the previous lemma to $\psi=(1-(1/r)^{\#\text{mutants}})/(1-(1/r)^n)$, invariant by the invariance theorem and equal to $1$ and $0$ on the two constant configurations; the absorption theorem gives the vanishing survival probability.

nodes.name: Isothermal theorem, neutral case
assumptions: On a connected regular graph with $r=1$
conclusions: the fixation probability is $k/n$
nodes.statement: On a connected regular graph with $r=1$, the fixation probability is $k/n$.
nodes.label: thm:neutral

nodes.statement_short: Same argument with the potential $\#\text{mutants}/n$.
nodes.statement: The same argument with $\psi=\#\text{mutants}/n$.

nodes.name: Moran's formula
conclusions: the fixation probability from $k$ mutants is $(1-r^{-k})/(1-r^{-n})$
nodes.statement: On the complete graph, the fixation probability from $k$ mutants is $(1-r^{-k})/(1-r^{-n})$.
nodes.label: thm:moran

nodes.statement_short: The complete graph is connected and regular; apply the isothermal theorem.
nodes.statement: The complete graph is connected and $(n-1)$-regular.
The converse of the isothermal theorem does not hold in general (Galanis, Göbel, Goldberg, Lapinskas and Richerby, Proposition~12), so only this direction is formalized.
nodes.name: Converse of the isothermal theorem fails
Death-Birth (pull) kernel
nodes.statement_short: A uniform vertex copies a uniform neighbour; neutral push is the Moran kernel with $r=1$.
nodes.statement: In one pull (death--Birth) step, a uniformly random vertex $u$ adopts the type of a uniformly random neighbour $w$ (an isolated vertex keeps its type), so the pair $(u,w)$ has weight $\frac1n\cdot\frac1{\deg u}$ for $w\sim u$. The neutral push (Birth--death) process is the Moran kernel with $r=1$.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: def:pull

nodes.name: Reproductive values
nodes.statement: For a configuration with mutant set $S$, $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}(S)=\sum_{v\in S}1/\deg v$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}(S)=\sum_{v\in S}\deg v$.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: def:repro

nodes.name: Reproductive values are invariant
nodes.statement_short: Degree-weighted mutant counts ($1/\deg$ for push, $\deg$ for pull) are martingales on every finite graph.
conclusions: $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}$ is invariant in expectation under neutral push
$\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}$ is invariant in expectation under pull
nodes.statement: On every finite graph, $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}$ is invariant in expectation under neutral push and $\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}$ is invariant in expectation under pull.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: thm:pushpull-invariance

nodes.statement_short: Expected changes are sums of antisymmetric functions over ordered adjacent pairs, hence vanish.
nodes.statement: Write $x_v\in\{0,1\}$ for the type of $v$. Under push, the pair (parent $u$, target $w\sim u$) has weight $\frac1n\frac1{\deg u}$ and changes $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}$ by $(x_u-x_w)/\deg w$, so the expected change is $\frac1n\sum_{u\sim w}(x_u-x_w)/(\deg u\deg w)$. Under pull, $u$ copies $w\sim u$ with weight $\frac1n\frac1{\deg u}$ and changes $\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}$ by $(x_w-x_u)\deg u$, so the expected change is $\frac1n\sum_{u\sim w}(x_w-x_u)$. Both sums are over ordered adjacent pairs of an antisymmetric function, hence vanish.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Push
nodes.statement: Write $x_v\in\{0,1\}$ for the type of $v$. Under push, the pair (parent $u$, target $w\sim u$) has weight $\frac1n\frac1{\deg u}$ and changes $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}$ by $(x_u-x_w)/\deg w$, so the expected change is $\frac1n\sum_{u\sim w}(x_u-x_w)/(\deg u\deg w)$.
nodes.statement_short: Expected change under push.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Pull
nodes.statement: Under pull, $u$ copies $w\sim u$ with weight $\frac1n\frac1{\deg u}$ and changes $\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}$ by $(x_w-x_u)\deg u$, so the expected change is $\frac1n\sum_{u\sim w}(x_w-x_u)$.
nodes.statement_short: Expected change under pull.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Antisymmetry
nodes.statement: Both sums are over ordered adjacent pairs of an antisymmetric function, hence vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Antisymmetric sums vanish.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Fixation or extinction under pull
conclusions: the probability that the pull process has not reached a constant configuration after $t$ steps tends to $0$
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, the probability that the pull process has not reached a constant configuration after $t$ steps tends to $0$.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: thm:pull-absorption

nodes.statement_short: Constant configurations are absorbing and reachable with positive probability; apply the shared absorption theorem.
nodes.statement: As for push: constant configurations are absorbing, and from any other configuration a resident adjacent to a mutant copies it with positive probability, so the number of mutants reaches $n$ with positive probability; the shared absorption theorem concludes.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Push and pull fixation
nodes.statement_short: Neutral push fixes $S$ with probability proportional to $\sum_{v\in S}1/\deg v$; pull with probability $\sum_{v\in S}\deg v/(2|E|)$.
assumptions: On a connected graph with at least two vertices
conclusions: the fixation probability of a mutant set $S$ is $\sum_{v\in S}\frac1{\deg v}\big/\sum_{v\in V}\frac1{\deg v}$ under neutral push and $\sum_{v\in S}\deg v/(2|E|)$ under pull
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with at least two vertices, the fixation probability of a mutant set $S$ is $\sum_{v\in S}\frac1{\deg v}\big/\sum_{v\in V}\frac1{\deg v}$ under neutral push and $\sum_{v\in S}\deg v/(2|E|)$ under pull.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: thm:pushpull

nodes.statement_short: Apply the fixation-limit lemma to the normalized reproductive values.
nodes.statement: Apply the fixation-limit lemma to the normalized reproductive values, which are invariant and equal to $1$ and $0$ on the two constant configurations; the denominators are positive because every degree is at least $1$.
nodes.section: 61 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.statement: The star with $n$ leaves is Mathlib's \texttt{starGraph} $c$ on $n+1$ vertices: the centre $c$ is adjacent to every leaf and leaves only to $c$.
nodes.name: Star graph

nodes.statement: Write \[ q=\frac{n+r}{r(nr+1)},\qquad \kappa=\frac{nr+1}{r(n+r)}=\frac1{r^2q}. \]
nodes.name: Star parameters $q$ and $\kappa$
Star potential
nodes.statement: For a configuration with $i$ mutant leaves, $\Phi=q^i$ if the centre is a resident and $\Phi=\kappa q^i$ if it is a mutant.
nodes.label: def:star-potential

nodes.name: The star potential is invariant
conclusions: $\Phi$ is invariant in expectation under one Birth--death step on the star
nodes.statement: For every $r>0$, $\Phi$ is invariant in expectation under one Birth--death step on the star.
nodes.label: thm:star-invariance

nodes.statement_short: Only centre-leaf pairs carry weight; along each edge the two contributions cancel by the choice of $q$ and $\kappa$.
nodes.statement: Only the ordered pairs $(c,\ell)$ and $(\ell,c)$ for a leaf $\ell$ carry weight, namely $\mathrm{fit}(c)/(nF)$ and $\mathrm{fit}(\ell)/F$. Along each edge the two contributions cancel: if $\ell$ is a mutant and $c$ a resident they give $\frac{q^{i-1}}F\big(\frac{1-q}n+rq(\kappa-1)\big)=0$, and if $c$ is a mutant and $\ell$ a resident they give $\frac{q^i}F\big(1-\kappa+\frac{r\kappa(q-1)}n\big)=0$; equal types change nothing.

nodes.name: Fixation on the star
nodes.statement_short: Exact fixation probability on the star via the normalized star potential, from a leaf, the centre, or a random vertex.
conclusions: the fixation probability from $s$ is $(1-\Phi(s))/(1-\kappa q^n)$
A single mutant fixes with probability $(1-q)/(1-\kappa q^n)$ from a leaf, $(1-\kappa)/(1-\kappa q^n)$ from the centre, and $(n(1-q)+(1-\kappa))/((n+1)(1-\kappa q^n))$ from a uniformly random vertex
nodes.statement: For $r\ne1$, the fixation probability from $s$ is $(1-\Phi(s))/(1-\kappa q^n)$. A single mutant fixes with probability $(1-q)/(1-\kappa q^n)$ from a leaf, $(1-\kappa)/(1-\kappa q^n)$ from the centre, and $(n(1-q)+(1-\kappa))/((n+1)(1-\kappa q^n))$ from a uniformly random vertex.
nodes.label: thm:star

nodes.statement_short: Bound the potential between $\kappa q^n$ and $1$ so the normalized potential is in $[0,1]$; apply the fixation-limit lemma.
nodes.statement: For $r>1$ we have $q\le1$ and $\kappa<1$, so $\kappa q^n\le\Phi\le1$; for $r<1$ all inequalities reverse. Hence the normalized potential is $1$ at fixation, $0$ at extinction and in $[0,1]$ otherwise, and the fixation-limit lemma applies.

nodes.name: Broom-Rychtář formula
nodes.statement_short: Closed formula with a geometric sum for the star fixation probability from a uniformly random vertex.
conclusions: a single mutant at a uniformly random vertex fixes with probability
nodes.statement: For every $r>0$, a single mutant at a uniformly random vertex fixes with probability \[ \frac{n\cdot\frac{nr}{nr+1}+\frac r{r+n}}{(n+1)\big(1+\frac n{n+r}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}q^j\big)}. \]
nodes.label: thm:star-sum

nodes.statement_short: Sum the geometric series for $r\ne1$; handle $r=1$ by push-pull fixation and $n=0$ directly.
nodes.statement: For $r\ne1$ and $n\ge1$, sum the geometric series: $1+\frac n{n+r}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}q^j= r^2(1-\kappa q^n)/(r^2-1)$. For $r=1$ both sides are $1/(n+1)$, by push--pull fixation; for $n=0$ both are $1$.

nodes.name: The star is an amplifier of selection
nodes.statement_short: On stars with $n\ge2$ leaves, advantageous mutants fix more often and disadvantageous ones less often than under Moran's formula.
conclusions: the fixation probability from a uniformly random vertex is larger than Moran's $(1-1/r)/(1-r^{-(n+1)})$ for $r>1$ and smaller for $0<r<1$
nodes.statement: For every $n\ge2$, the fixation probability from a uniformly random vertex is larger than Moran's $(1-1/r)/(1-r^{-(n+1)})$ for $r>1$ and smaller for $0<r<1$.
nodes.label: thm:star-amplifier

nodes.statement_short: Substitute $s=1/r$, reduce the sign of the difference via Bernoulli's inequality to a polynomial inequality with positive slack.
nodes.statement: Put $s=1/r$ and $t=(1+ns)/(n+s)$, so that $q=st$ and $\kappa=s/t$. The difference has the sign of $(1-s)\big(E(1-s^{n+1})-s^{n+1}(1-t^{n-1})\big)$ with $E=s^2(n-1)^2/((n+s)(1+ns))$. By Bernoulli, $1-t^{n-1}\le(n-1)(1-t)=(n-1)^2(1-s)/(n+s)$, which reduces the claim to $s^{n-1}(1-s)(1+ns)<1-s^{n+1}$. Its slack is $\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}(1-s)(s^k-s^n)$, a nonempty sum of positive terms on both sides of $s=1$.

nodes.name: Substitution
nodes.statement: Put $s=1/r$ and $t=(1+ns)/(n+s)$, so that $q=st$ and $\kappa=s/t$. The difference has the sign of $(1-s)\big(E(1-s^{n+1})-s^{n+1}(1-t^{n-1})\big)$ with $E=s^2(n-1)^2/((n+s)(1+ns))$.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $s,t$ and find the sign of the difference.

nodes.name: Bernoulli
nodes.statement: By Bernoulli, $1-t^{n-1}\le(n-1)(1-t)=(n-1)^2(1-s)/(n+s)$, which reduces the claim to $s^{n-1}(1-s)(1+ns)<1-s^{n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Bernoulli's inequality.

nodes.name: Slack
nodes.statement: Its slack is $\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}(1-s)(s^k-s^n)$, a nonempty sum of positive terms on both sides of $s=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Slack is a positive sum.

nodes.name: Large stars amplify r to r^2
conclusions: the fixation probability from a uniformly random vertex of the star with $n$ leaves tends to $1-1/r^2$ as $n\to\infty$
nodes.statement: For $r>1$, the fixation probability from a uniformly random vertex of the star with $n$ leaves tends to $1-1/r^2$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.label: thm:star-limit

nodes.statement_short: Take limits of each term of the star fixation formula as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement: $n(1-q)/(n+1)=\frac n{n+1}\cdot\frac n{n+1/r}\cdot(1-r^{-2})\to1-r^{-2}$, $(1-\kappa)/(n+1)\to0$, and $0\le\kappa q^n\le r^{-n}\to0$ because $q\le1/r$ for $n\ge1$.

nodes.name: Coloring and k-color distribution
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014)
nodes.statement_short: A coloring assigns one of k colors to each of n nodes; c_j counts nodes of color j and c is the k-color distribution.
nodes.statement: A \emph{coloring} is a map $x \colon [n] \to [k]$. The number of nodes of color $j$ is $c_j = |\{v : x(v) = j\}|$, and $\sum_j c_j = n$. The vector $c = (c_1,\dots,c_k)$ is the paper's $k$-color distribution ($k$-cd).
nodes.label: def:config

nodes.name: 3-input rule and 3-majority rule
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014)
nodes.statement_short: A 3-input rule picks one of its three inputs; 3-majority returns the majority color, or the first if all differ.
nodes.statement: A \emph{3-input rule} is a map $f \colon [k]^3 \to [k]$ with $f(a,b,c) \in \{a,b,c\}$. The \emph{3-majority rule} is $\mathrm{maj}_3(a,b,c) = b$ if $b = c$ and $a$ otherwise; it returns the majority color, and the first color if all three differ.
nodes.label: def:rule

nodes.name: One round and the 3-majority process
nodes.statement_short: A round gives every node three uniform samples; the next coloring applies the rule f to their colors, iterated over T rounds.
nodes.statement: A round is a map $r \colon [n] \to [n]^3$ (the three samples of every node), drawn uniformly. The next coloring under rule $f$ is $v \mapsto f(x(r_v^1), x(r_v^2), x(r_v^3))$. The process after $T$ rounds folds this step over $T$ independent uniform rounds.
nodes.label: def:step

nodes.name: Consensus
nodes.statement_short: Consensus on m means every node has color m; it is absorbing for every 3-input rule.
nodes.statement: $x$ is in \emph{consensus on $m$} if every node has color $m$, i.e.\ $c_m = n$. For every 3-input rule, consensus is absorbing.
nodes.label: def:mono

nodes.name: Markov kernel of the process
nodes.statement_short: The process is the finite Markov kernel whose row at x is the law of one round from x.
nodes.statement: The process with rule $f$ is the finite Markov kernel on colorings whose row at $x$ is the law of one round of $f$ from $x$. Its $T$-step event probabilities are the expectations over $T$ independent uniform rounds.
nodes.label: def:kernel

nodes.name: Adoption probability
nodes.statement_short: Under 3-majority a node adopts color j with probability x_j^2 + x_j(1 - sum_h x_h^2), independently across nodes.
conclusions: The new count of color $j$ is a sum of $n$ independent indicators, one per node.
Under 3-majority, a node adopts $j$ with probability $x_j^2 + x_j(1 - \sum_h x_h^2)$
nodes.statement: The new count of color $j$ is a sum of $n$ independent indicators, one per node. Under 3-majority, a node adopts $j$ with probability $x_j^2 + x_j(1 - \sum_h x_h^2)$, where $x_h = c_h/n$.
nodes.label: lem:adopt

nodes.name: Proof of adoption probability
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: sum the majority indicator over the three independent samples.
nodes.statement: The three samples are independent with law $(x_h)_h$. Summing the indicator of $\mathrm{maj}_3(a,b,c) = j$ first over $c$, then $b$, then $a$ gives the polynomial.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1 (next expected coloring)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement_short: Expected next count of color j is c_j(1 + (n c_j - sum_h c_h^2)/n^2).
assumptions: For every coloring and every color $j$
conclusions: \mu_j(c) = \E[C_{j,t+1} \mid C_t = c] = c_j\Bigl(1 + \frac{1}{n^2}\Bigl(n c_j - \sum_h c_h^2\Bigr)\Bigr).
nodes.statement: For every coloring and every color $j$, \[ \mu_j(c) = \E[C_{j,t+1} \mid C_t = c] = c_j\Bigl(1 + \frac{1}{n^2}\Bigl(n c_j - \sum_h c_h^2\Bigr)\Bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:2_1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the per-node adoption probability by n.
nodes.statement: Multiply the adoption probability of Lemma~\ref{lem:adopt} by $n$.

nodes.name: Plurality, bias, alpha and gamma (Section 3 quantities)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Section 3
nodes.statement_short: Defines the plurality size m(c), plurality set M(c), bias s(c), and the quantities alpha(c), gamma(c) of a k-cd.
nodes.statement: For a $k$-cd $c$ with $\sum_h c_h = n$: $m(c) = \max_h c_h$, $M(c) = \{j : c_j = m(c)\}$, the \emph{bias} $s(c) = m(c) - \max_{h \notin M(c)} c_h$ if $|M(c)| = 1$ and $0$ otherwise, $\alpha(c) = (n - m(c))\,s(c)/n^2$ and $\gamma(c) = (n\,m(c) - \sum_h c_h^2)/n^2 - \alpha(c)$.
nodes.label: def:quantities

nodes.name: Every other color trails by the bias
nodes.statement_short: Every non-plurality color is at least s(c) below m(c), with an identity expressing gamma(c) n^2 as a sum.
conclusions: $c_h + s(c) \le m(c)$ for every $h \ne m$, with equality for some $h$ when $k \ge 2$
$\gamma(c)\,n^2 = \sum_{h \ne m} c_h\,(m(c) - s(c) - c_h)$
$c_h + s(c) \le m(c)$ for every $h \ne m$, with equality for some $h$ when $k \ge 2$
$\gamma(c)\,n^2 = \sum_{h \ne m} c_h\,(m(c) - s(c) - c_h)$

nodes.statement: If $c_m = m(c)$ then $c_h + s(c) \le m(c)$ for every $h \ne m$, with equality for some $h$ when $k \ge 2$. Moreover $\gamma(c)\,n^2 = \sum_{h \ne m} c_h\,(m(c) - s(c) - c_h)$.
nodes.label: lem:bias_gap

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement_short: Bounds on the bias s(c), alpha(c) <= min(s/n, 1/4) and gamma(c) <= 1/8.
conclusions: (b) $0 \le \alpha(c) \le \min\{s(c)/n,\ 1/4\}$
(c) $0 \le \gamma(c) \le 1/8$
nodes.statement: For every $k$-cd $c$: (a) $0 \le s(c) \le m(c) - (n - m(c))/(k-1)$; (b) $0 \le \alpha(c) \le \min\{s(c)/n,\ 1/4\}$; (c) $0 \le \gamma(c) \le 1/8$.
nodes.label: lem:3_1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement_short: Part-by-part elementary bounds; (c) uses the gamma identity of the bias-gap lemma.
nodes.statement: (a) The $k-1$ other colors each have at most $m(c) - s(c)$ nodes. (b) $(n - m)m \le n^2/4$ and $s \le m$. (c) Use the identity of Lemma~\ref{lem:bias_gap}: every summand is nonnegative, the color attaining the bias contributes $0$, and the rest is at most $d(n - m - d) \le n^2/8$ with $d = m(c) - s(c)$.

nodes.name: Bound s(c) by counting the other colors
nodes.statement: (a) The $k-1$ other colors each have at most $m(c) - s(c)$ nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Bound s(c) by counting the other colors

nodes.name: Bound alpha via (n-m)m <= n^2/4
nodes.statement: (b) $(n - m)m \le n^2/4$ and $s \le m$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound alpha via (n-m)m <= n^2/4

nodes.name: Bound gamma using the bias-gap identity
nodes.statement: (c) Use the identity of Lemma~\ref{lem:bias_gap}: every summand is nonnegative, the color attaining the bias contributes $0$, and the rest is at most $d(n - m - d) \le n^2/8$ with $d = m(c) - s(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound gamma using the bias-gap identity

nodes.name: Lemma 3.2
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement_short: Expected next counts of the plurality color, of any color, and of the runner-up in terms of gamma, alpha and the bias.
assumptions: $\ell \ne m$ have the most nodes among the other colors
conclusions: (a) $\mu_m(c) = c_m(1 + \gamma + \alpha)$
(b) $\mu_j(c) = c_j(1 + \gamma + \alpha - (m(c) - c_j)/n)$ for every $j$
(c) $\mu_\ell(c) = c_\ell(1 + \gamma + \alpha - s(c)/n)$
nodes.statement: Let $m \in M(c)$ and let $\ell \ne m$ have the most nodes among the other colors. Then (a) $\mu_m(c) = c_m(1 + \gamma + \alpha)$; (b) $\mu_j(c) = c_j(1 + \gamma + \alpha - (m(c) - c_j)/n)$ for every $j$; (c) $\mu_\ell(c) = c_\ell(1 + \gamma + \alpha - s(c)/n)$.
nodes.label: lem:3_2

nodes.name: Concentration for sums of independent coordinates (Bernstein, Hoeffding, Chernoff, Markov)
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited): Bernstein, Hoeffding, Chernoff and Markov inequalities
nodes.statement_short: Collects Bernstein, Hoeffding, multiplicative Chernoff lower tail, Markov and closed-form Chernoff upper tail for sums of independent coordinates.
conclusions: Bernstein's inequality $\Pr(X \ge \E X + \lambda) \le \exp(-\lambda^2/(2\sigma^2(1 + b\lambda/(3\sigma^2))))$ when $Y_i - \E Y_i \le b$ and $\sum_i \mathrm{Var}\,Y_i \le \sigma^2$
Hoeffding's inequality for $\{0,1\}$ coordinates
the multiplicative Chernoff lower tail $\Pr(X \le (1-\delta)\mu) \le \exp(-\delta^2\mu/2)$
Markov's inequality $\Pr(X \ge 1) \le \E X$ for nonnegative coordinates
the closed-form Chernoff upper tail $\Pr(X \ge k) \le \exp(k - \mu - k\log(k/\mu))$ for $\E X \le \mu \le k$
nodes.statement: For $X = \sum_i Y_i(\omega_i)$ with independent uniform coordinates: Bernstein's inequality $\Pr(X \ge \E X + \lambda) \le \exp(-\lambda^2/(2\sigma^2(1 + b\lambda/(3\sigma^2))))$ when $Y_i - \E Y_i \le b$ and $\sum_i \mathrm{Var}\,Y_i \le \sigma^2$; Hoeffding's inequality for $\{0,1\}$ coordinates; the multiplicative Chernoff lower tail $\Pr(X \le (1-\delta)\mu) \le \exp(-\delta^2\mu/2)$; Markov's inequality $\Pr(X \ge 1) \le \E X$ for nonnegative coordinates; and the closed-form Chernoff upper tail $\Pr(X \ge k) \le \exp(k - \mu - k\log(k/\mu))$ for $\E X \le \mu \le k$. All are proved once in the shared \texttt{dynamics} library (\texttt{Dynamics/Concentration.lean}, \texttt{Dynamics/Chernoff.lean}, \texttt{Dynamics/Tail.lean}).
nodes.label: lem:tails

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 (increasing rate of the bias)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement_short: With a unique plurality, the gap to any other color grows by factor about 1+gamma+c_m alpha/(2s) except with exponentially small probability.
conclusions: \le \exp\Bigl(-\frac{c_m\alpha(c)^2}{25}\Bigr).
nodes.statement: If $M(c) = \{m\}$ then for every $j \ne m$, \[ \Pr\Bigl(C_{m,t+1} - C_{j,t+1} \le s(c)\Bigl(1 + \gamma(c) + \frac{c_m\alpha(c)}{2s(c)}\Bigr) \Bigm| C_t = c\Bigr) \le \exp\Bigl(-\frac{c_m\alpha(c)^2}{25}\Bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:3_3

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound the expected gap via Lemmas 3.1-3.2, then apply Bernstein's inequality to the sum of per-node differences.
nodes.statement: By Lemmas~\ref{lem:3_1} and~\ref{lem:3_2}, $\E[C_{m,t+1} - C_{j,t+1}] \ge s(1+\gamma) + c_m\alpha$. The difference is a sum of per-node variables in $\{-1,0,1\}$ with variance at most $3c_m$; apply Bernstein's inequality with $b = 2$ and $\lambda = c_m\alpha/2$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.4
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement_short: The plurality count grows by factor 1+gamma+alpha/2 except with probability exp(-c_m alpha^2/11).
conclusions: $\Pr(C_{m,t+1} \le c_m(1 + \gamma + \alpha/2) \mid C_t = c) \le \exp(-c_m\alpha^2/11)$
nodes.statement: If $M(c) = \{m\}$ then $\Pr(C_{m,t+1} \le c_m(1 + \gamma + \alpha/2) \mid C_t = c) \le \exp(-c_m\alpha^2/11)$.
nodes.label: lem:3_4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicative Chernoff lower tail with a suitable delta.
nodes.statement: The multiplicative Chernoff lower tail with $\delta = \alpha/(2(1 + \gamma + \alpha))$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.5 (large plurality and large bias)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement_short: With large plurality and bias, both the gap growth by 1+lambda/6 and growth of c_m fail with probability at most 1/n^2.
conclusions: \Pr\bigl(C_{m,t+1} - C_{j,t+1} \le s(c)(1 + \lambda/6)\bigr) \le 1/n^2
\Pr\bigl(C_{m,t+1} \le c_m\bigr) \le 1/n^2
nodes.statement: If $M(c) = \{m\}$, $0 < \lambda \le 2/3$, $\lambda n \le c_m \le (2/3)n$ and $s(c) \ge 22\sqrt{(1/\lambda)\,n\log n}$, then for every $j \ne m$ \[ \Pr\bigl(C_{m,t+1} - C_{j,t+1} \le s(c)(1 + \lambda/6)\bigr) \le 1/n^2 \quad\text{and}\quad \Pr\bigl(C_{m,t+1} \le c_m\bigr) \le 1/n^2. \]
nodes.label: lem:3_5

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement_short: Check the hypotheses make the parameters of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4 large enough.
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses $c_m\alpha/(2s) \ge \lambda/6$ and $c_m\alpha^2/25 \ge 2\log n$; conclude with Lemmas~\ref{lem:3_3} and~\ref{lem:3_4}.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.6
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided bound on the expected number of nodes not of color m after one round.
conclusions: (n - c_m)\Bigl(1 - \frac{c_m^2}{n^2}\Bigr) \le \E[\bar C_{m,t+1} \mid C_t = c] \le (n - c_m)\Bigl(1 - \frac{s(c)\,c_m}{n^2}\Bigr).
nodes.statement: For every $m \in M(c)$, writing $\bar C_{m,t+1} = n - C_{m,t+1}$, \[ (n - c_m)\Bigl(1 - \frac{c_m^2}{n^2}\Bigr) \le \E[\bar C_{m,t+1} \mid C_t = c] \le (n - c_m)\Bigl(1 - \frac{s(c)\,c_m}{n^2}\Bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:3_6

nodes.name: Lemma 3.7 (very large plurality)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 3.7
nodes.statement_short: With very large plurality, dissenters shrink by 17/18 w.h.p.; below n^{1/4} log n they vanish with probability 1 - n^{-1/5}.
conclusions: $\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} \ge n^{1/4}\log n) \le 1/n^2$
$\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} \ge n^{1/4}\log n) \le 1/n^2$

nodes.statement: Let $\log n \ge 40$, $M(c) = \{m\}$. (i) If $s(c) \ge n/3$ and $n - c_m \ge n^{1/4}\log n$ then $\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} \ge \frac{17}{18}(n - c_m)) \le 1/n^2$. (ii) If $n - c_m < n^{1/4}\log n$ then $\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} > 0) \le n^{-1/5}$ and $\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} \ge n^{1/4}\log n) \le 1/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:3_7

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.7
nodes.statement_short: Bound the expected dissenters with Lemma 3.6, then apply the Chernoff upper tail (i) and Markov's inequality (ii).
nodes.statement: The paper omits this proof. (i) By Lemma~\ref{lem:3_6} and $s\,c_m \ge n^2/9$, $\E\bar C_{m,t+1} \le \frac89(n - c_m)$; apply the closed-form Chernoff upper tail at ratio $17/16$. (ii) Here $s(c) \ge n - 2(n - c_m)$, so $\E\bar C_{m,t+1} \le 3(n-c_m)^2/n \le 3\log^2 n\, e^{-(\log n)/2}$; apply Markov's inequality for the first bound and the Chernoff upper tail for the second.

nodes.name: Lemma A.4 (nested phases)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma A.4
nodes.statement_short: For nested sets of a Markov chain that are sticky and successively reachable, the chain reaches the last set in lT steps with probability 1 - T(l eps + nu^l).
assumptions: $A_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq A_T$ be sets of states of a finite Markov chain such that from every state of $A_i$ the chain stays in $A_i$ with probability $\ge 1-\varepsilon$ and, for $i < T$, moves into $A_{i+1}$ with probability $\ge 1 - \nu$
conclusions: from any state of $A_1$, after $\ell T$ steps the chain is in $A_T$ with probability at least $1 - T(\ell\varepsilon + \nu^\ell)$
nodes.statement: Let $A_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq A_T$ be sets of states of a finite Markov chain such that from every state of $A_i$ the chain stays in $A_i$ with probability $\ge 1-\varepsilon$ and, for $i < T$, moves into $A_{i+1}$ with probability $\ge 1 - \nu$. Then from any state of $A_1$, after $\ell T$ steps the chain is in $A_T$ with probability at least $1 - T(\ell\varepsilon + \nu^\ell)$.

nodes.label: lem:A_4

nodes.name: Growth and saturation phases
nodes.statement_short: Defines nested growth phases (bias at least Lambda q^i), saturation phases (few dissenters) and the consensus phase.
nodes.statement: Fix $m$, $\lambda$, $\Lambda$ and let $q = 1 + 1/(6\lambda)$, $B = n^{1/4}\log n$. \emph{Growth phase $i$}: $c_m > \frac23 n$, or $M(c) = \{m\}$, $c_m \ge n/\lambda$ and $s(c) \ge \Lambda q^i$. \emph{Saturation phase $j$}: $n - c_m < \max\{\frac n3 (\frac{17}{18})^j,\ B\}$. \emph{Consensus}: $c_m = n$.
nodes.section: 65.5 Nested phases and the main theorem
nodes.label: def:phases

nodes.name: Saturation phases differ from the paper
nodes.statement_short: Saturation phases here only bound n - c_m < n/3, which already implies a unique plurality with bias n/3, unlike the paper's unpreserved condition.
nodes.statement: The paper's saturation phases also require $s(c) \ge n/3$, which Lemma~\ref{lem:3_7} does not show to be preserved. Here the saturation phases only bound $n - c_m < n/3$, which already implies $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge n/3$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:dissent}).
nodes.section: 65.5 Nested phases and the main theorem

nodes.name: A clear majority
nodes.statement_short: Fewer than n/3 dissenters, or a lead of g, gives a unique plurality with bias n/3 (resp. g); empty colors stay empty.
assumptions: $m$ leads every other color by at least $g > 0$ and $c_m \ge g$
conclusions: $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge n/3$
$M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge g$
A color without nodes stays without nodes.
$M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge n/3$

assumptions: $m$ leads every other color by at least $g > 0$ and $c_m \ge g$
conclusions: $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge g$
A color without nodes stays without nodes.

nodes.statement: If $n - c_m < n/3$ then $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge n/3$. If $m$ leads every other color by at least $g > 0$ and $c_m \ge g$, then $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge g$. A color without nodes stays without nodes.

nodes.label: lem:dissent

nodes.name: One round of each phase
nodes.statement_short: Each growth and saturation phase advances to the next with high probability in one round; the phases are nested.
conclusions: From growth phase $i$ the chain enters growth phase $i+1$ with probability $\ge 1 - 1/n$.
From saturation phase $j$ it enters saturation phase $j+1$ with probability $\ge 1 - 1/n^2$.
From fewer than $B$ dissenting nodes it reaches consensus with probability $\ge 1 - n^{-1/5}$, and consensus is kept with probability $1$.
The phase sets are nested, and growth phase $i$ lies in saturation phase $0$ once $\Lambda q^i > n$.
nodes.statement: Let $\log n \ge 40$, $k \ge 2$, $\lambda \ge 3$ and $\Lambda \ge 22\sqrt{\lambda n \log n}$. From growth phase $i$ the chain enters growth phase $i+1$ with probability $\ge 1 - 1/n$. From saturation phase $j$ it enters saturation phase $j+1$ with probability $\ge 1 - 1/n^2$. From fewer than $B$ dissenting nodes it reaches consensus with probability $\ge 1 - n^{-1/5}$, and consensus is kept with probability $1$. The phase sets are nested, and growth phase $i$ lies in saturation phase $0$ once $\Lambda q^i > n$.
nodes.section: 65.5 Nested phases and the main theorem
nodes.label: lem:phase_steps

nodes.name: Proof of one round of each phase
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis by phase: growth uses Lemma 3.5 with a union bound over colors; saturation uses Lemma 3.7.
nodes.statement: \emph{Growth, case $c_m > \frac23 n$}: saturation phase $0$ moves into saturation phase $1$, which lies in $\{c_m > \frac23 n\}$. \emph{Growth, otherwise}: apply Lemma~\ref{lem:3_5} with $1/\lambda$ to each other color $j$ that currently has a node, and to the growth of $c_m$. There are fewer than $n - c_m$ such colors, so a union bound gives failure probability at most $n/n^2$. Colors without nodes stay empty, and the color attaining the bias has a node (otherwise $c_m = n$), so after a successful round $m$ leads every other color by $s(c)\,q$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:dissent} applies. \emph{Saturation}: Lemma~\ref{lem:3_7}(i) above $B$ dissenters and Lemma~\ref{lem:3_7}(ii) below.
nodes.section: 65.5 Nested phases and the main theorem

nodes.name: Growth phase with c_m > 2n/3 reduces to saturation
nodes.statement: \emph{Growth, case $c_m > \frac23 n$}: saturation phase $0$ moves into saturation phase $1$, which lies in $\{c_m > \frac23 n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Growth phase with c_m > 2n/3 reduces to saturation

nodes.name: Growth otherwise: Lemma 3.5 plus union bound over colors

There are fewer than $n - c_m$ such colors, so a union bound gives failure probability at most $n/n^2$. Colors without nodes stay empty, and the color attaining the bias has a node (otherwise $c_m = n$), so after a successful round $m$ leads every other color by $s(c)\,q$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:dissent} applies.

nodes.name: Number of phases
nodes.statement_short: The total number of phases T = T1 + T2 + 1 is at most 13 lambda log n.
assumptions: $T_2 = \lceil \log n/\log(18/17)\rceil + 1$ saturation phases and one consensus phase
conclusions: $T = T_1 + T_2 + 1 \le 13\lambda\log n$
nodes.statement: With $T_1 = \lceil \log n/\log q\rceil$ growth phases, $T_2 = \lceil \log n/\log(18/17)\rceil + 1$ saturation phases and one consensus phase, $T = T_1 + T_2 + 1 \le 13\lambda\log n$ for $\lambda \ge 3$ and $\log n \ge 40$.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.8 (general upper bound for 3-majority plurality consensus)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Theorem 3.8 (repaired)
nodes.statement_short: With a unique plurality of size >= n/lambda and bias >= 22 sqrt(lambda n log n), 3-majority reaches consensus in O(lambda log n) rounds w.h.p.
conclusions: after $10T \le 130\lambda\log n$ rounds all nodes support $m$ with probability at least $1 - 11T/n \ge 1 - 143\lambda\log n/n$
nodes.statement: Let $\log n \ge 40$, $k \ge 2$ and $\lambda \ge 3$. If $M(c) = \{m\}$, $c_m \ge n/\lambda$ and $s(c) \ge 22\sqrt{\lambda n\log n}$, then after $10T \le 130\lambda\log n$ rounds all nodes support $m$ with probability at least $1 - 11T/n \ge 1 - 143\lambda\log n/n$.
nodes.section: 65.5 Nested phases and the main theorem
nodes.label: thm:3_8

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.8
nodes.statement_short: Apply the nested-phases Lemma A.4 to the growth, saturation and consensus phases with eps = 1/n, nu = n^{-1/5}, l = 10.
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:A_4} to the kernel of 3-majority with the $T_1$ growth phases, the $T_2$ saturation phases and consensus, $\varepsilon = 1/n$, $\nu = n^{-1/5}$ and $\ell = 10$, so that $\nu^\ell = n^{-2}$. The initial coloring is in growth phase $0$; growth phase $T_1$ lies in saturation phase $0$ because $\Lambda q^{T_1} \ge 22n$; saturation phase $T_2 - 1$ lies below $B$ dissenters because $\frac n3(\frac{17}{18})^{T_2-1} \le \frac13$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.10
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate Theorem 3.8 with lambda = min{2k,(n/log n)^{1/3}}, checking c_m >= n/lambda and lambda >= 3.
nodes.statement: Take $\lambda = \min\{2k, (n/\log n)^{1/3}\}$. If $\lambda = 2k$ then $c_m \ge n/k$ by pigeonhole; otherwise $\lambda^3 = n/\log n$, so $22\sqrt{\lambda n\log n} = 22n/\lambda$ and $c_m \ge s(c) \ge n/\lambda$. Moreover $\lambda \ge 3$ because $k \ge 2$ and $n = e^{\log n} \ge 27\log n$.

nodes.section: 65.5 Nested phases and the main theorem

nodes.name: Binary case of 3-majority
nodes.statement_short: With two colors the process is the binary 3-majority process, so a 3/5 majority wins in O(log n) rounds with probability 1 - 500/n.
conclusions: the set of nodes of color $1$ evolves exactly as the binary 3-majority process of the \texttt{three\_majority} package
all nodes support color $1$ after $O(\log n)$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 500/n$
nodes.statement: With $k = 2$ the set of nodes of color $1$ evolves exactly as the binary 3-majority process of the \texttt{three\_majority} package. Hence, if $c_1 \ge \frac35 n$ and $\log n \ge 30$, all nodes support color $1$ after $O(\log n)$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 500/n$.
nodes.label: thm:binary

nodes.name: Two opinions from a vanishing bias
nodes.statement_short: A binary majority leading by 22 sqrt(3 n log n) wins within 390 log n rounds with probability 1 - 429 log n/n.
assumptions: the initial majority leads by at least $22\sqrt{3n\log n}$ nodes
conclusions: all nodes adopt it within at most $390\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 429\log n/n$
nodes.statement: In the binary 3-majority process, if the initial majority leads by at least $22\sqrt{3n\log n}$ nodes (a fraction $\frac12 + O(\sqrt{\log n/n})$) and $\log n \ge 40$, all nodes adopt it within at most $390\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 429\log n/n$.
nodes.label: cor:binary_vanishing

nodes.name: Proof of two opinions from a vanishing bias
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.8 with k = 2 and lambda = 3, transferred to the binary process by the binary-case theorem.
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:3_8} with $k = 2$ and $\lambda = 3$: the majority color is the unique plurality, holds more than $n/2 \ge n/3$ nodes, and its bias is the gap; the conclusion transfers to the binary process through Theorem~\ref{thm:binary}.

nodes.name: Opinion-1 set and gap
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be the set of nodes with opinion $1$ and $s = |I| - (n - |I|)$ the gap.

nodes.name: One-round gap and its expectation
nodes.statement_short: The next gap s' is 2 sum_v Y_v - n with independent Bernoulli(3x^2 - 2x^3) indicators, so E s' = s(3/2 - s^2/(2n^2)).
nodes.statement: After one round, $s' = 2\sum_v Y_v - n$ for independent $\{0,1\}$-valued $Y_v$ with mean $p = 3x^2 - 2x^3$, $x = |I|/n$, so $\mathbb{E}s' = s\,(3/2 - s^2/(2n^2))$.

nodes.name: Jump near balance
nodes.statement_short: Near balance the gap jumps to at least sqrt(n)/5 in one round with probability at least 9/64.
conclusions: $|s'| \ge \sqrt n/5$ with probability at least $9/64$
nodes.statement: If $n \ge 5$ and $|s| \le 4\sqrt n/25$, then $|s'| \ge \sqrt n/5$ with probability at least $9/64$.
nodes.label: lem:jump_near_balance

nodes.name: Proof of jump near balance
nodes.statement_short: Paley-Zygmund on the centered sum, using variance >= n/5 and a fourth-moment bound.
nodes.statement: The centered sum $S = \sum_v (Y_v - p)$ has variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p) \ge n/5$ and fourth moment at most $\sigma^2 + 3\sigma^4$, so by Paley--Zygmund $4S^2 \ge \sigma^2$ with probability at least $9/64$. Then $|s'| = |2S + \mathbb{E}s'| \ge \sqrt{n/5} - \frac32|s| \ge \sqrt n/5$.

nodes.name: Growth away from balance
nodes.statement_short: Away from balance the gap grows by factor 11/8 up to 2 lambda with probability 1 - e^{-2 lambda^2/n}.
conclusions: $s' > \frac{11}{8}s - 2\lambda$ with probability at least $1 - e^{-2\lambda^2/n}$
nodes.statement: If $0 \le s \le n/2$ and $\lambda \ge 0$, then $s' > \frac{11}{8}s - 2\lambda$ with probability at least $1 - e^{-2\lambda^2/n}$.
nodes.label: lem:growth_far

nodes.name: Proof of growth away from balance
nodes.statement_short: Bound the expected gap below by 11/8 s and apply Hoeffding's inequality.
nodes.statement: $\mathbb{E}s' \ge \frac{11}{8}s$ for $0 \le s \le n/2$, and Hoeffding's inequality bounds the lower tail of $\sum_v Y_v$.

nodes.name: Symmetry breaking
nodes.statement_short: From any configuration the gap reaches 22 sqrt(3 n log n) within O(log n) rounds with probability 1 - 1/n.
conclusions: There is $C > 0$ such that
the gap reaches $22\sqrt{3n\log n}$ in absolute value within any $t \ge C\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 1/n$
nodes.statement: There is $C > 0$ such that, for $\log n \ge 40$, from any configuration the gap reaches $22\sqrt{3n\log n}$ in absolute value within any $t \ge C\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:symmetry_breaking

nodes.name: Proof of symmetry breaking
nodes.statement_short: Drift hitting-time bound of Doerr et al. applied to a discretized gap, with the jump and growth lemmas supplying drift in each regime.
nodes.statement: Apply the hitting-time bound of Doerr et al.\ (their Claim~2.9, \texttt{Dynamics.Kernel.drift\_hitting\_log}) to $X = \lfloor |s|/(\sqrt n/100)\rfloor$ with $q = n$, $c_1 = 5/4$, $c_2 = 1/320000$, $c_3 = 9/64$, $c_4 = 1000$, $c_6 = 1$; by the symmetry between the opinions assume $s \ge 0$. If $X = 0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:jump_near_balance} gives $X' \ge 20 \ge 1$ with probability $9/64$. If $1 \le X < 16$, the same lemma gives $X' \ge 20 \ge \frac54 X$ with probability $9/64 \ge 1 - e^{-X/320000}$. If $16 \le X < 1000\log n$, then $s \le n/2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:growth_far} with $\lambda = X\sqrt n/3200$ gives $s' > \frac{21}{16}X\sqrt n/100$, hence $X' \ge \frac54 X$, except with probability $e^{-X^2/5120000} \le e^{-X/320000}$. Reaching $X \ge 1000\log n$ means $|s| \ge 10\sqrt n\log n \ge 22\sqrt{3n\log n}$.

nodes.name: Set up the drift hitting-time bound for the scaled gap
nodes.statement: Apply the hitting-time bound of Doerr et al.\ (their Claim~2.9, \texttt{Dynamics.Kernel.drift\_hitting\_log}) to $X = \lfloor |s|/(\sqrt n/100)\rfloor$ with $q = n$, $c_1 = 5/4$, $c_2 = 1/320000$, $c_3 = 9/64$, $c_4 = 1000$, $c_6 = 1$; by the symmetry between the opinions assume $s \ge 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the drift hitting-time bound for the scaled gap

nodes.name: Case X = 0: jump near balance
nodes.statement: If $X = 0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:jump_near_balance} gives $X' \ge 20 \ge 1$ with probability $9/64$.
nodes.statement_short: Case X = 0: jump near balance

nodes.name: Case 1 <= X < 16: jump near balance again
nodes.statement: If $1 \le X < 16$, the same lemma gives $X' \ge 20 \ge \frac54 X$ with probability $9/64 \ge 1 - e^{-X/320000}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case 1 <= X < 16: jump near balance again

nodes.name: Case 16 <= X < 1000 log n: growth away from balance
nodes.statement: If $16 \le X < 1000\log n$, then $s \le n/2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:growth_far} with $\lambda = X\sqrt n/3200$ gives $s' > \frac{21}{16}X\sqrt n/100$, hence $X' \ge \frac54 X$, except with probability $e^{-X^2/5120000} \le e^{-X/320000}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case 16 <= X < 1000 log n: growth away from balance

nodes.name: Translate the hit back to the gap threshold
nodes.statement: Reaching $X \ge 1000\log n$ means $|s| \ge 10\sqrt n\log n \ge 22\sqrt{3n\log n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate the hit back to the gap threshold

nodes.name: Hit, then absorb
nodes.statement_short: Hitting a set from which an absorbing event is likely, then waiting, composes probabilities; two blocks give failure delta*eps.
assumptions: $P$ be an absorbing event of a finite Markov chain
from every state of $B$ the chain is in $P$ after $T$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$
from every state the chain is in $P$ after $T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$
from $a$ after $T_0$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta$
conclusions: from any state it is in $P$ at time $t + T$ with probability at least $\Pr(T_B \le t) - \varepsilon$
from $a$ it is in $P$ after $T_0 + T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta\varepsilon$

assumptions: from every state of $B$ the chain is in $P$ after $T$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$
conclusions: from any state it is in $P$ at time $t + T$ with probability at least $\Pr(T_B \le t) - \varepsilon$

assumptions: from every state the chain is in $P$ after $T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$
from $a$ after $T_0$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta$
conclusions: from $a$ it is in $P$ after $T_0 + T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta\varepsilon$

nodes.statement: Let $P$ be an absorbing event of a finite Markov chain. If from every state of $B$ the chain is in $P$ after $T$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$, then from any state it is in $P$ at time $t + T$ with probability at least $\Pr(T_B \le t) - \varepsilon$. If moreover from every state the chain is in $P$ after $T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$, and from $a$ after $T_0$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta$, then from $a$ it is in $P$ after $T_0 + T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: lem:hit_absorb

nodes.name: Proof of hit, then absorb
nodes.statement_short: Induction on t via the recursion for the hitting probability; second claim by the Markov property.
nodes.statement: The first claim by induction on $t$, through the recursion of $\Pr(T_B \le t)$ and the monotonicity in time of an absorbing event; the second by the Markov property at time $T_0$.

nodes.name: Two opinions from any configuration
nodes.statement_short: Binary 3-majority reaches consensus from any configuration, even balanced, in O(log n) rounds with probability 1 - O(log n/n), and 1 - 1/n for large n.
assumptions: from any configuration (in particular from a perfectly balanced one)
conclusions: all nodes hold the same opinion after any $T \ge C\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - C\log n/n$
for $\log n \ge C$, with probability at least $1 - 1/n$
nodes.statement: There is $C > 0$ such that, for $\log n \ge 40$, from any configuration (in particular from a perfectly balanced one) all nodes hold the same opinion after any $T \ge C\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - C\log n/n$; and, for $\log n \ge C$, with probability at least $1 - 1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:any_start

nodes.name: Proof of two opinions from any configuration
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry breaking followed by the vanishing-bias corollary, composed by the hit-then-absorb lemma; two blocks for the 1/n bound.
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetry_breaking}, then Corollary~\ref{cor:binary_vanishing} applied to the set of nodes of opinion $1$ or to its complement, composed by Lemma~\ref{lem:hit_absorb}; consensus on either opinion is absorbing, so further rounds keep it. For the second bound, two consecutive blocks each fail with probability at most $\varepsilon = C_0\log n/n$, and $\varepsilon^2 \le 1/n$.

nodes.name: Escaping a moving target
nodes.statement_short: If each round leaves the moving target set with probability at most p, after T rounds the process is outside it with probability at most Tp.
assumptions: for every $t < T$, one round from any state of $G_t$ misses $G_{t+1}$ with probability at most $p$
conclusions: after $T$ rounds it lies outside $G_T$ with probability at most $Tp$
nodes.statement: If a round-based process starts in $G_0$ and, for every $t < T$, one round from any state of $G_t$ misses $G_{t+1}$ with probability at most $p$, then after $T$ rounds it lies outside $G_T$ with probability at most $Tp$.
nodes.label: lem:escape

nodes.name: Proof of escaping a moving target
nodes.statement_short: Induction on T, conditioning on the first round.
nodes.statement: Induction on $T$, conditioning on the first round.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.1
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement_short: A color with at most n/k + b nodes exceeds n/k + (1+3/k)b after one round with probability at most 1/n^2.
conclusions: $\Pr(C_{j,t+1} \ge n/k + (1 + 3/k)b \mid C_t = c) \le 1/n^2$
nodes.statement: Let $k\sqrt{n\log n} \le b \le n/k$. If $c_j \le n/k + b$, then $\Pr(C_{j,t+1} \ge n/k + (1 + 3/k)b \mid C_t = c) \le 1/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:4_1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
