nodes.statement_short: Bound the expected count via Cauchy-Schwarz, then apply Hoeffding's inequality.
nodes.statement: By Cauchy--Schwarz $\sum_h c_h^2 \ge n^2/k$, so $\mu_j \le c_j(1 + c_j/n - 1/k)$. Writing $c_j = n/k + a$ with $a \le b$, this is at most $n/k + (1+1/k)b + b^2/n \le n/k + (1+2/k)b$. Hoeffding's inequality with deviation $b/k \ge \sqrt{n\log n}$ gives $1/n^2$.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz bound on the expected count
nodes.statement: By Cauchy--Schwarz $\sum_h c_h^2 \ge n^2/k$, so $\mu_j \le c_j(1 + c_j/n - 1/k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz bound on the expected count

nodes.name: Simplify the expected-count bound
nodes.statement: Writing $c_j = n/k + a$ with $a \le b$, this is at most $n/k + (1+1/k)b + b^2/n \le n/k + (1+2/k)b$.
nodes.statement_short: Simplify the expected-count bound

nodes.name: Apply Hoeffding's inequality
nodes.statement: Hoeffding's inequality with deviation $b/k \ge \sqrt{n\log n}$ gives $1/n^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Hoeffding's inequality

nodes.name: Theorem 4.2 (lower bound for 3-majority)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement_short: From nearly balanced k colors, 3-majority is monochromatic after T <= (k/3) log(n/(kb)) rounds with probability at most kT/n^2.
assumptions: every color starts with at most $n/k + b$ nodes, where $b \ge k\sqrt{n\log n}$
conclusions: the coloring after $T$ rounds is monochromatic with probability at most $kT/n^2$
nodes.statement: Let $k \ge 3$ and suppose every color starts with at most $n/k + b$ nodes, where $b \ge k\sqrt{n\log n}$. If $b(1 + 3/k)^T \le n/k$, in particular if $T \le \frac k3 \log\frac{n}{kb}$, then the coloring after $T$ rounds is monochromatic with probability at most $kT/n^2$.
nodes.label: thm:4_2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement_short: For each color apply the moving-target lemma with geometric thresholds and Lemma 4.1 per round; union over colors.
nodes.statement: For each color apply Lemma~\ref{lem:escape} to the thresholds $n/k + b(1+3/k)^t$, with Lemma~\ref{lem:4_1} for each round. A monochromatic coloring has a color with $n > 2n/k$ nodes, above its final threshold; sum over the $k$ colors.

nodes.name: Range of the lower bound
nodes.statement_short: The bound gives Omega(k log n) rounds only for k <= n^{1/4-delta}; the paper's claimed range and adaptive thresholds are flawed.
nodes.statement: With $b = \max\{(n/k)^{1-\varepsilon}, k\sqrt{n\log n}\}$ this gives $\Omega(k\log(n/(kb)))$ rounds, which is $\Omega(k\log n)$ for $k \le n^{1/4-\delta}$. The paper states $\Omega(k\log n)$ for all $k \le (n/\log n)^{1/4}$, but at that end $n/k = k\sqrt{n\log n}$ and the argument gives nothing. The paper's proof also chooses the thresholds after seeing the trajectory; the union bound needs the fixed schedule used here.

nodes.name: Conservative, clear-majority and uniform rules; Delta, delta and solvers
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Section 4
nodes.statement_short: Properties of 3-input rules: conservative, clear-majority, the counts Delta_r and delta_c, uniformity, and (s,eps)-solvers of plurality consensus.
nodes.statement: A rule is \emph{conservative} if it returns one of its inputs. It has the \emph{clear-majority} property if it returns the majority color whenever two inputs agree. For colors $r \ne b$, $\Delta_r$ counts the orderings of $(r,r,b)$ on which the rule returns $r$. For distinct $r,g,b$, $\delta_c$ counts the orderings of $(r,g,b)$ on which it returns $c$; the rule is \emph{uniform} if $\delta_r = 2$ for all distinct triples. It is an \emph{$(s,\varepsilon)$-solver} if from every coloring whose unique plurality color $m$ has bias at least $s$, consensus on $m$ is eventually reached with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: def:good_rules

nodes.name: Consensus needs survival
nodes.statement_short: Under a conservative rule an extinct color never returns, so consensus on m at time T is bounded by m surviving at time T_0.
conclusions: a color without nodes never returns
for all $T, T_0$, the probability of consensus on $m$ at time $T$ is at most the probability that $m$ has a node at time $T_0$
nodes.statement: Under a conservative rule a color without nodes never returns. Hence for all $T, T_0$, the probability of consensus on $m$ at time $T$ is at most the probability that $m$ has a node at time $T_0$.
nodes.label: lem:alive

nodes.name: Theorem 4.8(a) (clear majority)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Theorem 4.8(a)
nodes.statement_short: For two colors the adoption drift is x(1-x)(x(Delta_r-2)+(1-x)(2-Delta_b)); hence an (n/4,1/4)-solver has Delta_r = Delta_b = 3 or both <= 1.
assumptions: only colors $r, b$ present and $x$ the fraction of $r$
for an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver and every pair $r \ne b$
conclusions: a node adopts $r$ with probability $p(x)$, where $p(x) - x = x(1-x)\bigl(x(\Delta_r - 2) + (1-x)(2 - \Delta_b)\bigr)$
the number of $r$ nodes is a supermartingale, so from $5n/8$ nodes of $r$ (bias $n/4$) consensus on $r$ has probability at most $5/8$ at every time: the rule is not an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver
either $\Delta_r = \Delta_b = 3$ or $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$
a node adopts $r$ with probability $p(x)$, where $p(x) - x = x(1-x)\bigl(x(\Delta_r - 2) + (1-x)(2 - \Delta_b)\bigr)$
the number of $r$ nodes is a supermartingale, so from $5n/8$ nodes of $r$ (bias $n/4$) consensus on $r$ has probability at most $5/8$ at every time: the rule is not an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver

assumptions: for an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver and every pair $r \ne b$
conclusions: either $\Delta_r = \Delta_b = 3$ or $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$

nodes.statement: Let $8 \mid n$. With only colors $r, b$ present and $x$ the fraction of $r$, a node adopts $r$ with probability $p(x)$, where $p(x) - x = x(1-x)\bigl(x(\Delta_r - 2) + (1-x)(2 - \Delta_b)\bigr)$. If $\Delta_r \le 2 \le \Delta_b$, the number of $r$ nodes is a supermartingale, so from $5n/8$ nodes of $r$ (bias $n/4$) consensus on $r$ has probability at most $5/8$ at every time: the rule is not an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver. Consequently, for an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver and every pair $r \ne b$, either $\Delta_r = \Delta_b = 3$ or $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$.
nodes.label: thm:4_8_a

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.8(a)
nodes.statement_short: Supermartingale by induction on T, then Markov's inequality on X_T.
nodes.statement: $\E[X_T] \le X_0$ by induction on $T$, and $\Pr(X_T = n) \le \E[X_T]/n$.

nodes.name: The unformalized case of Theorem 4.8(a)
nodes.statement_short: The paper's claim that solvers have the clear-majority property fails for Delta_r, Delta_b <= 1 when red is the minority; not formalized.
nodes.statement: The paper claims that an $(n/4,1/4)$-solver has the clear-majority property, i.e.\ that $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$ is also impossible. Its proof uses the supermartingale property, but checks it only when red is the majority; for $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$ it fails when red is the minority, because the process is pulled to the interior point $x^* = (2 - \Delta_b)/(4 - \Delta_r - \Delta_b)$. That case is not formalized.

nodes.name: Adopting r among three colors
nodes.statement_short: With delta_r <= 1, color r's adoption probability is at most 0.97x for x <= 2/5, and it exceeds 2n/5 after a round only with probability e^{-9n/31250}.
assumptions: the rule be conservative with the clear-majority property
only $r, g, b$ be present and $\delta_r \le 1$
conclusions: $p(r) \le 3x^2 - 2x^3 + \delta_r x_r x_g x_b \le x(3x - 2x^2 + (1-x)^2/4)$
which is at most $0.97x$ for $x \le 2/5$
from $x \le 2/5$ one round ends above $2n/5$ with probability at most $e^{-9n/31250}$
nodes.statement: Let the rule be conservative with the clear-majority property, let only $r, g, b$ be present and $\delta_r \le 1$. Then $p(r) \le 3x^2 - 2x^3 + \delta_r x_r x_g x_b \le x(3x - 2x^2 + (1-x)^2/4)$, which is at most $0.97x$ for $x \le 2/5$; and from $x \le 2/5$ one round ends above $2n/5$ with probability at most $e^{-9n/31250}$.
nodes.label: lem:adopt3

nodes.name: Color r dies out
nodes.statement_short: Starting below 2n/5, color r survives T rounds with probability at most 0.97^T c_r + T e^{-9n/31250}.
assumptions: starting with at most $2n/5$ nodes of $r$
conclusions: the probability that $r$ still has a node after $T$ rounds is at most $0.97^T c_r + T e^{-9n/31250}$
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:adopt3}, starting with at most $2n/5$ nodes of $r$, the probability that $r$ still has a node after $T$ rounds is at most $0.97^T c_r + T e^{-9n/31250}$.
nodes.label: lem:extinct

nodes.name: Proof that r dies out
nodes.statement_short: Freeze the chain once r exceeds 2n/5; the potential C_r 1[C_r <= 2n/5] contracts by 0.97 and freezing is rare.
nodes.statement: Consider the chain frozen once $r$ exceeds $2n/5$. On it, $\Phi = C_r\,\mathbb 1[C_r \le 2n/5]$ contracts by $0.97$ in every state, it is frozen within $T$ rounds with probability at most $Te^{-9n/31250}$, and it agrees with the real chain until it is frozen.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.8(b) (uniform property)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Theorem 4.8(b)
nodes.statement_short: A clear-majority rule that is an (n/20,1/4)-solver must be uniform.
assumptions: A rule with the clear-majority property that is an $(n/20, 1/4)$-solver
conclusions: has the uniform property
nodes.statement: Let $60 \mid n$ and $\log n \ge 20$. A rule with the clear-majority property that is an $(n/20, 1/4)$-solver has the uniform property.
nodes.label: thm:4_8_b

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.8(b)
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a non-uniform triple has a color with delta_r <= 1, which dies out from a plurality start, so consensus on r is unlikely.
nodes.statement: If a triple is not uniform, some color $r$ of it has $\delta_r \le 1$, since the three counts sum to $6$. Start from $23n/60$ nodes of $r$, $n/3$ of $g$ and $17n/60$ of $b$: $r$ is the unique plurality color with bias $n/20$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:extinct} and~\ref{lem:alive}, with $T_0 = \lceil\log(8n)/\log(100/97)\rceil$, consensus on $r$ has probability at most $1/8 + 1/8$ at every time.

nodes.name: A non-uniform triple has a color with delta_r <= 1
nodes.statement: If a triple is not uniform, some color $r$ of it has $\delta_r \le 1$, since the three counts sum to $6$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-uniform triple has a color with delta_r <= 1

nodes.name: Choose a start where r is plurality with bias n/20
nodes.statement: Start from $23n/60$ nodes of $r$, $n/3$ of $g$ and $17n/60$ of $b$: $r$ is the unique plurality color with bias $n/20$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a start where r is plurality with bias n/20

nodes.name: Extinction plus survival lemma bound consensus on r
nodes.statement: By Lemmas~\ref{lem:extinct} and~\ref{lem:alive}, with $T_0 = \lceil\log(8n)/\log(100/97)\rceil$, consensus on $r$ has probability at most $1/8 + 1/8$ at every time.
nodes.statement_short: Extinction plus survival lemma bound consensus on r

nodes.name: The paper's proof of Lemma 4.10 is a sketch
nodes.statement_short: The paper only sketches special cases; the formal proof covers every non-uniform triple rigorously.
nodes.statement: The paper's proof (Lemma 4.10) is a sketch that treats $\delta_r = 1$ with $(\delta_g,\delta_b) \in \{(3,2),(4,1)\}$ and asserts that $r$ ``will not converge'' by iterating a one-round estimate. The proof here covers every non-uniform triple and makes the iteration rigorous.

nodes.name: h-plurality rule
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Section 4.3
nodes.statement_short: Each node samples h nodes and adopts a most frequent color, ties broken by a random ordering of the sample positions.
nodes.statement: Every node samples $h$ nodes and a uniformly random ordering $\sigma$ of the $h$ sample positions, and adopts the color of the position of smallest $\sigma$-rank among those whose color is most frequent. All tied colors appear equally often, so each is chosen with the same probability.
nodes.label: def:hplur

nodes.name: Adoption under h-plurality
nodes.statement_short: Under h-plurality a node adopts j with probability at most x_j + (h^2/2) x_j^2.
conclusions: A node adopts $j$ with probability at most $x_j + \frac{h^2}{2}x_j^2$.
nodes.statement: A node adopts $j$ with probability at most $x_j + \frac{h^2}{2}x_j^2$.
nodes.label: lem:hadopt

nodes.name: Proof of adoption under h-plurality
nodes.statement_short: Split on whether j is seen once (probability x_j) or at least twice (second factorial moment).
nodes.statement: If $j$ wins and is seen exactly once, all $h$ sampled colors are distinct and $j$ is at the position ranked first, which has probability $x_j$. Otherwise $j$ is seen at least twice, and $\Pr(N_j \ge 2) \le \E[N_j(N_j-1)]/2 = \binom h2 x_j^2$.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.11
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Lemma 4.11 (corrected factor)
nodes.statement_short: Under h-plurality a color of size at most a grows beyond a(1+2h^2/k) with probability exp(-2(a h^2/k)^2/n).
conclusions: which is at most $e^{-2nh^4/k^4}$ when $a \ge n/k$
nodes.statement: If $c_j \le a \le 2n/k$, then $\Pr(C_{j,t+1} \ge a(1 + 2h^2/k)) \le \exp(-2(ah^2/k)^2/n)$, which is at most $e^{-2nh^4/k^4}$ when $a \ge n/k$.
nodes.label: lem:4_11

nodes.name: Corrected factor in Lemma 4.11
nodes.statement_short: The paper's factor 1+h^2/k should be 1+2h^2/k, and c_j <= a is needed by the proof of Theorem 4.12.
nodes.statement: The paper states the factor $1 + h^2/k$ but its proof gives $1 + 2h^2/k$, which is also what Theorem~\ref{thm:4_12} uses. Allowing $c_j \le a$ instead of $c_j = a$ covers colors below $n/k$, which the paper's proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:4_12} needs but the lemma excludes.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.12 (lower bound for h-plurality)
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri, Trevisan (SPAA 2014), Theorem 4.12
nodes.statement_short: From nearly balanced colors, h-plurality is monochromatic after T <= (k/(2h^2)) log(4/3) rounds with probability at most kT e^{-2nh^4/k^4}.
assumptions: every color starts with at most $\frac32\cdot\frac nk$ nodes
conclusions: after $T$ rounds of $h$-plurality the coloring is monochromatic with probability at most $kT e^{-2nh^4/k^4}$
nodes.statement: Let $k \ge 3$. If every color starts with at most $\frac32\cdot\frac nk$ nodes and $T \le \frac{k}{2h^2}\log\frac43$, then after $T$ rounds of $h$-plurality the coloring is monochromatic with probability at most $kT e^{-2nh^4/k^4}$.
nodes.label: thm:4_12

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.12
nodes.statement_short: As for Theorem 4.2, with geometric thresholds (3/2)(n/k)(1+2h^2/k)^t.
nodes.statement: As for Theorem~\ref{thm:4_2}, with thresholds $\frac32\cdot\frac nk(1 + 2h^2/k)^t \le 2n/k$.

nodes.name: Vertex set of the complete graph
nodes.statement: Fix $n \ge 2$ and let $V = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ be the vertex set of the complete graph $K_n$.

nodes.name: Round configuration (push protocol)
nodes.statement_short: A round configuration assigns each node a uniformly random target among the other n-1 nodes; R_n is the uniform set of these.
nodes.statement: A \emph{round configuration} is a function $\omega \colon V \to V$ with $\omega(v) \ne v$ for all $v$. Let $R_n$ denote the (finite) set of round configurations; it carries the uniform probability measure, i.e.\ every node picks a uniformly random \emph{target} among the other $n-1$ nodes, independently of all other nodes.
nodes.label: def:round

nodes.name: Push step
nodes.statement_short: The next informed set adds the targets of all informed nodes: step(I, omega) = I union omega(I).
nodes.statement: For an \emph{informed set} $I \subseteq V$ and a round configuration $\omega \in R_n$, the next informed set is \[ \mathrm{step}(I,\omega) \;=\; I \,\cup\, \omega(I) \;=\; I \cup \{\omega(v) : v \in I\}. \] (Only informed nodes actually transmit; letting \emph{all} nodes draw a target and ignoring the choices of uninformed nodes is an equivalent and formalization-friendlier convention.)
nodes.label: def:step

nodes.name: Push process
nodes.statement_short: The push process iterates the step over T i.i.d. uniform rounds from {v_0}; m_t and U_t count informed and uninformed nodes.
nodes.statement: Fix a horizon $T \in \N$ and a start vertex $v_0 \in V$. The sample space is $\Omega = R_n^{\,T}$ (uniform measure, i.e.\ i.i.d.\ uniform rounds). For $\omega = (\omega_0,\dots,\omega_{T-1}) \in \Omega$ define $I_0(\omega) = \{v_0\}$ and $I_{t+1}(\omega) = \mathrm{step}(I_t(\omega), \omega_t)$ for $0 \le t < T$. We write $m_t = |I_t|$ and $U_t = n - m_t$ for the numbers of informed and uninformed nodes. Since $\Omega$ is finite, all probabilities are finite ratios and all expectations are finite sums; ``conditioning on $I_t$'' means partitioning $\Omega$ according to the first $t$ coordinates. In the formalization, a trajectory is simply a \texttt{List} of round configurations and $\mathrm{run}\ I\ l$ folds \texttt{step} over the list $l$.
nodes.label: def:process

nodes.name: Proof of monotonicity and at most doubling
nodes.statement_short: Both facts are immediate from the definition of the push step.
nodes.statement: Two trivial but load-bearing facts, both immediate from Definition~\ref{def:step}:

nodes.name: Monotonicity of the push process
nodes.statement_short: Informed sets only grow over time, pointwise on the sample space.
conclusions: $I_t(\omega) \subseteq I_{t+1}(\omega)$ for all $t$ and all $\omega$
$m_t$ is non-decreasing and $U_t$ is non-increasing in $t$, pointwise on $\Omega$
nodes.statement: $I_t(\omega) \subseteq I_{t+1}(\omega)$ for all $t$ and all $\omega$; hence $m_t$ is non-decreasing and $U_t$ is non-increasing in $t$, pointwise on $\Omega$.
nodes.label: lem:mono

nodes.name: At most doubling
nodes.statement_short: One push round at most doubles the informed set.
conclusions: $|I_{t+1}(\omega) \smallsetminus I_t(\omega)| \le |I_t(\omega)|$
$(\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)).\mathrm{card} \le 2\,I.\mathrm{card}$
nodes.statement: $|I_{t+1}(\omega) \smallsetminus I_t(\omega)| \le |I_t(\omega)|$; equivalently $(\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)).\mathrm{card} \le 2\,I.\mathrm{card}$.
nodes.label: lem:atmost

nodes.name: Push protocol informs K_n in O(log n) rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform push on K_n from one informed node informs everyone within ceil(117 log n)+23+ceil(6 log n) rounds with probability 1 - 2/n.
assumptions: T_1 \;=\; \ceil{117 \log n} + 23, \qquad T_2 \;=\; \ceil{6 \log n}, \qquad T \;=\; T_1 + T_2 .
conclusions: $\Pr\bigl[\, I_T = V \,\bigr] \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{2}{n}$
all nodes are informed after $O(\log n)$ rounds with high probability
nodes.statement: Let $n \ge 2$, let $v_0 \in V$, and set \[ T_1 \;=\; \ceil{117 \log n} + 23, \qquad T_2 \;=\; \ceil{6 \log n}, \qquad T \;=\; T_1 + T_2 . \] Then $\Pr\bigl[\, I_T = V \,\bigr] \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{2}{n}$. In particular all nodes are informed after $O(\log n)$ rounds with high probability.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Constants and the sharp bound for push
nodes.statement_short: The constants are crude; the sharp push time is log_2 n + ln n + o(log n) (Frieze-Grimmett, Pittel).
nodes.statement: The constants are deliberately crude: the proof is organized to minimize the analytic toolkit, not the round count. The sharp answer is $\log_2 n + \log n + o(\log n)$ (Frieze--Grimmett \cite{FG85}, Pittel \cite{Pittel87}). Replacing $2/n$ by $n^{-\alpha}$ for any fixed $\alpha \ge 1$ only changes the constants in $T_1, T_2$.

nodes.name: Two-phase proof sketch of the push theorem
nodes.statement_short: Two phases glued by monotonicity: an adaptive-trials growth phase to n/2, then expected contraction of the uninformed count plus Markov.
nodes.statement: The proof has two phases, glued by Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Growth phase} (Section~\ref{sec:growth}): while $m_t \le n/2$, each round multiplies $m_t$ by $\ge 9/8$ with probability $\ge 1/8$; an exponential-moment bound for adaptive trials shows that after $T_1$ rounds, $m_{T_1} > n/2$ except with probability $\le 1/n$. \item \textbf{Saturation phase} (Section~\ref{sec:saturation}): once $m_t \ge n/2$, the expected number of uninformed nodes contracts by a factor $2/3$ per round; after $T_2$ further rounds Markov's inequality gives $U_T = 0$ except with probability $\le 1/n$.

nodes.name: Split into two phases glued by monotonicity
nodes.statement: The proof has two phases, glued by Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}:
nodes.statement_short: Split into two phases glued by monotonicity

nodes.name: Growth phase via adaptive trials
nodes.statement: \textbf{Growth phase} (Section~\ref{sec:growth}): while $m_t \le n/2$, each round multiplies $m_t$ by $\ge 9/8$ with probability $\ge 1/8$; an exponential-moment bound for adaptive trials shows that after $T_1$ rounds, $m_{T_1} > n/2$ except with probability $\le 1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Growth phase via adaptive trials

nodes.name: Saturation phase via contraction and Markov
nodes.statement: \textbf{Saturation phase} (Section~\ref{sec:saturation}): once $m_t \ge n/2$, the expected number of uninformed nodes contracts by a factor $2/3$ per round; after $T_2$ further rounds Markov's inequality gives $U_T = 0$ except with probability $\le 1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Saturation phase via contraction and Markov

nodes.name: Average (uniform expectation)
nodes.statement_short: avg(f) is the uniform expectation of f over a finite type.
nodes.statement: For a finite type $\alpha$ and $f \colon \alpha \to \R$, $\mathrm{avg}(f) := \bigl(\sum_{a} f(a)\bigr) / |\alpha|$ is the expectation of $f$ under the uniform distribution on $\alpha$.
nodes.label: def:avg

nodes.name: Trajectory expectation expList
nodes.statement_short: expList is the expectation of a trajectory functional over T i.i.d. uniform draws, defined by recursion on T averaging the head draw first.
nodes.statement: For a finite type $\alpha$, $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ F$ is the expectation of a functional $F$ of a trajectory of $T$ i.i.d.\ uniform draws from $\alpha$, defined \emph{by recursion on $T$}: the head draw is averaged out first, i.e.\ $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ 0\ F = F(\,[]\,)$ and $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ (T{+}1)\ F = \mathrm{avg}\bigl(a \mapsto \mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ (l \mapsto F(a :: l))\bigr)$. This makes ``conditioning on the first round'' a definitional unfolding rather than a measure-theoretic construction.
nodes.label: def:expList

nodes.name: Basic properties of avg and expList
nodes.statement_short: avg and expList are monotone, additive and homogeneous and fix constants; this is how Markov and union bounds are used.
conclusions: $\mathrm{avg}$ and $\mathrm{expList}$ are monotone, additive, and homogeneous, and constants pass through unchanged.
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{avg}$ and $\mathrm{expList}$ are monotone, additive, and homogeneous, and constants pass through unchanged. These pointwise inequalities pushed through $\mathrm{avg\_le\_avg}$ / $\mathrm{expList\_le\_expList}$ are the only form in which Markov's inequality and union bounds are used below (Lemmas~\ref{lem:markov} and~\ref{lem:revmarkov}); they are not separately formalized lemmas.
nodes.label: lem:avg-basic

nodes.name: Faithfulness of the model
nodes.statement_short: The recursive expList equals the uniform average over all length-T sequences, i.e. the product probability space.
conclusions: $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ F$ equals the uniform average of $F$ over \emph{all} length-$T$ sequences of draws
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ F$ equals the uniform average of $F$ over \emph{all} length-$T$ sequences of draws, i.e.\ over the product probability space $\mathrm{Fin}\ T \to \alpha$ of $T$ i.i.d.\ uniform rounds. This confirms that the recursive definition of Definition~\ref{def:expList} is the textbook object.
nodes.label: thm:faithful

nodes.name: The quantity x = 1/(n-1)
nodes.statement: We write $x := \tfrac{1}{n-1}$, so $0 < x \le 1$ for $n \ge 2$.

nodes.name: Bernoulli's inequality
nodes.statement: For all real $y \ge -1$ (we only use $y\in[-1,1]$) and $m \in \N$: $(1+y)^m \ge 1 + my$. Equivalently, with $y = -x$: $1 - mx \le (1-x)^m$.
nodes.label: lem:bernoulli

nodes.name: Second-order Bonferroni lower bound
conclusions: 1-(1-x)^m \;\ge\; mx - \binom{m}{2}x^2 \;\ge\; mx\Bigl(1-\frac{mx}{2}\Bigr),
$mx/2 \le 1-(1-x)^m$ whenever $mx \le 1$
nodes.statement: For $0 \le x \le 1$ and $m \in \N$: \[ 1-(1-x)^m \;\ge\; mx - \binom{m}{2}x^2 \;\ge\; mx\Bigl(1-\frac{mx}{2}\Bigr), \] and consequently $mx/2 \le 1-(1-x)^m$ whenever $mx \le 1$.
nodes.label: lem:bonferroni

nodes.name: Upper bound without e
conclusions: $(1-x)^m \le \dfrac{1}{1+mx}$
nodes.statement: For $0 \le x \le 1$ and $m \in \N$: $(1-x)^m \le \dfrac{1}{1+mx}$.
nodes.label: lem:upper

nodes.name: Logarithm lower bound
conclusions: $1 - \tfrac1x \le \log x$
nodes.statement: For $x > 0$: $1 - \tfrac1x \le \log x$. (The formalization only needs this left inequality, applied at $x = 9/8,\ 16/15,\ 3/2$, together with Mathlib's numeric bound $\log 2 < 0.6931471808$.)
nodes.label: lem:logbounds

nodes.name: Markov's inequality, finite uniform version
assumptions: $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set with the uniform measure
conclusions: $\Pr[f \ge a] \le \E[f]/a$
if $f$ takes values in $\N$, then $\Pr[f \ne 0] \le \E[f]$
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set with the uniform measure, $f \colon \Omega \to \R$ with $f \ge 0$, and $a > 0$. Then $\Pr[f \ge a] \le \E[f]/a$. In particular, if $f$ takes values in $\N$, then $\Pr[f \ne 0] \le \E[f]$.
nodes.label: lem:markov

nodes.name: Reverse Markov inequality for bounded variables
conclusions: $\Pr[f \ge a] \ge \dfrac{\E[f] - a}{b}$
nodes.statement: Let $f \colon \Omega \to \R$ with $0 \le f \le b$ pointwise, $b > 0$, and let $0 < a < b$. Then $\Pr[f \ge a] \ge \dfrac{\E[f] - a}{b}$. (As with Lemma~\ref{lem:markov}, the formalization does not isolate this as a named lemma: each use site supplies its own pointwise bound and pushes it through $\mathrm{avg\_le\_avg}$, e.g.\ in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:goodround}.)
nodes.label: lem:revmarkov

nodes.name: Fixed informed set and uniform round
nodes.statement: Fix an informed set $I$ with $|I| = m \ge 1$ and let $\omega \in R_n$ be a uniform round configuration.

nodes.name: Contact probability
nodes.statement_short: An uninformed node is reached in one push round with probability exactly 1-(1-1/(n-1))^m.
conclusions: \Pr_\omega\bigl[u \in \mathrm{step}(I,\omega)\bigr] \;=\; 1 - \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{n-1}\Bigr)^{m}.
nodes.statement: For any fixed $u \notin I$, \[ \Pr_\omega\bigl[u \in \mathrm{step}(I,\omega)\bigr] \;=\; 1 - \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{n-1}\Bigr)^{m}. \] The Lean proof is the only place where a probability is \emph{computed} rather than estimated: it counts round configurations avoiding $u$ on $I$ via an explicit equivalence to a product of subtypes and \texttt{Fintype.card\_pi}.
nodes.label: lem:contact

nodes.name: Expected growth
nodes.statement_short: Exact formula for the expected next informed count; below n/2 the expected number of newly informed nodes is at least m/4.
assumptions: $N(\omega) = |\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)| - m$ be the number of newly informed nodes
conclusions: \E_\omega[|\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)|] \;=\; m + (n-m)\bigl(1-(1-x)^m\bigr),
$\E_\omega[N] \ge m/4$
nodes.statement: Let $N(\omega) = |\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)| - m$ be the number of newly informed nodes. The formalization gives the \emph{exact} formula \[ \E_\omega[|\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)|] \;=\; m + (n-m)\bigl(1-(1-x)^m\bigr), \] from which, if $1 \le m \le n/2$: $\E_\omega[N] \ge m/4$ (using Lemma~\ref{lem:bonferroni} and $n - m \ge n/2$, $mx \le 1$).
nodes.label: lem:expgrowth

nodes.name: A good round has constant probability
nodes.statement_short: Below n/2, a push round multiplies the informed set by 9/8 with probability at least 1/8.
conclusions: \Pr_\omega\bigl[\,|\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)| \ge \tfrac{9}{8}\,m\,\bigr] \ge \tfrac18
nodes.statement: If $1 \le m \le n/2$, then $\Pr_\omega\bigl[\,|\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)| \ge \tfrac{9}{8}\,m\,\bigr] \ge \tfrac18$.
nodes.label: lem:goodround

nodes.name: Contraction above half
nodes.statement_short: Above n/2 each uninformed node stays uninformed with probability <= 2/3, so the expected uninformed count contracts by 2/3.
conclusions: $\Pr_\omega[u \notin \mathrm{step}(I,\omega)] = (1-x)^m \le \tfrac23$
$\E_\omega[U'] \le \tfrac23(n-m)$
nodes.statement: If $m \ge n/2$, then for every fixed $u \notin I$, $\Pr_\omega[u \notin \mathrm{step}(I,\omega)] = (1-x)^m \le \tfrac23$, and consequently, with $U' := n - |\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)|$, $\E_\omega[U'] \le \tfrac23(n-m)$.
nodes.label: lem:contract

nodes.name: Good rounds and goodCount
nodes.statement_short: A round is good if it multiplies the informed set by 9/8 or the set already exceeds n/2; goodCount counts them, each good with conditional probability >= 1/8.
nodes.statement: A round is \emph{good} if it multiplies the informed set by $\ge 9/8$, or if the informed set already exceeds $n/2$: \[ X_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\Bigl[\, m_{t+1} \ge \tfrac98\, m_t \;\;\text{or}\;\; m_t > \tfrac n2 \,\Bigr] \in \{0,1\}. \] $\mathrm{goodCount}$ counts the good rounds along a trajectory. By Lemma~\ref{lem:goodround} (applied when $m_t \le n/2$; trivial otherwise), $\Pr[X_t = 1 \mid \omega_0,\dots,\omega_{t-1}] \ge \tfrac18$ for every prefix, since $\omega_t$ is independent of the prefix and $\mathrm{expList}$ conditions on it definitionally.
nodes.label: def:good

nodes.name: Exponential moment for adaptive trials
nodes.statement_short: E[(1/2)^goodCount] <= (15/16)^T over T rounds, by induction on T.
conclusions: \E\Bigl[\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^{\mathrm{goodCount}(I,\,\cdot\,)}\Bigr] \;\le\; \Bigl(\frac{15}{16}\Bigr)^{T}
nodes.statement: For every $T$ and every nonempty $I$, \[ \E\Bigl[\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^{\mathrm{goodCount}(I,\,\cdot\,)}\Bigr] \;\le\; \Bigl(\frac{15}{16}\Bigr)^{T} \] over $T$ rounds started at $I$. (This specializes the textbook ``$\E[s^G] \le (1-p(1-s))^T$ for adaptive $\{0,1\}$-trials with per-step success probability $\ge p$'' at $p = 1/8$, $s = 1/2$; the formalization proves the specialized statement directly by induction on $T$ rather than the general one, since only this instance is needed. The ensuing tail bound $\Pr[G < L] \le 2^{L}(15/16)^{T}$ — via $s^{L}\Pr[G<L] \le \E[s^G]$ — is likewise not isolated as a separate lemma; it is proved inline inside Lemma~\ref{lem:phase1} (\texttt{phase1}).
nodes.label: lem:adaptive

nodes.name: Enough good rounds force half-saturation
nodes.statement_short: Deterministically m_{T1} >= (9/8)^goodCount m_0 while below n/2, so L good rounds force exceeding n/2.
assumptions: the informed set never exceeds $n/2$ up to time $T_1$
conclusions: $m_{T_1} \ge (9/8)^{\mathrm{goodCount}} \cdot m_0$
nodes.statement: Let $L \in \N$ satisfy $(9/8)^L > n/2$. If the informed set never exceeds $n/2$ up to time $T_1$, then along that trajectory $m_{T_1} \ge (9/8)^{\mathrm{goodCount}} \cdot m_0$: every good round multiplies $m_t$ by $\ge 9/8$ and every round is non-decreasing (Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}), so $\mathrm{goodCount} \ge L$ would force $m_{T_1} > n/2$, a contradiction — hence $\mathrm{goodCount} < L \Rightarrow m_{T_1} \le n/2$ is impossible to rule out only via the deterministic growth bound stated here.
nodes.label: lem:force

nodes.name: Phase 1 (growth phase failure bound)
nodes.statement_short: If (9/8)^L >= n, the informed set stays below n/2 after T1 rounds with probability at most 2^L (15/16)^{T1}.
conclusions: after $T_1$ rounds the informed set is still $\le n/2$ with probability at most $2^{L}\,(15/16)^{T_1}$
nodes.statement: If $(9/8)^L \ge n$, then after $T_1$ rounds the informed set is still $\le n/2$ with probability at most $2^{L}\,(15/16)^{T_1}$.
nodes.label: lem:phase1

nodes.name: Admissible constants
nodes.statement_short: L = ceil(9 log n)+1 and T1 = ceil(117 log n)+23 satisfy (9/8)^L >= n and 2^L (15/16)^{T1} <= 1/n.
nodes.statement: With $L = \ceil{9 \log n} + 1$ we have $(9/8)^L \ge n$ (\texttt{numeric\_A}), and with $T_1 = \ceil{117 \log n} + 23$ we have $2^{L}(15/16)^{T_1} \le 1/n$ (\texttt{numeric\_B}), using $\log\tfrac98 \ge \tfrac19$, $\log\tfrac{16}{15} \ge \tfrac1{16}$ and $\log 2 < 0.6932$. Combined with Lemma~\ref{lem:phase1}: $\Pr[m_{T_1} \le n/2] \le 1/n$. The clean statement to formalize is that \emph{any} $L, T_1$ satisfying these two numeric inequalities work; the values above merely exhibit admissible ones.
nodes.label: lem:constants

nodes.name: Phase 2 (saturation)
nodes.statement_short: On the event that phase 1 succeeded, the expected uninformed count after s more rounds is at most (2/3)^s n.
nodes.statement: Let $A = \{m_{T_1} > n/2\}$ (an event determined by the first $T_1$ coordinates). Then for every $s \ge 0$, $\E\bigl[\, U_{T_1 + s}\, \mathbf{1}_A \,\bigr] \le (2/3)^{s}\, n$, by induction on $s$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:contract} at each step (monotonicity keeps $m_{T_1+s} > n/2$ on $A$).
nodes.label: lem:phase2

nodes.name: Saturation failure bound
nodes.statement_short: With T2 = ceil(6 log n), some node is uninformed on A with probability at most 1/n.
conclusions: $\Pr[\, U_T \ge 1 \text{ and } A \,] \le n\,(2/3)^{T_2} \le 1/n$
nodes.statement: With $T_2 = \ceil{6 \log n}$: $\Pr[\, U_T \ge 1 \text{ and } A \,] \le n\,(2/3)^{T_2} \le 1/n$. ($U_T$ is $\N$-valued, so Markov applied to $U_T \mathbf{1}_A$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:phase2} give the first inequality; $(2/3)^{T_2} n \le 1/n$ — \texttt{numeric\_C} — follows from $\log\tfrac32 \ge \tfrac13$ and $T_2 \ge 6\log n$.)
nodes.label: lem:phase2cor

nodes.name: Gluing the two phases
nodes.statement_short: The failure probability after T1+T2 rounds is at most 2^L (15/16)^{T1} + (2/3)^{T2} n.
assumptions: For all $L, T_1, T_2$ with $(9/8)^L \le n$
conclusions: \mathrm{prNotAllInformed}(n,v_0,T_1+T_2) \;\le\; 2^{L}\Bigl(\frac{15}{16}\Bigr)^{T_1} + \Bigl(\frac23\Bigr)^{T_2} n.
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{prNotAllInformed}(n,v_0,T)$ be the probability that some node is still uninformed after $T$ rounds started at $v_0$. For all $L, T_1, T_2$ with $(9/8)^L \le n$: \[ \mathrm{prNotAllInformed}(n,v_0,T_1+T_2) \;\le\; 2^{L}\Bigl(\frac{15}{16}\Bigr)^{T_1} + \Bigl(\frac23\Bigr)^{T_2} n. \] Failure requires either phase 1 to fail (informed set still $\le n/2$ after $T_1$ rounds, Lemma~\ref{lem:phase1}) or phase 2 to leave an uninformed node on the complementary event, controlled by Lemma~\ref{lem:phase2} via Markov.
nodes.label: lem:gluing

nodes.name: Proof of the push main theorem
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over the two phase failures: 1/n from the growth phase plus 1/n from saturation.
nodes.statement: With $T_1 = \ceil{117\log n} + 23$, $T_2 = \ceil{6\log n}$, $T = T_1+T_2$, Theorem~\ref{thm:main} follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:gluing}, Lemma~\ref{lem:constants} and Corollary~\ref{lem:phase2cor}: \[ \Pr[I_T \ne V] \;=\; \Pr[U_T \ge 1] \;\le\; \Pr[\,\overline{A}\,] + \Pr[\,U_T \ge 1 \text{ and } A\,] \;\le\; \frac1n + \frac1n \;=\; \frac2n . \]

nodes.name: PULL and PUSH-PULL rounds
nodes.statement_short: PULL adds every caller whose callee is informed; PUSH-PULL takes the union with the push step; failure is some node uninformed after T rounds.
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{pullStep}(I,\omega) = I \cup \{v : \omega(v) \in I\}$ and $\mathrm{pushPullStep}(I,\omega) = \mathrm{step}(I,\omega) \cup \mathrm{pullStep}(I,\omega)$; trajectories fold these steps over a list of i.i.d.\ uniform rounds, and the failure probabilities are the probabilities that some node is still uninformed after $T$ rounds started from $\{v_0\}$.
nodes.label: def:pull

nodes.name: Pathwise domination
conclusions: the PUSH--PULL informed set contains the PUSH and the PULL informed sets after every number of rounds
nodes.statement: With the same calls, the PUSH--PULL informed set contains the PUSH and the PULL informed sets after every number of rounds.
nodes.label: lem:pull-domination

nodes.name: Independent calls
nodes.statement_short: Calls in a uniform round are independent and uniform; an uninformed caller calls into I with probability |I|/(n-1).
conclusions: The calls $\omega(v)$, $v \in V$, of a uniform round are independent, each uniform among the other $n-1$ nodes
a caller $v \notin I$ calls into $I$ with probability $|I|/(n-1)$
nodes.statement: The calls $\omega(v)$, $v \in V$, of a uniform round are independent, each uniform among the other $n-1$ nodes; in particular a caller $v \notin I$ calls into $I$ with probability $|I|/(n-1)$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-indep

nodes.name: One PULL or PUSH-PULL round, exactly
nodes.statement_short: Exact one-round expectations for PULL and PUSH-PULL; PULL shrinks the uninformed count quadratically.
conclusions: From a single informed node a PULL round informs nobody with probability $(1 - \frac1{n-1})^{n-1}$.
After one PULL round, $\E|I'| = m + u\,\frac{m}{n-1}$ and $\E[n - |I'|] = \frac{u(u-1)}{n-1} \le \frac{u^2}{n}$ (quadratic shrinking).
After one PUSH--PULL round, $\E[n - |I'|] = \frac{u(u-1)}{n-1}\bigl(1 - \frac1{n-1}\bigr)^{m}$.
nodes.statement: Let $m = |I|$ and $u = n - m$. From a single informed node a PULL round informs nobody with probability $(1 - \frac1{n-1})^{n-1}$. After one PULL round, $\E|I'| = m + u\,\frac{m}{n-1}$ and $\E[n - |I'|] = \frac{u(u-1)}{n-1} \le \frac{u^2}{n}$ (quadratic shrinking). After one PUSH--PULL round, $\E[n - |I'|] = \frac{u(u-1)}{n-1}\bigl(1 - \frac1{n-1}\bigr)^{m}$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-oneround

nodes.name: Two-phase argument for any inflationary step
nodes.statement_short: Any inflationary spreading step with constant-probability good rounds and 2/3 contraction above n/2 informs all within ceil(160 log n) rounds w.p. 1 - 2/n.
assumptions: $f(I,a) \supseteq I$ be a spreading step driven by i.i.d.\ uniform rounds $a$
from every nonempty $I$ a round is good ($|f(I,a)| \ge \frac98 |I|$, or $|I| > n/2$) with probability at least $1/8$
for $|I| \ge n/2$ the expected number of uninformed nodes contracts by $2/3$
conclusions: after $\ceil{160 \log n}$ rounds from $\{v_0\}$, some node is uninformed with probability at most $2/n$
nodes.statement: Let $f(I,a) \supseteq I$ be a spreading step driven by i.i.d.\ uniform rounds $a$. Suppose that from every nonempty $I$ a round is good ($|f(I,a)| \ge \frac98 |I|$, or $|I| > n/2$) with probability at least $1/8$, and that for $|I| \ge n/2$ the expected number of uninformed nodes contracts by $2/3$. Then after $\ceil{160 \log n}$ rounds from $\{v_0\}$, some node is uninformed with probability at most $2/n$. The proof is the PUSH proof of Sections~\ref{sec:adaptive}--\ref{sec:proof-main}, which uses no other property of $\mathrm{step}$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-phases

nodes.name: The two inputs for PULL
nodes.statement_short: A PULL round is good with probability >= 1/8 and contracts the expected uninformed count by 2/3 above n/2.
conclusions: A PULL round is good with probability at least $1/8$
for $|I| \ge n/2$ it contracts the expected uninformed count by $2/3$
nodes.statement: A PULL round is good with probability at least $1/8$, and for $|I| \ge n/2$ it contracts the expected uninformed count by $2/3$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-good

nodes.name: Proof of the two inputs for PULL
nodes.statement_short: Contraction from the exact one-round formula; good rounds via a second-moment (Paley-Zygmund) bound on the number of successful callers.
nodes.statement: The contraction follows from $\frac{u(u-1)}{n-1} \le \frac23 u$ for $u \le n/2$. For good rounds, let $X$ be the number of uninformed callers that call into $I$, so $|I'| = |I| + X$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-indep}, $\mu = \E X = \frac{(n-m)m}{n-1} \ge \max(m/2, 1/2)$ for $m \le n/2$ and, the calls being pairwise independent, $\E X^2 \le \mu + \mu^2$. A round that is not good has $X < m/8 \le \mu/4$, so pointwise $X \le \mu/4 + X^2/(2t) + (t/2)\,\mathbf 1[\text{good}]$ with $t = 4(1+\mu)/3$; taking expectations gives $\Pr[\text{good}] \ge \frac{3\mu}{4t} \ge 3/16$ (a Paley--Zygmund bound). Unlike PUSH, the reverse Markov argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:goodround} does not apply, since a PULL round can inform many more than $|I|$ new nodes.

nodes.name: Contraction from the exact PULL formula
nodes.statement: The contraction follows from $\frac{u(u-1)}{n-1} \le \frac23 u$ for $u \le n/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Contraction from the exact PULL formula

nodes.name: Introduce X, the successful uninformed callers
nodes.statement: For good rounds, let $X$ be the number of uninformed callers that call into $I$, so $|I'| = |I| + X$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce X, the successful uninformed callers

nodes.name: First and second moments of X
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-indep}, $\mu = \E X = \frac{(n-m)m}{n-1} \ge \max(m/2, 1/2)$ for $m \le n/2$ and, the calls being pairwise independent, $\E X^2 \le \mu + \mu^2$.
nodes.statement_short: First and second moments of X

nodes.name: Paley-Zygmund style bound on Pr[good]
nodes.statement: A round that is not good has $X < m/8 \le \mu/4$, so pointwise $X \le \mu/4 + X^2/(2t) + (t/2)\,\mathbf 1[\text{good}]$ with $t = 4(1+\mu)/3$; taking expectations gives $\Pr[\text{good}] \ge \frac{3\mu}{4t} \ge 3/16$ (a Paley--Zygmund bound).
nodes.statement_short: Paley-Zygmund style bound on Pr[good]

nodes.name: Explain why reverse Markov fails for PULL
nodes.statement: Unlike PUSH, the reverse Markov argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:goodround} does not apply, since a PULL round can inform many more than $|I|$ new nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Explain why reverse Markov fails for PULL

nodes.name: PULL and PUSH-PULL inform K_n in O(log n) rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement_short: After ceil(160 log n) rounds of PULL or PUSH-PULL from one node, all are informed with probability 1 - 2/n.
conclusions: After $\ceil{160 \log n}$ rounds of PULL, or of PUSH--PULL, started from $\{v_0\}$, all nodes are informed with probability at least $1 - 2/n$.
nodes.statement: Let $n \ge 2$ and $v_0 \in V$. After $\ceil{160 \log n}$ rounds of PULL, or of PUSH--PULL, started from $\{v_0\}$, all nodes are informed with probability at least $1 - 2/n$.
nodes.label: thm:pull

nodes.name: Proof of the PULL and PUSH-PULL theorem
nodes.statement_short: Apply the generic two-phase lemma with the PULL inputs; PUSH-PULL dominates PULL pathwise.
nodes.statement: For PULL, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-phases} with the inputs of Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-good}. For PUSH--PULL, the failure event is contained in the PULL failure event by Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-domination}.

nodes.name: Undecided-state dynamics
nodes.statement_short: Each node samples a uniform node: undecided nodes adopt the sampled opinion, decided nodes meeting the other opinion become undecided.
nodes.statement: Each of $n$ nodes holds opinion $a$, opinion $b$, or is undecided. In a round every node samples a node uniformly at random (with replacement, possibly itself): an undecided node adopts the sampled opinion, and a decided node that samples the other opinion becomes undecided. We write $a$, $b$, $q$ for the numbers of $a$-, $b$- and undecided nodes.
nodes.label: def:usd

nodes.name: Per-node probabilities
assumptions: The state of a node after a round depends only on the node it samples, which is uniform
conclusions: an $a$-node stays $a$ with probability $1-b/n$ and an undecided node becomes $a$ with probability $a/n$
nodes.statement: The state of a node after a round depends only on the node it samples, which is uniform; so an $a$-node stays $a$ with probability $1-b/n$ and an undecided node becomes $a$ with probability $a/n$.
nodes.label: lem:node

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Averaging a function of one coordinate over sampling functions gives the uniform average.
nodes.statement: The average over all sampling functions of a function of one coordinate is the uniform average.

nodes.name: Expected counts and bias
conclusions:
After one round, the expected numbers of $a$-, $b$- and undecided nodes are $a(n-b+q)/n$,
$b(n-a+q)/n$ and $(q^2+2ab)/n$
the expected bias is $(a-b)(1+q/n)$
nodes.statement_short: One-round expected counts of the undecided-state dynamics; the bias grows by factor $1+q/n$ in expectation.
nodes.statement: After one round, the expected numbers of $a$-, $b$- and undecided nodes are $a(n-b+q)/n$, $b(n-a+q)/n$ and $(q^2+2ab)/n$; hence the expected bias is $(a-b)(1+q/n)$.
nodes.label: thm:expect

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Sum the per-node probabilities over nodes and simplify the bias.
nodes.statement: Sum Lemma~\ref{lem:node} over the nodes; $a(n-b+q)-b(n-a+q)=(a-b)(n+q)$.

nodes.name: Almost-sure absorption
conclusions: Monochromatic configurations are fixed points

from every configuration the probability of
not being monochromatic after $t$ rounds tends to $0$
nodes.statement: Monochromatic configurations are fixed points, and from every configuration the probability of not being monochromatic after $t$ rounds tends to $0$.
nodes.label: thm:absorbed

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit a positive-probability two-round path to a monochromatic configuration, then apply the shared absorption theorem.
nodes.statement: If some node $w$ is decided, the round in which everybody samples $w$, repeated twice, makes the configuration monochromatic; it has positive probability. Conclude with the shared absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Bias, deviation scale and good round
nodes.statement: Write $s=a-b$ for the bias, $\Lambda=\sqrt{n\log n}$, and call a round \emph{good} if the new counts of $a$-, $b$- and undecided nodes are within $\Lambda$ of their expectations (from below for $a$, from above for $b$, both ways for the undecided nodes).
nodes.statement_short: Bias $s=a-b$, scale $\Lambda=\sqrt{n\log n}$, and good rounds where all counts are within $\Lambda$ of their expectations.

nodes.name: Bad rounds
conclusions: A round is bad with probability at most $4e^{-2\Lambda^2/n}=4/n^2$.
nodes.statement: A round is bad with probability at most $4e^{-2\Lambda^2/n}=4/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:badround

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Each count is a sum of independent per-node indicators; Hoeffding's inequality on the four tails.
nodes.statement: Each count after the round is a sum of independent indicators, one per node, depending only on the node it samples; apply Hoeffding's inequality to the four tails.

nodes.name: Good rounds
conclusions: $s'>s(1+q/n)-2\Lambda$ and $q'>n/3-s^2/(2n)-\Lambda$
the potential $\Psi=12b+q$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\Psi']\le\frac56\Psi$, hence $\Psi'<\frac56\Psi+13\Lambda$ after a good round
$s'>s(1+q/n)-2\Lambda$ and $q'>n/3-s^2/(2n)-\Lambda$
the potential $\Psi=12b+q$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\Psi']\le\frac56\Psi$, hence $\Psi'<\frac56\Psi+13\Lambda$ after a good round

nodes.statement_short: In a good round the bias and undecided count obey explicit lower bounds, and the potential $\Psi=12b+q$ contracts by $5/6$ near consensus.
nodes.statement: After a good round, $s'>s(1+q/n)-2\Lambda$ and $q'>n/3-s^2/(2n)-\Lambda$. If $b+2q\le 2n/3$ and $q\le n/3$, the potential $\Psi=12b+q$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\Psi']\le\frac56\Psi$, hence $\Psi'<\frac56\Psi+13\Lambda$ after a good round.
nodes.label: lem:goodround

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Three algebraic identities/inequalities for the expected counts.

nodes.name: Phases
conclusions: after $T+1$ rounds $s\ge\min(400\Lambda(201/200)^T,7n/10)$ except with probability $(T+1)p$
after $18$ rounds $\Psi\le n/3$ except with probability $18p$
not all nodes hold $a$ after $T$ rounds with probability at most $(5/6)^T\Psi+Tp$
after $T+1$ rounds $s\ge\min(400\Lambda(201/200)^T,7n/10)$ except with probability $(T+1)p$
after $18$ rounds $\Psi\le n/3$ except with probability $18p$
not all nodes hold $a$ after $T$ rounds with probability at most $(5/6)^T\Psi+Tp$

nodes.statement_short: Three phases of the undecided-state majority dynamics: bias growth, a bridge to small $\Psi$, and a final geometric contraction.
nodes.statement: Let $2000\Lambda\le n$ and $p=4/n^2$. (Growth) From $s\ge 402\Lambda$, after $T+1$ rounds $s\ge\min(400\Lambda(201/200)^T,7n/10)$ except with probability $(T+1)p$. (Bridge) From $s\ge 7n/10$, after $18$ rounds $\Psi\le n/3$ except with probability $18p$. (Final) From $\Psi\le n/3$, not all nodes hold $a$ after $T$ rounds with probability at most $(5/6)^T\Psi+Tp$.
nodes.label: thm:phases

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Phase-by-phase: moving-target union bound for growth, contraction of $\Psi$ in the bridge, induction on $T$ for the final phase.
nodes.statement: Growth: the sets $\{s\ge g,\ (q\ge n/100\text{ or }s\ge g+n/20)\}$ are entered with $g=400\Lambda$ after one good round and $g$ grows by $201/200$ per good round (if $s\le 4n/5$ then $q'\ge n/100$); union bound over rounds with moving targets. Bridge: while $s\ge 2n/3$, $\Psi$ shrinks by $9/10$ per good round and $s$ loses at most $2\Lambda$. Final: induction on $T$, splitting on whether the first round stays in $\{\Psi\le n/3\}$; and $\Psi\ge 1$ unless all nodes hold $a$.

nodes.name: Growth phase
nodes.statement: Growth: the sets $\{s\ge g,\ (q\ge n/100\text{ or }s\ge g+n/20)\}$ are entered with $g=400\Lambda$ after one good round and $g$ grows by $201/200$ per good round (if $s\le 4n/5$ then $q'\ge n/100$); union bound over rounds with moving targets.
nodes.statement_short: Growth: bias target grows by 201/200 per good round; union bound with moving targets.

nodes.name: Bridge phase
nodes.statement: Bridge: while $s\ge 2n/3$, $\Psi$ shrinks by $9/10$ per good round and $s$ loses at most $2\Lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Bridge: $\Psi$ shrinks by 9/10 per good round.

nodes.name: Final phase
nodes.statement: Final: induction on $T$, splitting on whether the first round stays in $\{\Psi\le n/3\}$; and $\Psi\ge 1$ unless all nodes hold $a$.
nodes.statement_short: Final: induction on $T$ with the contraction of $\Psi$.

nodes.name: Majority phase
nodes.origin_citation: Clementi, Ghaffari, Gualà, Natale, Pasquale, Scornavacca (MFCS 2018), Thm 3.2; BCNPS SODA 2015 Thm 11
assumptions: every configuration (any number of undecided nodes) with $|a-b|\ge C\sqrt{n\log n}$
conclusions: all nodes hold the initial majority opinion after $\lceil C\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-2/n$
the same holds with a constant depending on $\alpha$

assumptions: every configuration (any number of undecided nodes) with $|a-b|\ge C\sqrt{n\log n}$
conclusions: all nodes hold the initial majority opinion after $\lceil C\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-2/n$
the same holds with a constant depending on $\alpha$

nodes.statement_short: Undecided-state dynamics reaches majority consensus in $O(\log n)$ rounds w.h.p. from bias $\Omega(\sqrt{n\log n})$.
nodes.statement: Let $C=10^4$. For every $n$ with $\log n\ge C$ and every configuration (any number of undecided nodes) with $|a-b|\ge C\sqrt{n\log n}$, all nodes hold the initial majority opinion after $\lceil C\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-2/n$. Without undecided nodes and with $a\ge(1+\alpha)b$, the same holds with a constant depending on $\alpha$ (SODA 2015, Theorem~11 for two colours).
nodes.label: thm:majority

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Chain the growth, bridge and final phases and sum failure probabilities; symmetry and absorption handle the remaining cases.
nodes.statement: Run $T_1+1$ growth rounds with $T_1=\lceil\log n/\log(201/200)\rceil$, $18$ bridge rounds and the remaining $T_3\ge 12\log n$ final rounds, so that $(5/6)^{T_3}\le n^{-2}$; the failure probability is at most $\lceil C\log n\rceil p+n^{-2}\cdot n/3\le 2/n$. A $b$-majority follows by exchanging the opinions. With $a\ge(1+\alpha)b$ and $q=0$ the bias is at least $\alpha n/(2+\alpha)$, which exceeds $C\sqrt{n\log n}$ once $\log n\ge C(1+3(2+\alpha)/\alpha)$; extra rounds do not hurt since the all-$a$ configuration is absorbing.

nodes.name: Chain the phases
nodes.statement: Run $T_1+1$ growth rounds with $T_1=\lceil\log n/\log(201/200)\rceil$, $18$ bridge rounds and the remaining $T_3\ge 12\log n$ final rounds, so that $(5/6)^{T_3}\le n^{-2}$; the failure probability is at most $\lceil C\log n\rceil p+n^{-2}\cdot n/3\le 2/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the three phases and bound the total failure probability by $2/n$.

nodes.name: b-majority by symmetry
nodes.statement: A $b$-majority follows by exchanging the opinions.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric case of a $b$-majority.

nodes.name: Multiplicative bias case
nodes.statement: With $a\ge(1+\alpha)b$ and $q=0$ the bias is at least $\alpha n/(2+\alpha)$, which exceeds $C\sqrt{n\log n}$ once $\log n\ge C(1+3(2+\alpha)/\alpha)$; extra rounds do not hurt since the all-$a$ configuration is absorbing.
nodes.statement_short: A multiplicative bias gives linear bias, reducing to the main case.

nodes.name: Undecided-state dynamics with k colours
nodes.statement: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale and Silvestri (\emph{Plurality consensus in the gossip model}, SODA 2015) analyse the undecided-state dynamics with $k$ colours: a state is a colour or the undecided state (Table~1), and with $c_i$ nodes of colour $i$ and $q$ undecided nodes one round gives in expectation $\mu_i=c_i(c_i+2q)/n$ nodes of colour $i$ and $\mu_q=(q^2+(n-q)^2-\sum_i c_i^2)/n$ undecided nodes (their (3)--(4)).
nodes.statement_short: The $k$-colour undecided-state dynamics, with colour counts $c_i$ and expected next counts $\mu_i$, $\mu_q$.

nodes.name: Monochromatic distance
nodes.statement: The monochromatic distance is $\mathrm{md}(c)=\sum_i(c_i/c_1)^2\in[1,k]$, $c_1$ the plurality.

nodes.name: Correction to the range of k in BCNPS Theorem 11
nodes.statement: The range of $k$ in Theorem~11 of the paper needs a minor correction: its proof invokes Lemma~10, which assumes $k=O((n/\log n)^{1/4})$, and the round-by-round argument closes for $k\le\varepsilon(\alpha)(n/\log n)^{1/3}$. The formalized statement takes $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/3}$ with $C=C(\alpha)$ (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/undecided/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#the-dynamics-with-k-colours-plurality-roadmap-und-3}{details}).
nodes.statement_short: BCNPS Theorem 11 holds for $k\lesssim(n/\log n)^{1/3}$, which is the range formalized.

nodes.name: Model
conclusions: Equations (3)--(4) hold
$1\le\mathrm{md}(c)\le k$
the two-colour dynamics is the binary dynamics under undecided $\mapsto u$, colour $0\mapsto a$, colour $1\mapsto b$
nodes.statement: Equations (3)--(4) hold, $1\le\mathrm{md}(c)\le k$, and the two-colour dynamics is the binary dynamics under undecided $\mapsto u$, colour $0\mapsto a$, colour $1\mapsto b$.
nodes.label: thm:pmodel

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Linearity over nodes; the binary case is checked on nine state pairs.
nodes.statement: Linearity over the nodes, as in the binary case; the binary update is checked on the nine pairs of states.

nodes.name: Good rounds (plurality)
assumptions: Let $\ell=3\log n$ and call a round good if every count is within $\sqrt{3\ell(\mu+2\ell)}$ of its mean $\mu$ (Bernstein)
conclusions: a round is bad with probability at most $(k+4)/n^3$
a good round keeps the invariant $c_i+12\sqrt{\ell c}\le\theta c$ ($i\ne m$), $S+12B\sqrt{\ell c}\le Bc$, multiplies $\Phi$ by $1+\kappa/(8000B)$ unless $4S+q\le n/10$, and keeps $\{4S+q\le n/10\}$
the first round from $q=0$, $(1+\alpha)c_i\le c_m$ enters the invariant with $\Phi\ge n/(2k^2)$
nodes.statement_short: Bernstein-good rounds are likely and preserve the plurality invariant while the potential $\Phi=\mu_m$ grows geometrically.
nodes.statement: Let $\ell=3\log n$ and call a round good if every count is within $\sqrt{3\ell(\mu+2\ell)}$ of its mean $\mu$ (Bernstein); a round is bad with probability at most $(k+4)/n^3$. Let $\theta=1/(1+\alpha)$, $\kappa=1-\theta$, $B=2\,\mathrm{md}(x_0)$, $S$ the nodes of colours other than $m$, $c=c_m$, $\Phi=\mu_m$. If $n\ge 2\cdot10^{12}K^2k^3\log n$ with $K=(1+\alpha)^2/\alpha$, a good round keeps the invariant $c_i+12\sqrt{\ell c}\le\theta c$ ($i\ne m$), $S+12B\sqrt{\ell c}\le Bc$, multiplies $\Phi$ by $1+\kappa/(8000B)$ unless $4S+q\le n/10$, and keeps $\{4S+q\le n/10\}$; the first round from $q=0$, $(1+\alpha)c_i\le c_m$ enters the invariant with $\Phi\ge n/(2k^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:pgood

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Drift-versus-deviation estimates for the colour ratios and for $\Phi$, using the plurality drift; first round handled separately.
nodes.statement: For the ratios: if $X\le tc/2$ one round cannot double it; if fewer than $n/20$ nodes are decided, $c$ grows by $16/9$, which absorbs the slack; otherwise $c\ge n/(20(1+B))$ and the deterministic drift $X\mu_m-\mu_Xc\ge\frac t2\kappa c^3/n$ beats the deviations, which needs $c^3\gtrsim n^2\log n$, i.e.\ $k\lesssim(n/\log n)^{1/3}$. For $\Phi$: $\mu_m+2\mu_q=n+(n-c-2q)^2/n+2W/n$ with $W=\sum_{j\ne m}c_j(c-c_j)\ge\kappa cS$ (the plurality drift, Lemma~1 of the paper). In the first round $q=0$, so the ratios square and $\mu_S=(\mathrm{md}-1)\mu_m$.

nodes.name: Ratio invariant
nodes.statement: For the ratios: if $X\le tc/2$ one round cannot double it; if fewer than $n/20$ nodes are decided, $c$ grows by $16/9$, which absorbs the slack; otherwise $c\ge n/(20(1+B))$ and the deterministic drift $X\mu_m-\mu_Xc\ge\frac t2\kappa c^3/n$ beats the deviations, which needs $c^3\gtrsim n^2\log n$, i.e.\ $k\lesssim(n/\log n)^{1/3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Drift beats deviations to keep the ratio invariant.

nodes.name: Growth of Phi
nodes.statement: For $\Phi$: $\mu_m+2\mu_q=n+(n-c-2q)^2/n+2W/n$ with $W=\sum_{j\ne m}c_j(c-c_j)\ge\kappa cS$ (the plurality drift, Lemma~1 of the paper).
nodes.statement_short: Plurality drift makes $\Phi$ grow.

nodes.name: First round
nodes.statement: In the first round $q=0$, so the ratios square and $\mu_S=(\mathrm{md}-1)\mu_m$.
nodes.statement_short: First round squares the ratios.

nodes.name: Plurality consensus
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri (SODA 2015), Thm 11
assumptions: every configuration without undecided nodes in which colour $m$ has at least $1+\alpha$ times as many nodes as every other colour
conclusions: all nodes hold $m$ after $\lceil C\,\mathrm{md}(x)\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-6/n$
nodes.statement_short: With a multiplicative plurality bias, undecided-state dynamics reaches plurality consensus in $O(\mathrm{md}\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha>0$ and $C=10^5((1+\alpha)^2/\alpha)^2$. For every $n$ with $\log n\ge C$, every $k$ with $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/3}$ and every configuration without undecided nodes in which colour $m$ has at least $1+\alpha$ times as many nodes as every other colour, all nodes hold $m$ after $\lceil C\,\mathrm{md}(x)\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-6/n$ (SODA 2015, Theorem~11; the range of $k$ is discussed in \texttt{FORMALIZATION\_DIFFERENCES.md}).
nodes.label: thm:plurality

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Enter the invariant, grow $\Phi$ with moving targets until $4S+q\le n/10$, then contract $4S+q$; union-bound the failures.
nodes.statement: One round into the invariant, then $T_2=\lceil\log(4k^2)/\log(1+\kappa/(8000B))\rceil\le 96000K\,\mathrm{md}\log n+1$ rounds with moving targets $\Phi\ge\frac n{2k^2}(1+\kappa/(8000B))^t$ or $4S+q\le n/10$, which end in $\{4S+q\le n/10\}$ since $\Phi\le n$; then $T_3=\lceil 8\log n\rceil$ rounds in which $4S+q$ contracts by $3/4$ in expectation. The failure probability is at most $T(k+4)/n^3+(3/4)^{T_3}n/10\le 6/n$.

nodes.name: Ratios R and Lambda
nodes.statement: With $R(c)=\sum_i c_i/c_1$ and $\Lambda(c)=R(c)^2/\mathrm{md}(c)$: after the first round most nodes are undecided (Lemma~3); their number $q$ then descends to about $n/2$ within $O(\log n)$ rounds while no colour exceeds $\gamma n/\mathrm{md}$ (Lemma~6); from there no colour grows faster than by a factor $1+O(1/\mathrm{md})$ per round (Lemma~7).
nodes.statement_short: Defines $R=\sum c_i/c_1$ and $\Lambda=R^2/\mathrm{md}$ and outlines the three-lemma lower-bound argument.

nodes.name: Corrections to BCNPS Lemmas 6 and 7
nodes.statement: Lemmas~6 and~7 need minor corrections: the window $|Q-n/2|\le 2\gamma^2/\mathrm{md}(\bar c)$ should read $2\gamma^2n/\mathrm{md}(\bar c)$; the proof of (17) uses the initial instead of the current monochromatic distance; in Lemma~7 the growth factor is $1+(4\gamma^2+2\gamma+1)/\mathrm{md}$, the lower bound (23) on $E[\Delta']$ reverses the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, and the proof needs $\gamma\ge1$ (any $\gamma>1/2$ would do) rather than an arbitrary $\gamma>0$; and both lemmas must bound the largest colour, not only the initial plurality (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/undecided/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#the-lower-bound-with-k-colours-lowerbound-roadmap-und-3}{details}).
nodes.statement_short: Lists the minor corrections needed in Lemmas 6 and 7 of BCNPS (window scaling, current md, growth factor, $\gamma\ge1$, largest colour).

nodes.name: Ratios and expectations
conclusions: $\mathrm{md}\le R\le k$ and $\mathrm{md}\le\Lambda\le k$
without undecided nodes $R=n/c_1$ and $\Lambda=n^2/\sum_ic_i^2$
$\mu_i=(1+(2\delta+c_i)/n)\,c_i$ and $E[Q'-n/2]=(2\delta^2-\sum_jc_j^2)/n$
nodes.statement_short: Basic bounds on $R$, $\Lambda$ and the expectations rewritten around $q=n/2$.
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{md}\le R\le k$ and $\mathrm{md}\le\Lambda\le k$; without undecided nodes $R=n/c_1$ and $\Lambda=n^2/\sum_ic_i^2$. With $\delta=q-n/2$: $\mu_i=(1+(2\delta+c_i)/n)\,c_i$ and $E[Q'-n/2]=(2\delta^2-\sum_jc_j^2)/n$ (the paper's (20) and (19)).
nodes.label: lem:lb-basic

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Elementary ratio bounds and Cauchy--Schwarz; the expectations are (3)--(4) rewritten.
nodes.statement: $c_i/c_1\in[0,1]$ gives $(c_i/c_1)^2\le c_i/c_1\le1$; Cauchy--Schwarz gives $R^2\le k\,\mathrm{md}$. The expectations are (3)--(4) rewritten with $q=n/2+\delta$.

nodes.name: First round; Lemma 3
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri (SODA 2015), Lemma 3
assumptions: From a configuration $x$ without undecided nodes, with plurality colour $m$
conclusions: $c_m\ge n/(2R^2)$, every colour has at most $2n/R^2$ nodes, and $n(1-2/\Lambda)\le q\le n(1-1/(2\Lambda))$
nodes.statement_short: After one round from an undecided-free configuration most nodes become undecided, w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Let $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/2}$. From a configuration $x$ without undecided nodes, with plurality colour $m$, after one round, with probability at least $1-C/n$: $c_m\ge n/(2R^2)$, every colour has at most $2n/R^2$ nodes, and $n(1-2/\Lambda)\le q\le n(1-1/(2\Lambda))$ ($R$, $\Lambda$ of $x$).
nodes.label: lem:lb-first

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Compute the first-round expectations with $q=0$ and control deviations in a good round.
nodes.statement: With $q=0$, $\mu_i=c_i^2/n\le\mu_m=n/R^2$ and $\mu_q=n-\sum_ic_i^2/n=n(1-1/\Lambda)$; in a good round (Lemma~\ref{lem:pgood}, deviation level $3\log n$) the deviations are small compared with $\mu_m\ge n/k^2\ge C^2\log n$ and with $n/\Lambda\ge n/k$. Proved with $C=100$.

nodes.name: Descent of the undecided nodes; Lemma 6
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri (SODA 2015), Lemma 6 (corrected)
assumptions: If every colour is at most $\gamma n/D$, with $\gamma\ge1$ and $0<D\le k$
conclusions: there is a round $t\le C\log n$ such that, with probability at least $1-C/n$, every colour is at most $\gamma n/\mathrm{md}(x)$ at each round $s\le t$, and at round $t$ also $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/\mathrm{md}(x)$
after one round $Q'\le(1+\delta^2)n/2$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$
$Q'\ge n/2-2\gamma^2n/D$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$
after one round $Q'\le(1+\delta^2)n/2$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$

assumptions: If every colour is at most $\gamma n/D$, with $\gamma\ge1$ and $0<D\le k$
conclusions: $Q'\ge n/2-2\gamma^2n/D$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$

nodes.statement_short: The number of undecided nodes descends to about $n/2$ within $O(\log n)$ rounds while every colour stays $O(n/\mathrm{md})$.
nodes.statement: Let $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/6}$. If $q=(1+\delta)n/2$ with $1-\delta\ge1/(2k)$, then after one round $Q'\le(1+\delta^2)n/2$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$ (16). If every colour is at most $\gamma n/D$, with $\gamma\ge1$ and $0<D\le k$, then $Q'\ge n/2-2\gamma^2n/D$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$ (17, corrected). Hence there are $\gamma\ge1$ and $C$ such that, for $x$ without undecided nodes with $\mathrm{md}(x)\ge C$ and $y$ satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-first}, there is a round $t\le C\log n$ such that, with probability at least $1-C/n$, every colour is at most $\gamma n/\mathrm{md}(x)$ at each round $s\le t$, and at round $t$ also $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/\mathrm{md}(x)$.
nodes.label: lem:lb-descent

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mu_q$ from both sides, choose the descent round deterministically and iterate an explicit colour envelope with moving targets.
nodes.statement: (16): $\mu_q=(1+\delta^2)n/2-\sum_jc_j^2/n$ and $\sum_jc_j^2\ge(n-q)^2/k$. (17): $\mu_q\ge n/2-\sum_jc_j^2/n$ and $\sum_jc_j^2\le(\max_jc_j)(n-q)\le\gamma n^2/D$. The round $t$ is deterministic: the first $s$ with $(1-1/\Lambda)^{2^s}\le4\gamma^2/\mathrm{md}$. The colours follow an explicit envelope (at most $8n/D$, then at most $\gamma n/D$ with $\gamma=24$), iterated with moving targets. Proved with $\gamma=24$ and $C=10^6$.

nodes.name: Upper bound (16)
nodes.statement: (16): $\mu_q=(1+\delta^2)n/2-\sum_jc_j^2/n$ and $\sum_jc_j^2\ge(n-q)^2/k$.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound on $Q'$.

nodes.name: Lower bound (17)
nodes.statement: (17): $\mu_q\ge n/2-\sum_jc_j^2/n$ and $\sum_jc_j^2\le(\max_jc_j)(n-q)\le\gamma n^2/D$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound on $Q'$.

nodes.name: Choice of round t
nodes.statement: The round $t$ is deterministic: the first $s$ with $(1-1/\Lambda)^{2^s}\le4\gamma^2/\mathrm{md}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the descent round $t$.

nodes.name: Colour envelope
nodes.statement: The colours follow an explicit envelope (at most $8n/D$, then at most $\gamma n/D$ with $\gamma=24$), iterated with moving targets. Proved with $\gamma=24$ and $C=10^6$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate a colour envelope with moving targets.

nodes.name: Plateau; Lemma 7
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri (SODA 2015), Lemma 7 (corrected)
assumptions: If $C\le D\le k$, $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/D$ and every colour is at most $\gamma n/D$
conclusions: for every $T\le D/C$, after $T$ rounds, with probability at least $1-C/n$, every colour is at most $2\gamma n/D$ and $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/D$
nodes.statement_short: Near $q\approx n/2$, colours grow by at most a factor 2 over $D/C$ rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma\ge1$ and $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/4}$. If $C\le D\le k$, $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/D$ and every colour is at most $\gamma n/D$, then for every $T\le D/C$, after $T$ rounds, with probability at least $1-C/n$, every colour is at most $2\gamma n/D$ and $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/D$.
nodes.label: lem:lb-plateau

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: One-round growth factor bound via (19)--(20), iterated over $D/C$ rounds.
nodes.statement: One round multiplies the bound $B\in[\gamma n/D,2\gamma n/D]$ on the colours by at most $1+(4\gamma^2+2\gamma+1)/D$ and keeps the window, with probability at least $1-C/n^2$: by (20), $2\delta+c_i\le(4\gamma^2+2\gamma)n/D$, and by (19) $E[\Delta']\le 8\gamma^4n/D^2$ and $E[\Delta']\ge-(\max_jc_j)(n-q)/n\ge-(4\gamma/3)n/D$. Iterate for $T\le D/C$ rounds, during which the factor stays at most $2$. Proved with $C=30\gamma^2$.

nodes.name: One-round bound
nodes.statement: One round multiplies the bound $B\in[\gamma n/D,2\gamma n/D]$ on the colours by at most $1+(4\gamma^2+2\gamma+1)/D$ and keeps the window, with probability at least $1-C/n^2$: by (20), $2\delta+c_i\le(4\gamma^2+2\gamma)n/D$, and by (19) $E[\Delta']\le 8\gamma^4n/D^2$ and $E[\Delta']\ge-(\max_jc_j)(n-q)/n\ge-(4\gamma/3)n/D$.
nodes.statement_short: One round grows colours by at most $1+O(\gamma^2/D)$ and keeps the window.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: Iterate for $T\le D/C$ rounds, during which the factor stays at most $2$. Proved with $C=30\gamma^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate over $T\le D/C$ rounds.

nodes.name: Lower bound; Theorem 8
nodes.origin_citation: Becchetti, Clementi, Natale, Pasquale, Silvestri (SODA 2015), Thm 8
also_stated_at: The same paper (SODA 2015, Theorem~8) shows that, without any bias, the dynamics needs $\Omega(\mathrm{md}(c))$ rounds.
conclusions: for every $T$ with $CT\le\mathrm{md}(x)$, after $T$ rounds every colour has at most $Cn/\mathrm{md}(x)$ nodes with probability at least $1-C/n$
for every $T$ with $C(T+1)\le\mathrm{md}(x)$, all nodes hold the same colour after $T$ rounds with probability at most $C/n$
the convergence time is $\Omega(\mathrm{md}(x))$ with probability at least $1-C/n$
nodes.statement_short: Without bias, the $k$-colour undecided-state dynamics needs $\Omega(\mathrm{md}(x))$ rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement: There is $C>0$ such that, for every $n$ with $\log n\ge C$, every $k$ with $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/6}$ and every configuration $x$ without undecided nodes: for every $T$ with $CT\le\mathrm{md}(x)$, after $T$ rounds every colour has at most $Cn/\mathrm{md}(x)$ nodes with probability at least $1-C/n$; and for every $T$ with $C(T+1)\le\mathrm{md}(x)$, all nodes hold the same colour after $T$ rounds with probability at most $C/n$. Since monochromatic configurations are absorbing, the convergence time is $\Omega(\mathrm{md}(x))$ with probability at least $1-C/n$.
nodes.label: thm:lb

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Compose the first-round, descent and plateau lemmas by the Markov property.
nodes.statement: Compose Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-first}, Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent} and Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-plateau} (with the $\gamma$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent}, $D=\mathrm{md}(x)$) by the Markov property; a round $T$ up to the descent round is covered by the bound at every round of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent}. A monochromatic configuration has $n>Cn/\mathrm{md}(x)$ nodes of one colour once $\mathrm{md}(x)>C$. Proved with $C=1017429$ for the first form and $2C$ for the second.

nodes.name: Compose the lemmas
nodes.statement: Compose Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-first}, Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent} and Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-plateau} (with the $\gamma$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent}, $D=\mathrm{md}(x)$) by the Markov property; a round $T$ up to the descent round is covered by the bound at every round of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent}.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the three lemmas via the Markov property.

nodes.name: No early consensus
nodes.statement: A monochromatic configuration has $n>Cn/\mathrm{md}(x)$ nodes of one colour once $\mathrm{md}(x)>C$. Proved with $C=1017429$ for the first form and $2C$ for the second.
nodes.statement_short: Monochromatic configurations violate the colour bound.

nodes.name: Sequential undecided-state dynamics
nodes.statement_short: Population-protocol version: a uniform ordered pair interacts and only the responder updates (AAE approximate majority).
nodes.statement: At each step an ordered pair (initiator, responder) of distinct agents is drawn uniformly among the $n(n-1)$ such pairs, independently of the past; only the responder updates, by the rule of Definition~\ref{def:usd} applied to the initiator's state. This is the approximate-majority protocol of Angluin, Aspnes and Eisenstat (Distributed Computing 21, 2008), with $x$, $y$ and blank written $a$, $b$ and $u$.
nodes.label: def:seq

nodes.name: One-step formula
conclusions: The expectation of a function of the next configuration that depends only on the states of the initiator and the responder is its value on idle interactions plus the four state-changing transitions $xb$, $yb$, $xy$, $yx$, weighted by $aq$, $bq$, $ab$, $ab$ pairs out of $n(n-1)$
nodes.statement: The expectation of a function of the next configuration that depends only on the states of the initiator and the responder is its value on idle interactions plus the four state-changing transitions $xb$, $yb$, $xy$, $yx$, weighted by $aq$, $bq$, $ab$, $ab$ pairs out of $n(n-1)$ (with $q$ the number of blank agents).
nodes.label: lem:seq-step

nodes.name: Weighted supermartingales
assumptions: If one step never increases $e^{\varphi}F$ in expectation
conclusions: $e^{\sum_{\text{path}}\varphi}F$ has expectation at most $F$ at every finite time

Markov's inequality bounds the probability
that the path sum of $\varphi$ is large
nodes.statement: If one step never increases $e^{\varphi}F$ in expectation, then $e^{\sum_{\text{path}}\varphi}F$ has expectation at most $F$ at every finite time, and Markov's inequality bounds the probability that the path sum of $\varphi$ is large.
nodes.label: lem:seq-mart

nodes.name: Six potentials
conclusions: satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:seq-mart} with suitable weights
nodes.statement_short: Six explicit potentials are weighted supermartingales for the sequential dynamics.
nodes.statement: The potentials $1/((a-b)^2+4n)$ (state-changing interactions), $1$ (central region), $1/(a+b)$ (blank corner), $3b+q+1$ and $3a+q+1$ (the two opinion corners), and $e^{-\lambda\max(a-b,0)}$ (the gap stays positive) satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:seq-mart} with suitable weights.
nodes.label: lem:seq-pot

nodes.name: Convergence; AAE Theorem 1
assumptions: from every non-blank configuration of $n\ge2$ agents
conclusions: all agents agree, with probability at least $1-C/n^c$
nodes.statement: For every $c$ there is $C$ such that from every non-blank configuration of $n\ge2$ agents, after $T\ge Cn\log n$ interactions all agents agree, with probability at least $1-C/n^c$.
nodes.label: thm:seq-conv

nodes.name: Correctness; AAE Theorem 2
conclusions: all agents hold $a$, with probability at least $1-C/n^c$
nodes.statement: For every $c$ there is $C$ such that if initially $a-b\ge C\sqrt n\log n$, then after $T\ge Cn\log n$ interactions all agents hold $a$, with probability at least $1-C/n^c$.
nodes.label: thm:seq-maj

nodes.name: Finite weighted expectations
nodes.genus: nonnegative real weights summing to one
nodes.statement: A distribution has nonnegative real weights summing to one. A kernel is a family of such distributions, one for each state. Expectations are finite sums. These are shared library definitions, not numbered results of the paper.
nodes.label: def:weights

nodes.name: Stationary distribution exists
conclusions: has a stationary distribution
nodes.statement: Every finite nonempty stochastic matrix has a stationary distribution.
nodes.label: thm:stationary

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Cesàro averages of evolved distributions plus compactness of the simplex.
nodes.statement: The shared library uses Ces\`aro averages of evolved distributions and compactness of the finite probability simplex. This supplies the existence fact recalled before Lemma 2.2; uniqueness is not required.

nodes.name: Finite-chain absorption
assumptions: An absorbing target accessible from every state of a finite chain
conclusions:
admits a
uniform positive success probability in a fixed number of rounds

The survival
probability decays geometrically in blocks and tends to zero
nodes.statement: An absorbing target accessible from every state of a finite chain admits a uniform positive success probability in a fixed number of rounds. The survival probability decays geometrically in blocks and tends to zero.
nodes.label: thm:generic-absorption

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Common block length beyond all access times gives a uniform contraction; iterate.
nodes.statement: Take a common block length exceeding all finitely many access times, then a maximum survival probability strictly below one. Iterate the resulting contraction.

nodes.name: Finite-horizon optional stopping
assumptions: If an observable equals $\varphi_A$ on $A$, $\varphi_B$ on $B$, lies in $[\varphi_B+m,\varphi_B+M]$ elsewhere, and keeps its expectation up to time $T$
conclusions: $\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_B-(\varphi_A-\varphi_B)\Pr(X_T\in A)$ lies between $m$ and $M$ times the probability of lying in neither event at time $T$
nodes.statement_short: Finite-horizon optional stopping bound for a martingale observable between two target sets.
nodes.statement: If an observable equals $\varphi_A$ on $A$, $\varphi_B$ on $B$, lies in $[\varphi_B+m,\varphi_B+M]$ elsewhere, and keeps its expectation up to time $T$, then $\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_B-(\varphi_A-\varphi_B)\Pr(X_T\in A)$ lies between $m$ and $M$ times the probability of lying in neither event at time $T$.
nodes.label: thm:optional-stopping

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the observable pointwise on $A$ and off $A\cup B$, take expectations and bound.
nodes.statement: A shared library result (roadmap FND-4): decompose the observable pointwise into its values on $A$ and off $A\cup B$, take expectations, and bound the second part.

nodes.name: Synchronous copying
nodes.statement_short: Each vertex independently samples a vertex from its row of $H$ and copies its colour.
nodes.statement: A configuration is $s:V\to C$. Independently sample $r(i)$ according to row $H_i$, then set the next configuration to $i\mapsto s(r(i))$.
nodes.label: def:step

nodes.name: Configuration transition formula
conclusions: the transition probability is \[P_{st}=\prod_i\sum_{j:s(j)=t(i)}H_{ij}.\]
nodes.statement: For configurations $s,t$, the transition probability is \[P_{st}=\prod_i\sum_{j:s(j)=t(i)}H_{ij}.\] For Boolean colors a white target vertex contributes $\sum_j H_{ij}s(j)$; a black target contributes its complement, giving the paper's product formula.
nodes.label: lem:product

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Pushforward of independent samples; factor the equality indicator over vertices.
nodes.statement: The configuration distribution is the pushforward of the independently sampled neighbors. Factor its equality indicator into a product over vertices.

nodes.name: Monochromatic-edge propagation
conclusions:
every Boolean configuration has a possible
finite path to a constant configuration
nodes.statement: On a connected nonbipartite graph every Boolean configuration has a possible finite path to a constant configuration.
nodes.label: lem:propagation

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number of vertices outside a monochromatic region grown from a monochromatic edge. Nonbipartiteness supplies the initial monochromatic edge.
nodes.statement: A coloring without a monochromatic edge would be a proper two-coloring. Starting with a monochromatic edge, each vertex of its region can keep that color by sampling an internal neighbor. Connectedness supplies an edge leaving every proper region. One more vertex can copy across that edge. Induction on the number of vertices outside the region gives consensus.

nodes.name: Monochromatic edge exists
nodes.statement: A coloring without a monochromatic edge would be a proper two-coloring.
nodes.statement_short: Nonbipartiteness gives a monochromatic edge.

nodes.name: Region keeps its color
nodes.statement: Starting with a monochromatic edge, each vertex of its region can keep that color by sampling an internal neighbor.
nodes.statement_short: The monochromatic region can persist.

nodes.name: Region grows
nodes.statement: Connectedness supplies an edge leaving every proper region. One more vertex can copy across that edge.
nodes.statement_short: Grow the region by one vertex across a boundary edge.
