nodes.name: Induction
nodes.statement: Induction on the number of vertices outside the region gives consensus.
nodes.statement_short: Induct to reach consensus.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1: absorption
conclusions:
Both constant configurations
are absorbing
the probability of remaining nonconstant tends to zero
nodes.statement: Assume $H_{ij}>0$ whenever $i,j$ are adjacent; extra support, such as self-loops, is allowed. Both constant configurations are absorbing, and the probability of remaining nonconstant tends to zero. This is the finite-time survival formulation of the paper's transience claim.
nodes.label: lem:21

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Propagation gives accessibility; apply the finite-chain absorption theorem.
nodes.statement: Every possible copying round has positive probability. Thus graph propagation gives accessibility. Apply the shared finite-chain absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Accessibility
nodes.statement: Every possible copying round has positive probability. Thus graph propagation gives accessibility.
nodes.statement_short: Propagation paths have positive probability.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.3: invariant stationary weight
conclusions: the expected white mass at every finite time is the initial mass $\sum_i\pi_i s(i)$
nodes.statement: For any stationary distribution $\pi$, the expected white mass at every finite time is the initial mass $\sum_i\pi_i s(i)$. No graph connectivity assumption is imposed on this invariant.
nodes.label: lem:23

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: One-step preservation from $\pi H=\pi$, then induction.
nodes.statement: A vertex's expected next color indicator is $\sum_jH_{ij}s(j)$. Interchanging finite sums and using $\pi H=\pi$ proves one-step preservation; induction proves the iterated statement.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.2: limiting identification
conclusions:
The discrepancy between expected stationary white mass and all-white
probability lies between zero and nonconsensus probability
all-white probability converges to initial stationary white mass
nodes.statement: The discrepancy between expected stationary white mass and all-white probability lies between zero and nonconsensus probability. Consequently all-white probability converges to initial stationary white mass. The implementation combines the paper's limiting identification with the invariant from Lemma 2.3 when stating the limit.
nodes.label: lem:22

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Optional stopping with the two consensus states bounds the discrepancy; squeeze using absorption.
nodes.statement: Pointwise, the white mass agrees with the all-white indicator on constant configurations and lies in $[0,1]$ elsewhere. Finite-horizon optional stopping, with the two consensus configurations as targets and the invariant of Lemma 2.3, bounds the discrepancy; squeeze it using Lemma 2.1.

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 (Hassin--Peleg)
assumptions:
Define eventual all-white probability as the supremum of the increasing
finite-time all-white probabilities.
conclusions: It equals the initial stationary white mass.
nodes.statement: Define eventual all-white probability as the supremum of the increasing finite-time all-white probabilities. It equals the initial stationary white mass.
nodes.label: thm:21

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Monotone bounded probabilities converge; identify the limit by Lemma 2.2.
nodes.statement: Consensus is absorbing, so the probabilities increase and are bounded by one. Their supremum is their limit. Identify this limit using Lemma 2.2.

nodes.name: Monotone limit
nodes.statement: Consensus is absorbing, so the probabilities increase and are bounded by one. Their supremum is their limit.
nodes.statement_short: Supremum equals limit by monotonicity.

nodes.name: Identify limit
nodes.statement: Identify this limit using Lemma 2.2.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.2 identifies the limit.

nodes.name: Corollary 2.2 and regular graphs
conclusions: $\pi_i=d_i/(2|E|)$, so all-white consensus has probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=1}d_i/(2|E|)$

On a regular graph this is the initial
fraction of white vertices.
nodes.statement: For uniform neighbor sampling, $\pi_i=d_i/(2|E|)$, so all-white consensus has probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=1}d_i/(2|E|)$. On a regular graph this is the initial fraction of white vertices.
nodes.label: cor:22

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Verify degree weights are stationary; equal degrees give uniform weights.
nodes.statement: The degree-sum formula normalizes these weights. In the stationarity equation, the degree cancels the reciprocal sampling degree; undirected adjacency gives the remaining column sum. Equal degrees then give uniform vertex weights.

nodes.name: Normalization
nodes.statement: The degree-sum formula normalizes these weights.
nodes.statement_short: Degree weights sum to one.

nodes.name: Stationarity
nodes.statement: In the stationarity equation, the degree cancels the reciprocal sampling degree; undirected adjacency gives the remaining column sum.
nodes.statement_short: Degree weights satisfy stationarity.

nodes.name: Regular graphs
nodes.statement: Equal degrees then give uniform vertex weights.
nodes.statement_short: Regular case.

nodes.name: Consensus in a specified color
assumptions: For a finite color set and any specified color $c$
conclusions: its eventual consensus probability is $\sum_{i:s(i)=c}\pi_i$
These probabilities sum to one.
nodes.statement: For a finite color set and any specified color $c$, its eventual consensus probability is $\sum_{i:s(i)=c}\pi_i$. These probabilities sum to one.
nodes.label: thm:colors

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Project to the Boolean indicator of colour $c$ and apply Theorem 2.1.
nodes.statement: The color-indicator projection commutes with every copying step and with iterated expectations. Its all-white event is exactly all-$c$ consensus. Apply Theorem 2.1 to this Boolean projection.

nodes.name: Projection
nodes.statement: The color-indicator projection commutes with every copying step and with iterated expectations. Its all-white event is exactly all-$c$ consensus.
nodes.statement_short: Boolean projection of colour $c$.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem 2.1 to this Boolean projection.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2.1.

nodes.name: Rounds, backward map, Wright--Fisher sampling
nodes.statement_short: Backward map $r_1\circ\cdots\circ r_T$ of a run, disagreement indicator, and Wright--Fisher (uniform with self-loops) sampling.
nodes.statement: A run applies rounds $r_1,\dots,r_T\colon V\to V$ in order. Its backward map is $r_1\circ r_2\circ\cdots\circ r_T$. The disagreement indicator is $0$ on constant configurations and $1$ otherwise. Wright--Fisher sampling picks every row uniformly on $V$, self included, i.e.\ the complete graph with self-loops.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: def:backward

nodes.name: Duality with coalescing walks
conclusions: the configuration is $s\circ r_1\circ\cdots\circ r_T$

If the backward map is constant, the
configuration is a consensus.
nodes.statement: After rounds $r_1,\dots,r_T$ the configuration is $s\circ r_1\circ\cdots\circ r_T$: running the voter forward reads the initial colours through the backward map, whose point images are coalescing random walks. If the backward map is constant, the configuration is a consensus.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: lem:duality

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the list of rounds.
nodes.statement: Induction on the list of rounds, since one round maps $s$ to $s\circ r$.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Rounds are independent and uniform
conclusions: a round is uniform on $V\to V$

the $T$-step
configuration kernel is the average over $T$ independent uniform rounds
nodes.statement: Under Wright--Fisher sampling a round is uniform on $V\to V$, so the $T$-step configuration kernel is the average over $T$ independent uniform rounds.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: lem:wf-rounds

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Product weights are uniform; induct on $T$.
nodes.statement: The product weights are all $n^{-n}$; induct on $T$, peeling off the first round.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Meeting probability
conclusions: Two coordinates of a uniform map $V\to V$ agree with probability $1/n$
the backward walks from two distinct vertices have not met after $T$ rounds with probability exactly $(1-1/n)^T$
nodes.statement: Two coordinates of a uniform map $V\to V$ agree with probability $1/n$. Hence the backward walks from two distinct vertices have not met after $T$ rounds with probability exactly $(1-1/n)^T$.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: lem:meeting

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Peel off the first round and induct on $T$.
nodes.statement: Peel off the first round, swap it with the remaining average, and multiply by the one-round probability of not meeting; induct on $T$.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Consensus time
conclusions: The probability that no consensus is reached after $T$ rounds is at most $(n-1)(1-1/n)^T$
consensus is reached within $2n\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1-1/n$
nodes.statement: The probability that no consensus is reached after $T$ rounds is at most $(n-1)(1-1/n)^T$. Consequently consensus is reached within $2n\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1-1/n$.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: thm:consensus-time

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over the other $n-1$ backward walks meeting a fixed one, plus $(1-1/n)^T\le e^{-T/n}$.
nodes.statement: Consensus holds once every backward walk has met the walk of a fixed vertex; apply the union bound over the other $n-1$ vertices and the meeting probability, then $(1-1/n)^T\le e^{-T/n}\le n^{-2}$ for $T\ge 2n\log n$.
nodes.section: 89 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Propagation through the kernel support
assumptions: On a connected graph whose edges are charged by $H$
conclusions:
a monochromatic region in which
every vertex charges a vertex of the region grows to consensus through possible rounds
the region $\{v\}$ qualifies, so nonconsensus probability tends to zero, bipartite graphs included

assumptions: On a connected graph whose edges are charged by $H$
conclusions:
a monochromatic region in which
every vertex charges a vertex of the region grows to consensus through possible rounds
the region $\{v\}$ qualifies, so nonconsensus probability tends to zero, bipartite graphs included

nodes.statement: Call a round possible for $H$ when every vertex samples a vertex of positive weight in its row. On a connected graph whose edges are charged by $H$, a monochromatic region in which every vertex charges a vertex of the region grows to consensus through possible rounds. If $H_{vv}>0$ for one vertex $v$, the region $\{v\}$ qualifies, so nonconsensus probability tends to zero, bipartite graphs included.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: lem:kernel-propagation

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Grow the region as in Lemma 2.1 and apply finite-chain absorption.
nodes.statement: As in Lemma~2.1: a boundary vertex copies its neighbour in the region, vertices of the region copy inside it, and all other vertices copy any vertex of positive weight. Possible rounds have positive probability, and the finite-chain absorption theorem applies.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Hassin--Peleg self-loop remark (p. 254)
assumptions: On a connected graph, bipartite or not
if $H$ charges every edge and $H_{vv}>0$ for some vertex $v$
conclusions: consensus in colour $c$ has probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=c}\pi_i$ for every stationary $\pi$
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, bipartite or not, if $H$ charges every edge and $H_{vv}>0$ for some vertex $v$, then consensus in colour $c$ has probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=c}\pi_i$ for every stationary $\pi$.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: thm:selfloop

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Nonconsensus vanishes, so Lemma 2.2 and the colour projection apply.
nodes.statement: Lemma~2.2 only needs nonconsensus probability to vanish; then project colours as in Section~2.3.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Lazy voter
conclusions: The lazy kernel $(I+H)/2$ has the stationary distributions of $H$ and positive self-loops
On any connected graph the lazy voter $(I+D^{-1}A)/2$ reaches consensus in colour $c$ with probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=c} d_i/2m$
nodes.statement: The lazy kernel $(I+H)/2$ has the stationary distributions of $H$ and positive self-loops. On any connected graph the lazy voter $(I+D^{-1}A)/2$ reaches consensus in colour $c$ with probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=c} d_i/2m$.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: thm:lazy

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Apply the self-loop remark to the lazy kernel with degree weights.
nodes.statement: Apply the Remark to $(I+H)/2$; for uniform neighbour sampling use the degree distribution.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Neutral Wright--Fisher fixation
assumptions: If every offspring picks a uniform parent, itself included
conclusions: allele $a$ fixes with probability $c_a/n$
nodes.statement: If every offspring picks a uniform parent, itself included, allele $a$ fixes with probability $c_a/n$, where $c_a$ is its initial number of copies.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: thm:wright-fisher

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Uniform weights are stationary and positive; apply Section 2.3 or the self-loop remark.
nodes.statement: The uniform distribution is stationary and every entry is positive. For $n\ge 3$ the complete graph is nonbipartite and Section~2.3 applies; for every $n$ the Remark applies.
nodes.section: 90 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Correction to the survey's Theorem 8
nodes.statement: For the synchronous voter with plain uniform-neighbour sampling, Theorem~8 of the survey needs a minor correction (a nonbipartiteness hypothesis, or a lazy walk); this section formalizes the lazy version, and Section~\ref{sec:hp-plain-walk} the plain walk on nonbipartite graphs (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/voter/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#41-survey-theorem-8-needs-a-minor-correction-the-lazy-walk-is-formalized}{details}).
nodes.statement_short: Survey Theorem 8 needs a nonbipartiteness hypothesis or a lazy walk for the plain synchronous voter.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Two-token walk, lazy sampling
nodes.statement_short: Two tokens moved by the same voter rounds (independent off the diagonal, together on it); the lazy kernel stays put with probability 1/2.
nodes.statement: For a sampling kernel $H$, two tokens move with the rounds of the voter dynamics: the token at $x$ moves to $r(x)$, where $r$ is drawn from the independent product of the rows of $H$. Off the diagonal the tokens make independent $H$-steps; on the diagonal they move together. The lazy kernel of a graph samples the vertex itself with probability $1/2$ and otherwise a uniformly random neighbour. Rounds can also be composed on the left, $W\mapsto r\circ W$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus
nodes.label: def:pairwalk

nodes.name: Duality for every kernel
conclusions: the probability that no consensus is reached after $T$ rounds is at most the sum over $v\neq u_0$ of the probability that the tokens started at $v$ and $u_0$ are apart after $T$ steps
nodes.statement: For every sampling kernel, the probability that no consensus is reached after $T$ rounds is at most the sum over $v\neq u_0$ of the probability that the tokens started at $v$ and $u_0$ are apart after $T$ steps.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus
nodes.label: lem:duality-general

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Left and right compositions of i.i.d. rounds have the same law; read at two vertices this is the two-token walk; union bound.
nodes.statement: The voter dynamics on maps started from the identity composes the rounds on the right; composing them on the left gives the same finite-time expectations, since the rounds are independent and identically distributed (induction on $T$, exchanging two finite expectations). The left composition read at two vertices is the two-token walk. Conclude with the pointwise union bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:consensus-time}.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Left vs right composition
nodes.statement: The voter dynamics on maps started from the identity composes the rounds on the right; composing them on the left gives the same finite-time expectations, since the rounds are independent and identically distributed (induction on $T$, exchanging two finite expectations).
nodes.statement_short: Left and right compositions agree in law.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Two-token reading
nodes.statement: The left composition read at two vertices is the two-token walk.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the two-token walk.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: Conclude with the pointwise union bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:consensus-time}.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over vertices.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Hassin--Peleg Theorem 2.4, tail form
assumptions: If from every pair of vertices the tokens are apart after $T_0$ steps with probability at most $1/2$
conclusions: consensus fails after $kT_0$ rounds with probability at most $(n-1)2^{-k}$
nodes.statement: If from every pair of vertices the tokens are apart after $T_0$ steps with probability at most $1/2$, then consensus fails after $kT_0$ rounds with probability at most $(n-1)2^{-k}$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus
nodes.label: thm:hp24

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Submultiplicativity in blocks of $T_0$ steps plus the duality lemma.
nodes.statement: The diagonal is absorbing, so the probabilities of being apart are submultiplicative in blocks of $T_0$ steps; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:duality-general}.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Hitting times of the lazy walk; Fact 2.3
assumptions: On a connected graph with Laplacian $L$ and $\mathrm{vol}=\sum_z d_z$
conclusions: the system $h(y)=0$, $(Lh)(x)=2d_x$ for $x\neq y$ has a nonnegative solution $h_y$
$\sum_z d_z h_y(z)-\mathrm{vol}\,h_y(x)=\sum_z d_z h_x(z)-\mathrm{vol}\,h_x(y)$
$h_y(x)+h_x(y)\le 4\,\mathrm{vol}\,(n-1)\le 4n^3$
nodes.statement_short: Lazy-walk hitting times solve a Laplacian system, satisfy a symmetry identity, and have commute time at most $4n^3$.
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with Laplacian $L$ and $\mathrm{vol}=\sum_z d_z$, the system $h(y)=0$, $(Lh)(x)=2d_x$ for $x\neq y$ has a nonnegative solution $h_y$, the expected hitting time of $y$ for the lazy walk. It satisfies $\sum_z d_z h_y(z)-\mathrm{vol}\,h_y(x)=\sum_z d_z h_x(z)-\mathrm{vol}\,h_x(y)$ and $h_y(x)+h_x(y)\le 4\,\mathrm{vol}\,(n-1)\le 4n^3$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus
nodes.label: lem:hitting

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Maximum principle for solvability, symmetry of $L$ for the identity, energy plus Cauchy--Schwarz along a path for the bound.
nodes.statement: The maximum principle makes the linear system injective, hence surjective. The identity is the symmetry of $L$. For the bound, $\psi=h_y-h_x$ has energy $\psi^\top L\psi=2\,\mathrm{vol}\,(h_y(x)+h_x(y))$; apply Cauchy--Schwarz along a path from $x$ to $y$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Solvability
nodes.statement: The maximum principle makes the linear system injective, hence surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Maximum principle gives a solution.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Symmetry identity
nodes.statement: The identity is the symmetry of $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Identity from symmetry of $L$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Commute-time bound
nodes.statement: For the bound, $\psi=h_y-h_x$ has energy $\psi^\top L\psi=2\,\mathrm{vol}\,(h_y(x)+h_x(y))$; apply Cauchy--Schwarz along a path from $x$ to $y$.
nodes.statement_short: Energy and Cauchy--Schwarz bound the commute time.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Sequential and synchronous walks
assumptions: If a nonnegative potential $F$ drops by one in expectation under a step of either token
conclusions: the sequential walks are apart after $T$ steps with probability at most $F/T$
at most $3/4$ once $T\ge 2\sup F$
nodes.statement: Let the two tokens move one at a time, meeting being checked after each move. If a nonnegative potential $F$ drops by one in expectation under a step of either token, the sequential walks are apart after $T$ steps with probability at most $F/T$. For a lazy kernel, the synchronous tokens are apart after $T+1$ steps with probability at most the average of the indicator of starting apart and the sequential survival; hence at most $3/4$ once $T\ge 2\sup F$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus
nodes.label: lem:sequential

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Two inductions on $T$, using laziness when a token lands on the other's old position.
nodes.statement: Two inductions on $T$. When the first token lands on the old position of the second, the second stays put with probability at least $1/2$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Meeting time of lazy walks; Lemma 2.4
nodes.origin_citation: Hassin & Peleg 2001, Lemma 2.4; Kanade, Mallmann-Trenn, Sauerwald (SODA 2019) Prop. B.9
assumptions: On a connected graph with $n$ vertices
conclusions: two lazy walks are apart after $3(16n^3+1)\le 51n^3$ steps with probability at most $1/2$, and after $51kn^3$ steps with probability at most $2^{-k}$, from every pair of start vertices
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with $n$ vertices, two lazy walks are apart after $3(16n^3+1)\le 51n^3$ steps with probability at most $1/2$, and after $51kn^3$ steps with probability at most $2^{-k}$, from every pair of start vertices.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus
nodes.label: thm:meeting-lazy

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Hitting-time potential bounded by $8n^3$ in the sequential-walk lemma, then submultiplicativity.
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sequential} to the potential $h_y(x)-\sum_z d_z h_y(z)/\mathrm{vol}+4n^3$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting}, bounded by $8n^3$, then submultiplicativity.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Hassin--Peleg Theorem 2.5; Survey Theorem 8
assumptions: On every connected graph with $n$ vertices and from every initial colouring
conclusions: the lazy voter dynamics reaches consensus within $255\,n^3\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1-1/n$
nodes.statement: On every connected graph with $n$ vertices and from every initial colouring, the lazy voter dynamics reaches consensus within $255\,n^3\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1-1/n$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus
nodes.label: thm:hp25

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Duality plus the lazy meeting-time bound with $k=\lfloor T/(51n^3)\rfloor$.
nodes.statement: With $k=\lfloor T/(51n^3)\rfloor$, Lemma~\ref{lem:duality-general} and Theorem~\ref{thm:meeting-lazy} bound the failure probability by $(n-1)2^{-k}\le 1/n$.
nodes.section: 91 Section 2.4 on connected graphs: meeting time and $O(n^3\log n)$ consensus

nodes.name: Plain synchronous voter
nodes.statement: Hassin and Peleg's own setting is the plain synchronous voter, in which every vertex copies a uniformly random neighbour, on a connected nonbipartite graph.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Correction to Hassin--Peleg Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement: The proof of Lemma~2.4 needs a minor correction: it uses $\mathrm{Diam}(\tilde G)\le n$, but the diameter of $\tilde G$ can be $2n-3$ (a path ending in a triangle); $\mathrm{Diam}(\tilde G)\le 2n-1$ only changes the constant, and our route does not use the diameter (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/voter/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#43-the-plain-walk-on-connected-nonbipartite-graphs-lemma-24-and-theorem-25}{details}).
nodes.statement_short: Hassin--Peleg's Lemma 2.4 proof uses a wrong diameter bound for the double cover; the constant changes only.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Hitting times h
nodes.statement: Hitting times $h$ are those of Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting}, twice the hitting times of the plain walk.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Bipartite double cover
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde G=G\times K_2$ with edges between layers along edges of $G$.
nodes.statement: The graph $\tilde G=G\times K_2$ has vertices $(a,i)$, $a\in V$, $i\in\{0,1\}$, and $(a,i)\sim(b,j)$ iff $a\sim b$ in $G$ and $i\neq j$. Swapping the layers is an automorphism, degrees are those of $G$, and $\mathrm{vol}\,\tilde G=2\,\mathrm{vol}\,G$.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover
nodes.label: def:double-cover

nodes.name: Connectivity of the double cover
conclusions: $\tilde G$ is connected
nodes.statement: If $G$ is connected and not $2$-colourable, then $\tilde G$ is connected.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover
nodes.label: lem:double-cover-connected

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Lift walks to the cover; disconnection would give a proper 2-colouring.
nodes.statement: Walks of $G$ lift to $\tilde G$, flipping the layer at every step. If $\tilde G$ were disconnected, ``$(w,0)$ is reachable from $(x_0,0)$'' would be a proper $2$-colouring of $G$.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Hitting times on the double cover
conclusions: The hitting-time system has a unique solution
$\tilde h_{(y,1-j)}(x,1-i)=\tilde h_{(y,j)}(x,i)$
A plain step away from $y$ lowers $h_y$ by $2$ in expectation
nodes.statement: The hitting-time system has a unique solution, so the hitting times of $\tilde G$ satisfy $\tilde h_{(y,1-j)}(x,1-i)=\tilde h_{(y,j)}(x,i)$. A plain step away from $y$ lowers $h_y$ by $2$ in expectation, and a plain step of $\tilde G$ from $(x,i)$ is a plain step of $G$ from $x$ followed by a flip of the layer.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover
nodes.label: lem:hitting-flip

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Layer swap maps solutions to solutions; uniqueness by maximum principle.
nodes.statement: Swapping the layers maps solutions to solutions; the maximum principle gives uniqueness. The first-step equation is the row $x$ of the Laplacian system.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Additive drift for two tokens
assumptions: If a nonnegative potential $F$ drops by at least $c$ in expectation under one step of the two-token walk from every pair of distinct vertices
conclusions: $cT\cdot\Pr[\text{apart after }T\text{ steps}]\le F$
nodes.statement: If a nonnegative potential $F$ drops by at least $c$ in expectation under one step of the two-token walk from every pair of distinct vertices, then $cT\cdot\Pr[\text{apart after }T\text{ steps}]\le F$.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover
nodes.label: lem:additive-drift

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Truncate $F$ on the diagonal and induct on $T$, using that being apart is antitone.
nodes.statement: Truncate $F$ to $0$ on the diagonal, show $\mathbb E[F'_T]+c\sum_{t<T}\Pr[\text{apart at }t]\le F'$ by induction on $T$, and use that being apart is antitone in $t$.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Exact drift of the potential
assumptions: Let $\Phi$ be the Coppersmith--Tetali--Winkler potential of $\tilde G$
conclusions: Every hitting time of $\tilde G$ is at most $16n^3$, $0\le\Psi\le 32n^3$
for $x\neq y$ one synchronous plain step of the two tokens lowers $\Psi$ by exactly $4$ in expectation
nodes.statement_short: The Coppersmith--Tetali--Winkler potential on the double cover drops by exactly 4 per synchronous plain step.
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi$ be the Coppersmith--Tetali--Winkler potential of $\tilde G$ (as in Theorem~\ref{thm:meeting-lazy}) and $\Psi(x,y)=\Phi((x,0),(y,0))$. Every hitting time of $\tilde G$ is at most $16n^3$, $0\le\Psi\le 32n^3$, and for $x\neq y$ one synchronous plain step of the two tokens lowers $\Psi$ by exactly $4$ in expectation.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover
nodes.label: lem:plain-drift

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Commute bound on the double cover, then split a synchronous step into two token moves on $\tilde G$, each lowering the potential by 2.
nodes.statement: The bound is the commute bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting} on $\tilde G$ ($2n$ vertices, volume at most $2n^2$). A synchronous step at $(x,y)$ is, on $\tilde G$, a move of the first token from $(x,0)$ to layer $1$ followed by a move of the second token from $(y,0)$ to layer $1$. Between the two moves the tokens lie in different layers, hence are distinct, and each move lowers $\Phi$ by $2$. The layer symmetry of Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting-flip} returns both tokens to layer $0$.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Potential bound
nodes.statement: The bound is the commute bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting} on $\tilde G$ ($2n$ vertices, volume at most $2n^2$).
nodes.statement_short: Bound via the commute bound.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Split the step
nodes.statement: A synchronous step at $(x,y)$ is, on $\tilde G$, a move of the first token from $(x,0)$ to layer $1$ followed by a move of the second token from $(y,0)$ to layer $1$. Between the two moves the tokens lie in different layers, hence are distinct, and each move lowers $\Phi$ by $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Each of two token moves lowers $\Phi$ by 2.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Layer symmetry
nodes.statement: The layer symmetry of Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting-flip} returns both tokens to layer $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Layer symmetry returns to layer 0.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover

nodes.name: Meeting time of plain walks; Lemma 2.4
assumptions: On a connected nonbipartite graph with $n$ vertices
conclusions: two synchronous plain walks are apart after $T$ steps with probability at most $8n^3/T$
after $16n^3$ steps with probability at most $1/2$, and after $16kn^3$ steps with probability at most $2^{-k}$
nodes.statement: On a connected nonbipartite graph with $n$ vertices, two synchronous plain walks are apart after $T$ steps with probability at most $8n^3/T$; hence after $16n^3$ steps with probability at most $1/2$, and after $16kn^3$ steps with probability at most $2^{-k}$, from every pair of start vertices.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover
nodes.label: thm:meeting-plain

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Additive drift with $c=4$ and the exact potential drift, then submultiplicativity.
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:additive-drift} with $c=4$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:plain-drift} give $4T\cdot\Pr[\text{apart}]\le 32n^3$; then submultiplicativity in blocks.

nodes.name: Hassin--Peleg Theorem 2.5, plain walk
assumptions: On every connected nonbipartite graph with $n$ vertices and from every initial colouring
conclusions: the plain voter dynamics fails to reach consensus after $16kn^3$ rounds with probability at most $(n-1)2^{-k}$
reaches consensus within $80\,n^3\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1-1/n$
nodes.statement: On every connected nonbipartite graph with $n$ vertices and from every initial colouring, the plain voter dynamics fails to reach consensus after $16kn^3$ rounds with probability at most $(n-1)2^{-k}$, and reaches consensus within $80\,n^3\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1-1/n$.
nodes.section: 92 Section 2.4 for the plain walk: the bipartite double cover
nodes.label: thm:hp25-plain

nodes.statement_short: As for the lazy case, with the plain meeting-time bound.
nodes.statement: As for Theorem~\ref{thm:hp25}, with $k=\lfloor T/(16n^3)\rfloor$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:meeting-plain}.

nodes.name: Process of BGKM16
nodes.statement: The process is the lazy voter $(I+D^{-1}A)/2$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy}.

nodes.name: Corrections to BGKM16 Lemmas 2.1 and 2.4
nodes.statement: Lemma~2.1 of BGKM16 needs a minor correction (its sum should run over the minority side, which is what its proof gives), and so do the statement of Lemma~2.4 (it prints $1/n^2$ for $1-1/n^2$) and the sign of an exponent in its proof; the corrected versions are formalized (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/voter/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#51-lemma-21-of-bgkm16-needs-a-minor-correction}{details on Lemma~2.1}, \href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/voter/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#5-consensus-time-via-conductance-berenbrinkgiakkoupiskermarrecmallmann-trenn}{details on Lemma~2.4} in Section~5.5 there).
nodes.statement_short: BGKM16 Lemma 2.1 (sum over minority side) and Lemma 2.4 (statement and an exponent sign) need minor corrections.

nodes.name: Volume, conductance, minority side, potential
nodes.statement_short: Volume, conductance, disagreeing-neighbour counts, the minority side $s_t$ and potential $\Psi=\sqrt{\mathrm{vol}(s_t)}$.
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{vol}(S)=\sum_{u\in S}d_u$; the conductance $\varphi(G)$ is the minimum of $|\mathrm{cut}(U,V\setminus U)|/\mathrm{vol}(U)$ over $0<\mathrm{vol}(U)\le m$; $\lambda_u$ is the number of neighbours of $u$ with another opinion; for two opinions $s_t$ is the side of smaller volume and $\Psi=\sqrt{\mathrm{vol}(s_t)}$.
nodes.label: def:conductance

nodes.name: Independent coordinates
nodes.origin_citation: Berenbrink, Giakkoupis, Kermarrec, Mallmann-Trenn (ICALP 2016), Lemma A.1
conclusions: Resampling one coordinate of an independent point does not change its law
centred coordinate functions have additive second and third moments
the replacement of all of them improves $\mathbb{E}f(c+\sum_i g_i(x_i))$
nodes.statement: Resampling one coordinate of an independent point does not change its law. Consequently centred coordinate functions have additive second and third moments, and if replacing each coordinate function improves $\mathbb{E}f(z+\cdot)$ for all admissible $z$, then the replacement of all of them improves $\mathbb{E}f(c+\sum_i g_i(x_i))$ (BGKM16 Lemma~A.1).
nodes.label: lem:indep

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Reindex pairs by swapping one coordinate; induct over replaced coordinates.
nodes.statement: Reindex the pairs $(x,a)$ by $(x[i\mapsto a],x_i)$; induct over the set of replaced coordinates.

nodes.name: BGKM16 Lemma 2.1, corrected
conclusions: $\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{t+1}\mid s_t]\le\Psi-\sum_{u\in s_t}\lambda_u d_u/(32\Psi^3) \le\Psi-d_{\min}\varphi/(32\Psi)$
nodes.statement_short: The square-root-volume potential of the minority side has negative drift proportional to conductance.
nodes.statement: If $s_t\neq\emptyset$, then $\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{t+1}\mid s_t]\le\Psi-\sum_{u\in s_t}\lambda_u d_u/(32\Psi^3) \le\Psi-d_{\min}\varphi/(32\Psi)$. The paper prints the sum over all of $V$; this needs a minor correction (the inequality does not hold on the star $K_{1,15}$), and its proof gives the sum over $s_t$ (\href{https://github.com/formal-dynamics/leanamics/blob/main/voter/FORMALIZATION_DIFFERENCES.md#51-lemma-21-of-bgkm16-needs-a-minor-correction}{details}).
nodes.label: lem:bgkm-21

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\Psi_{t+1}$ by a square root, replace moves via concavity, third-order expansion with moment bounds, and conductance.
nodes.statement: $\Psi_{t+1}$ is at most the root of the new volume $P+\sum_u X_u$ of the opinion of $s_t$. Replace $X_u$ for $u\notin s_t$ by $Y_u=\lambda_u\mathbf{1}[\text{move}]$ (concavity of $\sqrt{\cdot}$), expand $\sqrt{P+x}$ to third order, and use $\mathbb{E}\Delta'=0$, $\mathbb{E}\Delta'^2\ge\sum_{s_t}\lambda_ud_u/4$, $\mathbb{E}\Delta'^3\le0$. The conductance gives $\sum_{s_t}\lambda_ud_u\ge d_{\min}\varphi\,\mathrm{vol}(s_t)$.

nodes.name: Square-root bound
nodes.statement: $\Psi_{t+1}$ is at most the root of the new volume $P+\sum_u X_u$ of the opinion of $s_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\Psi_{t+1}$ by a square root of the new volume.

nodes.name: Third-order expansion
nodes.statement: Replace $X_u$ for $u\notin s_t$ by $Y_u=\lambda_u\mathbf{1}[\text{move}]$ (concavity of $\sqrt{\cdot}$), expand $\sqrt{P+x}$ to third order, and use $\mathbb{E}\Delta'=0$, $\mathbb{E}\Delta'^2\ge\sum_{s_t}\lambda_ud_u/4$, $\mathbb{E}\Delta'^3\le0$.
nodes.statement_short: Concavity and moment bounds give the drift.

nodes.name: Conductance
nodes.statement: The conductance gives $\sum_{s_t}\lambda_ud_u\ge d_{\min}\varphi\,\mathrm{vol}(s_t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conductance converts to the second form.

nodes.name: BGKM16 Lemma 2.2 and Theorem 1.1 (i), two opinions
nodes.origin_citation: Berenbrink, Giakkoupis, Kermarrec, Mallmann-Trenn (ICALP 2016), Lemma 2.2, Thm 1.1(i)
assumptions: On dynamic graphs with fixed degrees
conclusions: the opinions still disagree at time $T$ with probability at most $1/2$

the expected
consensus time is at most twice that
the same holds once $128\,\mathrm{vol}(s_0)\le d_{\min}\sum_{t<T}\varphi_t$
the opinions still disagree at time $T$ with probability at most $1/2$

assumptions: On dynamic graphs with fixed degrees
conclusions: the same holds once $128\,\mathrm{vol}(s_0)\le d_{\min}\sum_{t<T}\varphi_t$

nodes.statement: If $128\,\mathrm{vol}(s_0)\le d_{\min}\varphi T$, the opinions still disagree at time $T$ with probability at most $1/2$; in particular after $128m/(d_{\min}\varphi)$ rounds, and the expected consensus time is at most twice that. On dynamic graphs with fixed degrees the same holds once $128\,\mathrm{vol}(s_0)\le d_{\min}\sum_{t<T}\varphi_t$.
nodes.label: thm:bgkm-two

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Additive drift lemma with drift $d_{\min}\varphi_t/32$; restarting bounds the expectation.
nodes.statement: The drift lemma of the shared library (FND-5) with drift $d_{\min}\varphi_t/32$; restarting bounds the expected time.

nodes.name: BGKM16 Theorem 1.1 (i), any number of opinions
conclusions: the expected consensus time is at most $b\,m/(d_{\min}\varphi)$ and consensus holds within $b\,m/(d_{\min}\varphi)$ rounds with probability at least $1/2$
nodes.statement: There is a constant $b$ such that the expected consensus time is at most $b\,m/(d_{\min}\varphi)$ and consensus holds within $b\,m/(d_{\min}\varphi)$ rounds with probability at least $1/2$, for every number of opinions.
nodes.label: thm:bgkm-many

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Project to two-opinion processes and reduce the number of opinions geometrically.
nodes.statement: Project each opinion to the two-opinion process ``$i$ against the rest''. From $\ell\le\theta$ opinions, after $384\,\mathrm{vol}(V)/(\theta d_{\min}\varphi)$ rounds at most $5\theta/6$ remain with probability at least $1/3$ (BGKM16 Lemma~2.3). Summing over the levels $\theta_j=n(5/6)^j$ gives a geometric series; Markov's inequality gives the probability form.

nodes.name: Projection
nodes.statement: Project each opinion to the two-opinion process ``$i$ against the rest''.
nodes.statement_short: Two-opinion projections.

nodes.name: Opinion reduction
nodes.statement: From $\ell\le\theta$ opinions, after $384\,\mathrm{vol}(V)/(\theta d_{\min}\varphi)$ rounds at most $5\theta/6$ remain with probability at least $1/3$ (BGKM16 Lemma~2.3).
nodes.statement_short: Opinions drop by factor 5/6 per level with constant probability.

nodes.name: Geometric sum
nodes.statement: Summing over the levels $\theta_j=n(5/6)^j$ gives a geometric series; Markov's inequality gives the probability form.
nodes.statement_short: Geometric series and Markov.

nodes.name: Multiplicative drift of the potential
assumptions: On a graph with $n$ vertices and conductance $\varphi$, from every two-opinion configuration
conclusions: $\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{t+1}\mid s_t]\le(1-\varphi^2/(32n))\,\Psi(s_t)$
$1\le\Psi\le n$ before consensus
nodes.statement: On a graph with $n$ vertices and conductance $\varphi$, from every two-opinion configuration, $\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{t+1}\mid s_t]\le(1-\varphi^2/(32n))\,\Psi(s_t)$. Moreover $1\le\Psi\le n$ before consensus.
nodes.label: lem:bgkm-mul

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy--Schwarz turns the additive drift into a multiplicative one.
nodes.statement: $\lambda_ud_u\ge\lambda_u^2$ and Cauchy--Schwarz over the at most $n$ vertices of $s_t$ give $\sum_{s_t}\lambda_ud_u\ge(\sum_{s_t}\lambda_u)^2/n\ge\varphi^2\Psi^4/n$; insert this into Lemma~\ref{lem:bgkm-21}. Volumes are integers and $\mathrm{vol}(s_t)\le m\le n^2$.

nodes.name: BGKM16 Lemma 2.4 and Theorem 1.1 (ii)
nodes.origin_citation: Berenbrink, Giakkoupis, Kermarrec, Mallmann-Trenn (ICALP 2016), Lemma 2.4 (corrected), Thm 1.1(ii)
conclusions: the opinions still disagree at time $T$ with probability at most $1/n^2$ for two opinions and at most $1/n$ for any number of opinions

On a static
graph the expected consensus time is at most $2T$.
nodes.statement: If $96\,n\ln n\le\sum_{t<T}\varphi_t^2$ (static graph: $96\,n\ln n\le\varphi^2T$), the opinions still disagree at time $T$ with probability at most $1/n^2$ for two opinions and at most $1/n$ for any number of opinions, on static graphs and on dynamic graphs with fixed degrees. On a static graph the expected consensus time is at most $2T$.
nodes.label: thm:bgkm-sq

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicative drift gives an $n^{-2}$ tail; union bound over opinion projections; restart for expectations.
nodes.statement: The multiplicative drift lemma of the shared library (FND-5) gives $\Pr(\Psi_T>0)\le\Psi(s_0)\prod_{t<T}(1-\varphi_t^2/(32n))\le n\cdot e^{-3\ln n}$. For many opinions apply this to each projection ``$i$ against the rest'' (the projection commutes with a round, whatever graph the adversary chooses) and take a union bound over the at most $n$ opinions present initially; restarting bounds the expected time.

nodes.name: BGKM16 Theorem 1.1
conclusions: The consensus time is at most $\min\{\tau,\tau'\}$ with probability at least $1/2$
nodes.statement_short: Voter consensus time is at most the minimum of the conductance and squared-conductance bounds, with probability 1/2.
nodes.statement: The consensus time is at most $\min\{\tau,\tau'\}$ with probability at least $1/2$: on a static graph for every number of opinions, with $\tau=b\,m/(d_{\min}\varphi)$ and $\tau'=b\,n\ln n/\varphi^2$ for a constant $b$; on a dynamic graph with fixed degrees for two opinions, with $\tau$ the first time with $d_{\min}\sum_{t<\tau}\varphi_t\ge128\,\mathrm{vol}(s_0)$ and $\tau'$ the first time with $\sum_{t<\tau'}\varphi_t^2\ge96\,n\ln n$.
nodes.label: thm:bgkm-min

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two-opinion, many-opinion and squared-conductance theorems.
nodes.statement: Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:bgkm-two}, \ref{thm:bgkm-many} and \ref{thm:bgkm-sq}, using $1/n\le1/2$ for $n\ge2$; with one vertex there is nothing to agree on.

nodes.name: Triangle and a nonuniform matrix
nodes.statement: One white vertex on a triangle wins with probability $1/3$. The stochastic matrix whose two rows are $(1/3,2/3)$ has stationary weights $(1/3,2/3)$, providing a nonuniform invariant example.
nodes.label: lem:examples

nodes.name: Wright--Fisher sampling on three individuals
nodes.statement: On three individuals, let every offspring pick a uniform parent, itself included. This kernel has self-loops, so it is supported beyond the edges of the triangle. Theorem~2.1 still applies, and one allele copy fixes with probability $1/3$.
nodes.label: lem:wf

nodes.name: Bipartite two-cycle
nodes.statement: On the two-vertex graph, every vertex must copy the other vertex. The alternating coloring flips each round and returns after two rounds; neither coloring is constant. Thus connectedness alone is insufficient.
nodes.label: lem:cycle
